title: Workload and Power Simulator

body:
The simulated cluster runs the real Joulie components on emulated bare-metal nodes, on one machine with Docker. The agent discovers and caps emulated hardware through the same files and tools it uses on a real node, the controller manager reads node power from the simulator’s OpenTelemetry metrics in Prometheus, and the scheduler extender scores real pods. The scripts in scripts/simcluster drive it, tests/simcluster checks it end to end, and CI runs it on every pull request that touches what it builds.
Use it to see a change to the agent, the controller manager, the extender, the chart or the simulator work across components. A change to discovery or capping alone is checked faster by the hwemu tests in cmd/agent (go test ./cmd/agent/ -run Hwemu).
Architecture host: Docker container $SIMCLUSTER_NAME (--privileged): one k3s server Node <name>-infra: the only real kubelet (joulie.io/infra=true, joulie.io/hwemu-host=true) monitoring Prometheus with its OTLP receiver; the Collector in mode otel-collector joulie-sim the simulator in emulate mode, writing /var/lib/joulie-hwemu/<node>/ joulie-system the controller manager; the scheduler extender on the host network joulie-system joulie-agent-emu-<i>: one agent per eligible fake Node, mounting its tree KWOK keeps the fake Nodes Ready fake Nodes rendered from the cluster spec One k3s server in Docker. The container $SIMCLUSTER_NAME (default joulie-sim) runs the k3s image pinned in scripts/simcluster/versions.env. Its own kubelet is the only real Node, <name>-infra, and runs every pod that really runs. The k3s state and the hwemu trees live in the named volumes <name>-k3s and <name>-hwemu, so they outlive a restart of the container: the trees, the limits agents wrote and the energy ledgers that keep exported counters from going back. The trees need no tmpfs: 200 emulated nodes take about 0.2 s per tick on the volume (Tick cost). Fake Nodes. clusterspec render-nodes turns the cluster spec into Node objects with the labels, taints, capacity and architecture of their hardware profiles, and KWOK v0.8.0 keeps them Ready. Every fake Node carries sim.joulie.io/cluster=<spec> and sim.joulie.io/pool=<pool>. Emulated hardware. The simulator runs in emulate mode with the same spec: one tree per fake Node under /var/lib/joulie-hwemu on the infra Node, all stepped on one tick. Emulated agents. The agent binary is the one a release ships, unmodified. With agent.mode: emulated the chart renders one Deployment joulie-agent-emu-<i> per entry of agent.emulated.nodes, on the infra Node, mounting its Node’s tree where the agent reads /sys, /proc/cpuinfo and the GPU tools (Agent chart values). Which Nodes get one is decided as in a real install: simcluster agents renders the chart’s agent DaemonSet with the same values files as the install and keeps the Nodes it would reach. The node selector must match, every NoSchedule and NoExecute taint must be tolerated (counting the tolerations the DaemonSet controller adds), and the architecture must match the image. Every other Node is printed with its reason. Scheduler. The k3s scheduler calls the extender through scripts/simcluster/manifests/scheduler-config.yaml, the same file the Dagger integration job uses. The extender runs on the infra Node’s host network. Telemetry. The simulator pushes OTLP straight into Prometheus, and the controller manager reads node power and the facility from there with its default settings, or with the settings of the chosen telemetry mode. Access. Every cluster HTTP call goes through the API server’s service proxy. The only published port is the API server’s, on 127.0.0.1, at a port Docker picks. The kubeconfig is $SIMCLUSTER_DIR/kubeconfig; ~/.kube is never read or written. Images. One go build (linux/amd64, CGO off) builds the agent, controller manager, extender, simulator and fakesmi from the working tree. Each binary is wrapped in the distroless image its release uses, tagged joulie.local/joulie-<component>:dev-<first 12 hex of the binary's sha256> (for the simulator image, which also carries fakesmi, a hash of both binaries) and imported into the cluster’s containerd. Pods pull with IfNotPresent, and the deploy checks each pod’s image ID against images.env. Requirements Host. amd64 Linux with Docker allowed to run a --privileged container: k3s runs its kubelet and containerd inside it. The images are built for linux/amd64 only. Tools. docker, kubectl, helm, jq, sha256sum and Go. The scripts build with the toolchain go.mod names (they set GOTOOLCHAIN), so the images match what CI builds. CI installs the Helm release that HELM_VERSION in versions.env pins. k3s 1.34 on a cgroup v1 host. stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup prints tmpfs on cgroup v1. k3s 1.35 and later refuse cgroup v1 unless the kubelet runs with fail-cgroupv1=false; up.sh adds that flag on such a host for such a k3s, but only the pinned 1.34 is tested there. fs.inotify.max_user_instances. Every pod of the cluster runs on the one infra kubelet, so all their containers and file watches share the host’s per-user inotify limit with the host’s own programs. 128 is a common default. The smoke spec fits in it, but a scale run with many emulated agents may exhaust it. The scripts never change host settings: check it with sysctl fs.inotify.max_user_instances and raise it by hand before a large run. Pod capacity. Every emulated agent is a pod on the infra Node. up.sh sizes its kubelet for the agents plus 50, at least 110 pods: up to 250 pods with the default /24 per Node, up to 1000 with a /22 per Node and the cluster CIDR 10.64.0.0/12. Beyond 1000 it fails with “split across k3s agents”. A running container created for fewer pods is never resized: up.sh asks for a recreate. Network on the first run. The k3s system images, KWOK, Prometheus, the Collector and the distroless base are pulled once; third-party images are pulled by the digest versions.env pins. With SIMCLUSTER_AIRGAP=1 the k3s system images come from the release’s air-gap bundle, kept in $SIMCLUSTER_DIR/images for later runs. Quick start make simcluster-smoke SIMCLUSTER_KEEP=1 D=~/.cache/joulie/simcluster/joulie-sim-smoke jq '{status: ."test.suite.run.status", failures, knownDefects}' $D/runs/latest/summary.json export KUBECONFIG=$D/kubeconfig kubectl get nodes -L sim.joulie.io/pool kubectl get nodetwins -o custom-columns=NODE:.spec.nodeName,SRC:.status.powerMeasurement.source,W:.status.powerMeasurement.measuredNodePowerW make simcluster-down SIMCLUSTER_NAME=joulie-sim-smoke make simcluster-smoke creates the cluster joulie-sim-smoke from tests/simcluster/specs/smoke.yaml, deploys with tests/simcluster/smoke-values.yaml, runs TestSimclusterE2E, collects the results and deletes the cluster unless SIMCLUSTER_KEEP=1. The smoke spec has eight Nodes: an Intel Xeon with RAPL, an AMD EPYC with energy counters only, an AMD EPYC with HSMP, an H100 NVL node, an H100 SXM node with persistence mode off, an MI300X node, a virtual machine, and a managed Intel node whose taint the agent does not tolerate. The smoke values put every node in performance with CPU and GPU caps at 80 %; the test lowers them to 50 % halfway.
To keep a cluster and work on it step by step:
make simcluster-up # k3s, KWOK, Prometheus, the fake Nodes make simcluster-deploy # images, simulator, Joulie; waits until every component reports make simcluster-status Targets Each target runs one script of scripts/simcluster and nothing else, so make -n shows what will run. The scripts also run directly, and each starts with its usage.
Target Script What it does simcluster-up up.sh Creates the k3s container, or reuses an existing one, starting it when stopped, if it was created for at least as many pods and as large pod CIDRs, with the same scheduler configuration and k3s image; otherwise it says to recreate. Installs KWOK, Prometheus and, in mode otel-collector, the Collector. Applies the spec’s Nodes and deletes the fake Nodes the spec no longer names. simcluster-images images.sh Builds and imports the Joulie images, and the pinned third-party ones, and writes images.env. An unchanged binary keeps its tag and is not imported again. simcluster-deploy deploy.sh Images, CRDs, the simulator, the agent placement, Joulie. Waits for the rollouts, one NodeHardware per emulated agent, the series of every measured Node and a NodeTwin per managed Node, then checks every pod’s image. -f <values> adds a Joulie values file when run directly. simcluster-reload C=<component> reload.sh Rebuilds and rolls out agent, controller-manager, scheduler, simulator or all; see the dev loop. simcluster-status status.sh Prints every Node with its pool, profile and NodeTwin power. Exits 1 when a Node is NotReady, a pod without joulie.io/workload-class is bound to a fake Node, a pod runs another image than images.env names, an emulated agent’s Node has no NodeHardware, or a measured Node has no series. simcluster-tree [NODE=<node>] tree.sh Without a Node, lists the Nodes that have a tree; with one, prints every file of its tree with its first line: the energy counters, limits, frequencies and GPU state its agent sees. simcluster-logs C=<component> [NODE=<node>] logs.sh The last 200 lines of agent (one Node’s, or every agent’s), controller-manager, scheduler, simulator, prometheus, otelcol, kwok or k3s. Run directly, it passes further flags such as -f to kubectl logs. simcluster-smoke smoke.sh See Quick start. simcluster-down down.sh Removes the container with its anonymous volumes and the named volumes <name>-k3s and <name>-hwemu. Keeps images/, runs/ and bin/ of the state directory. Settings The scripts read these variables from the environment; make passes on the ones that are set.
Variable Default Effect SIMCLUSTER_NAME joulie-sim; joulie-sim-smoke for the smoke run Container name and prefix of its volumes. It must match ^joulie-sim(-[a-z0-9]+)*$: the scripts touch no container or volume named otherwise. SIMCLUSTER_DIR ${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/joulie/simcluster/<name> State directory, outside the repository (below). SIMCLUSTER_SPEC tests/simcluster/specs/smoke.yaml The cluster spec. tests/simcluster/specs/medium.yaml has 50 Nodes, 46 of them reached by the agent, with GPU sharing, AMD GPUs with a pinned power cap, Nodes without NFD labels or GPU driver tools, and an unmanaged pool. SIMCLUSTER_NODES (empty) Instead of a spec, this many Nodes of one profile, for scale runs. SIMCLUSTER_SCALE_PROFILE intel-xeon-2s-rapl The profile of SIMCLUSTER_NODES. SIMCLUSTER_TELEMETRY otel The telemetry mode. SIMCLUSTER_POWER_SCOPE components The node power scope Joulie reads: components (CPU packages and GPUs) or host (hw.host.*, otel modes only). SIMCLUSTER_TIMING dev The timing profile, a file scripts/simcluster/timing/<name>.env. SIMCLUSTER_PROFILES_DIR (empty) Local hardware profiles, read by the host tools only. The simulator in the cluster reads its builtin profiles, so up.sh refuses a spec that needs a local one. SIMCLUSTER_EXTRA_VALUES (empty) Joulie values files, space separated, installed after the generated ones. They also decide which Nodes get an emulated agent. SIMCLUSTER_KEEP 0 1 keeps the smoke cluster after the run. SIMCLUSTER_AIRGAP 0 1 loads the k3s system images from the release’s air-gap bundle. SIMCLUSTER_FORCE_RELOAD 0 1 makes every reload a reload.sh --force. COMPONENT (or C), NODE (empty) The component and the Node of simcluster-reload, simcluster-logs and simcluster-tree. The state directory holds kubeconfig; cluster.env (how the container was created); telemetry.env, spec.yaml, images.env, deploy.env and crds.sha (what is installed); values/ and render/ (generated values files, renders and configurations); bin/ (the binaries, with the host tools in bin/host); images/ (image tarballs); and runs/ (the run results).
Telemetry modes A mode sets how the emulated Nodes’ power reaches Prometheus and which Joulie input settings read it. Every mode is checked against the emulator’s truth, read from the simulator’s /debug/emulate.
SIMCLUSTER_TELEMETRY Path to Prometheus Joulie settings beyond the defaults Checked against otel (default) the simulator pushes OTLP; Prometheus promotes k8s.node.name and host.name none CPU packages plus GPUs otel-unpromoted as otel, without promotion none: auto falls back to joining target_info CPU packages plus GPUs otel-labels-unpromoted as otel-unpromoted PROMETHEUS_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=labels no data, with the promotion hint in the log otel-utf8 as otel, names translated with NoUTF8EscapingWithSuffixes PROMETHEUS_NAME_TRANSLATION=NoUTF8EscapingWithSuffixes CPU packages plus GPUs otel-collector the simulator pushes to an OpenTelemetry Collector, whose prometheus exporter Prometheus scrapes with honor_labels: true none CPU packages plus GPUs kepler the simulator also serves Kepler 0.12 series NODE_POWER_PRESET=kepler CPU packages plus NVIDIA GPUs kepler-legacy the simulator also serves Kepler 0.7 series, scraped with honor_labels: false NODE_POWER_PRESET=kepler-legacy CPU packages plus NVIDIA GPUs With SIMCLUSTER_POWER_SCOPE=host, an otel mode also sets NODE_POWER_SCOPE=host and is checked against whole-host power. Each check passes within 3 % of the truth, and never needs to be closer than 1 W. simcluster telemetry prints what a mode generates, for example go run ./simulator/cmd/simcluster telemetry --part prom-config --mode otel-utf8; the parts are prom-config, otelcol-config, sim-values, joulie-values, checks and wait.
Timing Timing names map onto the real settings, so a nightly run in production timing exercises the values a real install uses.
Timing setting dev production Becomes CONTROLLER_RECONCILE_INTERVAL 10s 1m controller manager RECONCILE_INTERVAL AGENT_RECONCILE_INTERVAL 5s 20s agent RECONCILE_INTERVAL AGENT_SPEC_READ_TIMEOUT 60s 5m agent SPEC_READ_TIMEOUT PROM_SCRAPE_INTERVAL 5s 1m Prometheus scrape_interval OTLP_EXPORT_INTERVAL_MS 5000 60000 simulator otel.exportIntervalMillis RATE_WINDOW 30s 5m controller manager PROMETHEUS_RATE_WINDOW FACILITY_POLL_INTERVAL 10s 30s controller manager FACILITY_POLL_INTERVAL A rate window shorter than four export intervals reads too few samples.
What a real Prometheus needs The harness configures its Prometheus the way a production one must be configured for Joulie’s OpenTelemetry inputs:
global: {scrape_interval: 5s} # 1m in production timing storage: {tsdb: {out_of_order_time_window: 30m}} otlp: promote_resource_attributes: [k8s.node.name, host.name] translation_strategy: UnderscoreEscapingWithSuffixes Prometheus runs with --web.enable-otlp-receiver, which serves /api/v1/otlp/v1/metrics. On a real cluster:
Without the receiver flag (enableOTLPReceiver with the Prometheus Operator), Prometheus has no OTLP endpoint to push to. Prometheus promotes no resource attribute by default. Without the promotion, Joulie’s auto mode joins target_info for the node name (mode otel-unpromoted); a join must group target_info with max by (job, instance, <id>), or a restarted producer’s second target_info series fails it. otlp.translation_strategy must match Joulie’s PROMETHEUS_NAME_TRANSLATION, or no series is selected (mode otel-utf8). OTLP samples carry the producer’s timestamps, hence the out-of-order window. rate() under-reads a series younger than its window: after a producer starts, wait one window before trusting the reading. A scraped Kepler 0.7 keeps its own instance label only as exported_instance (honor_labels: false); a Collector’s prometheus exporter is scraped with honor_labels: true. The kube-prometheus-stack values (values/prometheus-grafana.yaml) and the full list are under Prometheus settings and Pitfalls.
The dev loop make simcluster-up && make simcluster-deploy # once # edit the agent make simcluster-reload C=agent # rebuild, import, roll out; prints the seconds make simcluster-logs C=agent NODE=intel-0 make simcluster-tree NODE=intel-0 make simcluster-status A reload follows the binary, not the sources. The image tag is the binary’s sha256, so reload.sh imports and upgrades only when the binary changed; an unchanged binary changes nothing, with no import, no upgrade and no restart. Touching a source file is therefore a no-op. To restart a component anyway, use reload.sh <component> --force (through make, SIMCLUSTER_FORCE_RELOAD=1), which sets the pod template annotation sim.joulie.io/reload to the current time. A reload rolls out one component. The others keep their images and pods even when shared code changed their binaries too; reload them, or all. A reload re-reads the charts and values files, reruns the release’s helm upgrade with only the component’s tag changed, and re-applies the CRDs when they changed. The values files are those of the last deploy, as deploy.env records them, a scenario’s simulator.set (SIMCLUSTER_SIM_EXTRA_VALUES) included. Another spec or mode. up.sh with another SIMCLUSTER_SPEC applies its Nodes and deletes the ones it no longer names; deploy.sh sets Prometheus up again when the mode or the timing changed. Reading Prometheus and the truth, through the API server proxy: export KUBECONFIG=~/.cache/joulie/simcluster/joulie-sim/kubeconfig P=/api/v1/namespaces/monitoring/services/prometheus-operated:9090/proxy/api/v1/query pq() { kubectl get --raw "$P?query=$(jq -rn --arg q "$1" '$q|@uri')" | jq -c '[.data.result[] | [.metric.k8s_node_name, .value[1]]]'; } pq 'sum by (k8s_node_name) (rate(hw_host_energy_joules_total[30s]))' kubectl get --raw /api/v1/namespaces/joulie-sim/services/joulie-telemetry-sim:80/proxy/debug/emulate | jq '[.nodes[] | {name, hostW: .host.powerW}]' Deviations from a real cluster KWOK taint. Every fake Node carries the KWOK annotation and the taint kwok.x-k8s.io/node=fake:NoSchedule, which keeps infrastructure pods off it. A pod meant for a fake Node must tolerate it. Placement ignores this taint, since a real Node does not have it. The sim.joulie.io/cluster selector. The infra Node runs a real kubelet, so a workload pod could land there. The simulator’s workload pods select sim.joulie.io/cluster=<spec> by default, and nothing without joulie.io/workload-class may be bound to a fake Node (E02, status.sh). Agents are Deployments, unprivileged. On a real node the agent is a DaemonSet pod with host network and privileges. An emulated agent is a Deployment on the infra Node with privileged: false and no host network, and its NODE_NAME is a literal. A privileged pod would see the infra host’s real devices on every fake Node, and only one host-network agent fits on a Node. /dev/nvidiactl is a file. On NVIDIA Nodes the tree has an empty regular file mounted at /dev/nvidiactl, where a privileged agent on a real node sees the driver’s character device. The agent only checks that it exists. Tool stubs. nvidia-smi, rocm-smi and amd-smi are links to fakesmi, first on the agent’s PATH. fakesmi checks what the real tool needs before it runs (the ELF loader, the NVML library, a script’s interpreter; see Simulator hardware emulation). Under toolDelivery: mounted, the default, the harness mounts one stub file at the first path of each requirement, standing in for a node where the chart’s hooks deliver the driver; the stub is never run. A pool listed with toolDelivery: none under spec.harness.pools gets nothing, so its tools fail as on a node without driver tools (MD03). Only a profile whose tools list requirements can fail this way: a tool without requirements always runs. Locked limits fail with EISDIR. A limit the firmware locks, or a disabled one, is a directory in place of the attribute, so a write fails with EISDIR instead of the kernel’s error for that attribute. This stays until the emulation mounts such limits read-only. Fake Nodes have no kubelet. KWOK moves a pod bound to a fake Node through its phases (its stages, plus scripts/simcluster/manifests/stage-*.yaml); no container runs, and the Node’s power is the simulator’s model of its load. Known defects A defect the run reproduces today, and that waits for a fix or a decision, is registered in tests/simcluster/known_defects_test.go. Its check asserts the defect’s observation, so the run stays green while the defect lasts, and summary.json lists it under knownDefects. The day it no longer reproduces, the run fails with “remove it from tests/simcluster/known_defects_test.go”: the fix has landed, and the check must assert the fixed behaviour instead.
ID Check Observation Changes with D1 E11 The MI300X agent’s GPU inventory fails: no rocm-smi release has --showpowercap, so the GPU status is none/error with “unrecognized arguments: –showpowercap”. the agent reading the MI300X cap without that flag D15 E12 A managed Node the agent DaemonSet does not reach (here an untolerated taint) gets a NodeTwin with a cap, but no NodeHardware and no controlStatus, and its hardware keeps the uncapped limit: the cap is planned, never enforced. The chart now tolerates the GPU vendor taints by default (agent.tolerations), so GPU Nodes are reached. tolerating every taint, or the controller manager planning only Nodes that run an agent D18 MD01 (medium) MIG-mixed and renamed time-slicing GPU Nodes get no GPU intent (none/none/“no GPU cap intent”) and a CPU percent cap, as if they had no GPU: the controller manager counts only */gpu resources (discoverGPUCount), not nvidia.com/mig-* or nvidia.com/gpu.shared. the controller manager counting those resources D17 is fixed: a scheduler extender on the host network could not roll out on a single Node, because a rolling update starts the new pod before it stops the old one and both need the host port. The chart now deploys it with strategy Recreate when schedulerExtender.hostNetwork is true (case C07 of scripts/verify-chart-renders.sh; E14 rolls it out). Recreate leaves a moment with no extender, which is safe here because the scheduler configuration marks it ignorable: true; for a configuration that does not, see Scheduler extender.
End-to-end checks TestSimclusterE2E (tests/simcluster, build tag simcluster) runs against the deployed cluster. smoke.sh runs it with SIMCLUSTER_DIR and SIMCLUSTER_RUN_DIR set; without SIMCLUSTER_DIR it skips. It changes the cluster as it goes (the caps go to 50 %, the extender is reloaded), so it expects a fresh deploy. The caps go to 50 % only when E09.50pct or E10.50pct runs, so a -run filter that leaves both out keeps a cluster at its deployed caps.
ID Checks E01 every spec Node is Ready, with the labels, taints, capacity and architecture clusterspec renders E02 no pod without joulie.io/workload-class is bound to a fake Node E03 every container runs the image just built and imported E04 one emulated agent exists for exactly the Nodes the agent DaemonSet would reach E05 each NodeHardware equals the in-process golden of its profile (cmd/agent/testdata/hwemu) E06 Prometheus holds series for every Node with a measured CPU package E07 every check query of the mode equals the emulated truth (E07c: the Kepler 0.7 data shape) E08 each NodeTwin’s measured power is the truth, or prometheus-no-data where nothing measures E09, E10 lowering the CPU and GPU caps from 80 % to 50 % lowers the enforced limits and the NodeTwins’ measured power (RAPL, DVFS, NVIDIA) E11 the control status of each hardware family E12 D15, above E13 the extender filters and scores a real pod E14 a forced extender reload rolls out; an agent reload with an unchanged binary does nothing E15 status.sh exits 0 E16 the facility inputs reach the NodeTwin gauges and the cooling stress MD01 to MD04 medium spec only: D18; no NFD labels caps through DVFS; no driver tools leaves the GPUs alone; an unmanaged pool has series and nothing else GS01 governor control on only: each agent’s NodeHardware lists the governor presets its profile accepts, with the result each gives GS02 governor control on only: each NodeTwin asks for the preset its profile and node state (performance or eco) call for, and the agent’s result for it is the one its profile predicts GS03 governor control on only: the emulated files hold the native words of every applied or equivalent result GS04 governor control on only, and last: after one helm upgrade to GOVERNOR_CONTROL=off, every governor result is restored or gone, and every file (governor, EPP, boost, AMD level and overdrive table, NVIDIA locks) is back at the baseline NodeHardware recorded GS01 to GS04 skip unless the deployed controller manager runs with GOVERNOR_CONTROL not off. experiments/05-governor-exploration/scripts/run_tier_b.sh deploys tests/simcluster/specs/governor.yaml, one pool per CPU frequency driver and per GPU family, with governor control on, and runs them (see Governor exploration). GS04 changes the release, so the cluster needs a fresh deploy afterwards.
Run results Each smoke run writes $SIMCLUSTER_DIR/runs/<UTC>-<spec>-<mode>-<sha12>[-dirty]/, and runs/latest points at the newest. down.sh keeps them.
summary.json, schema joulie.simcluster.summary/v1: test.suite.name, test.suite.run.status (success, failure, timed_out or aborted), exitCode, failures, warnings, knownDefects, one entry per check under assertions (test.case.name, test.case.result.status, observed and expected), the spec, mode, scope and timing, the git commit and whether the tree was dirty, the images, and the semantic conventions schema URL. otlp/harness.metrics.jsonl and otlp/harness.logs.jsonl: one OTLP JSON object per line, with a joulie.scenario.assertion.evaluated log record and joulie.scenario.assertion.value points per check. k8s/ (the Nodes, NodeHardware, NodeTwins, pods and events at the end), logs/ (every pod in joulie-system, joulie-sim and monitoring, and k3s), values.effective.yaml and values.simulator.effective.yaml, images.env, deploy.env, cluster.env, and smoke.log, everything the run printed. The scenario runner writes the same layout and schema, so one reader serves both.
CI .github/workflows/simcluster.yml has two jobs; the Dagger integration job (integration-tests.yml) stays as it is.
smoke, on pull requests and pushes to main that touch cmd/, pkg/, api/, charts/, config/, simulator/, ci/, scripts/simcluster/, tests/simcluster/, values/simcluster*.yaml, the Makefile, go.mod, go.sum or the workflow, and on demand. It vets the test, runs the harness’s own tests (TestE2E*), then make simcluster-smoke, with a 30 minute timeout around the test’s 20. The air-gap bundle is cached by the hash of versions.env. nightly, daily at 03:23 UTC and on demand: the medium spec in production timing, and the smoke spec once for each of otel-unpromoted, otel-labels-unpromoted, otel-utf8, otel-collector, kepler, kepler-legacy, and otel with host scope. One failing variant does not cancel the others. Every job uploads its runs/ directory, also when it fails.

title: Simulated Cluster

body:
A workload scenario runs a workload through the simulated cluster and checks what happened: whether the jobs completed, where they were placed, how long they took, what energy they used, and how Joulie’s settings compare with each other or with no Joulie at all. The jobs are real Kubernetes Jobs, scheduled by the real scheduler and the Joulie extender onto KWOK Nodes, and the simulator’s v1 workload engine drives them on the emulated hardware, so a cap the agent writes slows the jobs on that Node.
A scenario is one file in tests/simcluster/scenarios/. scripts/simcluster/scenario.sh runs it and simscenario (simulator/cmd/simscenario) validates, plans and evaluates it.
Quick start make simcluster-scenario SCENARIO=tests/simcluster/scenarios/smoke.yaml jq '{status: ."test.suite.run.status", failures, jobs}' ~/.cache/joulie/simcluster/joulie-sim/runs/latest/summary.json make simcluster-down The first command creates the cluster (or reuses a running one), deploys the simulator and Joulie built from the working tree, runs the scenario’s jobs and evaluates them. It exits 0 when every assertion of severity fail passed, 1 when one failed, and 2 when the scenario is invalid or a variant could not be run. The cluster is kept, so a second scenario on the same spec starts in seconds; make simcluster-down deletes it.
To check a scenario without a cluster:
go run ./simulator/cmd/simscenario validate tests/simcluster/scenarios/nightly-mixed.yaml go build -o /tmp/bin/ ./simulator/cmd/workloadgen go run ./simulator/cmd/simscenario plan tests/simcluster/scenarios/nightly-mixed.yaml -out /tmp/plan -workloadgen /tmp/bin/workloadgen plan writes the trace and prints the offered load of each resource: the sum over the jobs due in the window of request times ideal runtime, over capacity times the window. It refuses a load above 0.9, which would queue jobs past any drain.
The library Scenario Cluster spec, timing Workload Checks smoke smoke, dev; about 7 minutes 9 inline jobs: CPU and GPU, both classes, NVIDIA and AMD every job completes through KWOK; no stall; no Job left incomplete and no stray pod on a fake Node; 9 joulie.sim.job.completed events; energy above 0 J perf-isolation policy, dev performance and standard CPU jobs, and one standard job pinned to the eco Node intel-2 no performance pod is bound to a Node that was eco for longer than the placement grace; standard jobs completed on an eco Node and intel-2 drew CPU energy, so the check is not vacuous cap-cost policy, dev CPU jobs that nearly fill an intel Node; GPU jobs with no CPU feed the median slowdown of CPU jobs on the eco Node exceeds that on performance Nodes by more than 5 %; the median slowdown of the GPU jobs stays within 2 % deadlock-visible smoke, dev one gang of 2 pods of 8 GPUs, both pinned to nvl-0, which has 8 the run reports joulie.sim.run.stalled and a gang_incomplete stall, and the gang never completes nightly-mixed nightly, production; 60 minutes of arrivals, 20 to drain workloadgen seed 7, offered load 0.5 to 0.8 of CPUs and both GPU kinds at least 95 % of the due jobs complete; no performance pod on eco; no run stall; the NodeTwins’ measured power within 15 % of the emulated energy rate at p95 (warning) weekly-compare nightly, production the nightly workload, three variants on fresh clusters: joulie-off, queue-aware, kepler-compat per variant as nightly; Joulie spends no more energy than joulie-off, and its performance jobs take at most 10 % longer at p95 (warnings) cap-cost sets GPU_ECO_CAP_PCT_OF_MAX=100. The controller never caps the CPU of a GPU Node, so with the eco GPU cap at 100 % nothing on a GPU Node is capped, and the GPU check measures what the eco profile costs a GPU job whose CPU feed intensity is 0: nothing. perf-isolation and cap-cost pin static_partition with STATIC_HP_FRAC=0.5, which on the policy spec puts intel-2, epyc-1 and nvl-1 in eco; TestEcoNodesTheScenariosNameAreEco checks that against policy.BuildStaticPlan.
The specs the library adds, in tests/simcluster/specs/, carry no baseLoad, so a Node idles until a run’s jobs load it:
policy.yaml: 3 intel-xeon-2s-rapl, 2 amd-epyc-2s-energy-only, 2 nvidia-h100-nvl-8gpu. Every family has more than one Node, so the policy keeps an eco Node in each. nightly.yaml: 16 intel-xeon-2s-rapl, 12 amd-epyc-2s-energy-only, 4 amd-epyc-2s-hsmp, 8 nvidia-h100-nvl-8gpu, 4 nvidia-h100-sxm-8gpu, 4 amd-instinct-mi300x-8gpu, 2 vm-no-powercap. The tests in simulator/pkg/scenario/scenarios_test.go check the library without a cluster: every scenario validates and plans under the load limit, every job fits some Node of its spec (resources, node selector and taints), the nightly load stays between 0.5 and 0.8, and the deadlock gang fits its Node one pod at a time but never whole.
How a run works scenario.sh <file>:
builds simscenario and workloadgen, validates the scenario and plans the run directory: scenario.effective.yaml (the scenario with its defaults filled in) and, per variant, trace.jsonl and variant.env; per variant: deletes the cluster first when the scenario isolates its variants (it lists more than one, or sets isolation: cluster), then runs up.sh, which creates the cluster or reuses a running one and switches it to the variant’s spec; runs deploy.sh with the variant’s spec, timing, telemetry mode and Joulie values files. joulie.set and simulator.set become values files, rendered by helm from the --set arguments so they mean exactly what --set means; with joulie.enabled: false, uninstalls Joulie, deletes its NodeTwins and NodeHardwares, removes the joulie.io/power-profile labels and, once no Joulie pod is left, renders the Nodes’ hwemu trees again: an agent writes its limits into the tree and never restores them, so without this the variant would run under the caps the agents wrote during the deploy; deletes and creates the run’s namespaces, and copies the trace into the simulator’s run directory, <SIM_HWEMU_ROOT>/_runs/<run id>/trace.jsonl, with docker exec; simscenario run: checks the KWOK pod-complete Stage, snapshots the Nodes and Joulie’s objects, starts the run through the simulator’s run API, captures the NodeTwins every capture interval until the run finishes, its deadline (duration plus drain) passes or it stays stalled for abortOnRunStalled, snapshots again, finishes the run (deleting its Job objects), records the Prometheus captures and collects the component logs. Everything goes through the API server, nothing is port-forwarded; copies the simulator’s otlp/ files out of the cluster, and simscenario evaluate writes the variant’s summary.json; simscenario summarize writes the run’s summary.json with the comparisons across variants, and runs/latest points at the run directory. Scenario files A scenario is decoded strictly: an unknown key anywhere, including inside an assertion, is an error. Durations are Go durations such as 90s or 4m.
Key Meaning schemaVersion 1 name the file stem, a DNS label cluster.spec, cluster.timing a cluster spec, relative to the repository root; dev (default) or production seed seeds the plan and workloadgen duration, drain the submission window (at most 6 h; jobs due later are dropped) and the extra time for submitted jobs to finish abortOnRunStalled end the run once joulie.sim.run.stalled has lasted this long isolation cluster (each variant on a fresh cluster, the default with several variants) or reuse (allowed with one variant only) workload the run’s settings and exactly one source: jobs, generate or trace (below) joulie enabled (default true), inputPreset (otel, kepler or kepler-legacy), set (Helm --set pairs) and values (values files) simulator.set Helm --set pairs for the simulator release variants up to 4, each a name, a description and its own joulie and simulator, merged key by key over the top level capture interval of the NodeTwin captures (default 15s) and prometheus range queries recorded as gauges named joulie.capture.* assertions, compare below A scenario may not set NODE_POWER_* or FACILITY_*, neither in joulie.set nor in a values file: it reaches Joulie’s inputs only through joulie.inputPreset, so it always tests a preset Joulie ships.
joulie.set and simulator.set take --set syntax: {a,b} is a list, and a comma inside a value needs a backslash.
The workload workload.namespace, owner, intent, completion, jobTTL, stallReport, baseSpeedPerCore and placement become the run’s options (the SIM_WORKLOAD_* defaults of the configuration reference apply to what is unset). baseSpeedPerCore (default 1) sizes the trace and is sent with the run, so ideal runtimes hold whatever the simulator was deployed with. placement replaces the simulator’s default node selector (sim.joulie.io/cluster=<spec>) and tolerations (the KWOK taint); an empty list or map clears the default, an unset one keeps it.
The sources:
jobs: inline job kinds. Each is name, class (performance or standard), count groups submitted every apart, pods per group (a gang with gang: true), requests (cpu and memory), gpus (resource: nvidia.com/gpu, amd.com/gpu, nvidia.com/gpu.shared or nvidia.com/mig-<profile>, and count), the ideal runtime, workClass, profile (cpuUtilization, gpuUtilization, memoryIntensity, ioIntensity, cpuFeedIntensityGpu, and peerTransferIntensity, the share of a multi-GPU job’s GPU time spent copying between its GPUs, see Peer transfers), sensitivity, and the pod’s affinity, nodeSelector and tolerations. generate.workloadgen: workloadgen flags without the dash, from an allowlist. The runner sets seed, base-speed-per-core, out and schema-version (always v3) itself. trace: a v3 trace file, relative to the repository root. k3s does not run the ExtendedResourceToleration admission plugin, so nothing adds the GPU vendor’s toleration to a pod that requests GPUs. The GPU profiles taint their Nodes (nvidia.com/gpu, amd.com/gpu), so a GPU job needs that toleration in its tolerations, or the run’s placement.tolerations (as the nightly scenarios do, restating the KWOK toleration the list replaces).
Assertions Every assertion has a name, a type and a severity (fail, the default, or warn), and an expect comparator such as ">= 0.95", "== 0", "< 90s" or "> 0 J". An assertion with nothing to evaluate fails with “no data”.
Type Fields Observed jobs a job filter (class, workload, nodeProfile); expect per count: completedFraction, completed, failed, incomplete the jobs due before the duration latency a job filter, metric (duration, queueWait, runTime, slowdown), quantile (0.5 to 1, or max), optional reference filter the quantile over completed jobs, or its ratio to the reference jobs’ quantile stall expect per reason: gangIncomplete, noProgress, runStalled stall events placement class, forbidden schedulable classes, graceSeconds binds of that class to a Node that had held a forbidden class for at least the grace (default the extender’s CACHE_TTL plus the reconcile interval) energy scope (total, class:<class>, node:<node>), hwType (cpu, gpu, all), perJob joulie.sim.workload.energy at the end events event, where attribute values matching log records objects expect per count: jobsNotComplete, strayPodsOnFakeNodes, nodeHardwares, controlBlocked the objects at the end twinPower warmup, tolerance, quantile, nodes the quantile of the relative error between each NodeTwin’s measured power and its Node’s energy rate promql query, at: end one instant query at the end of the run slowdown is run time over ideal run time, so queueing does not count. The nodeProfile of a job is its Node’s power profile when its pod was bound.
Comparisons compare entries take a metric of a variant over the same metric of a reference variant, with an expect on the ratio and a severity. Metrics: energy.total, class.<class>.energy, class.<class>.throughput, and class.<class>.<duration|queueWait|slowdown>.<p50|p95|max>.
Results A run directory, $SIMCLUSTER_DIR/runs/<UTC>-<scenario>-<sha12>[-dirty]/, holds scenario.effective.yaml, scenario.log and a summary.json; each variant writes <variant>/ (a scenario without variants writes these at the top):
summary.json, schema joulie.simcluster.summary/v1, the same as the smoke test’s: test.suite.name, test.suite.run.status, exitCode, failures, warnings, one entry per check under assertions, and for scenarios jobs, classes (throughput, energy, slowdown and duration quantiles per class), energy (boundary cpu packages + gpus) and comparisons; otlp/simulator.metrics.jsonl and otlp/simulator.logs.jsonl, the simulator’s run records, and otlp/harness.metrics.jsonl and otlp/harness.logs.jsonl, the runner’s: OTLP JSON Lines with the names of Simulator Metrics; trace.jsonl, variant.env, run-status.json, values.effective.yaml, values.simulator.effective.yaml, images.env, the snapshots in k8s/ and the component logs in logs/. With SIMCLUSTER_VALIDATE_OTLP=1, every line of every OTLP file is also posted to an OpenTelemetry Collector (OTELCOL_IMAGE pinned to OTELCOL_DIGEST of scripts/simcluster/versions.env, one container in Docker for the whole scenario, with the OTLP receiver and the file exporter). Each post must answer HTTP 200 with no rejected points or records, and the Collector must write as many data points and log records as were sent; otherwise the variant fails.
Settings Besides those of up.sh and deploy.sh (Simulated Cluster); each variant’s variant.env sets the spec, timing, telemetry mode and power scope.
Variable Effect SCENARIO the scenario file, for make simcluster-scenario SCENARIO_VARIANTS run only these variants, space separated. The run is then not summarized, so the variants can run on separate machines and simscenario summarize can compare them afterwards SCENARIO_RUN_DIR the run directory, instead of a new one under runs/; runs/latest is then left alone SIMCLUSTER_VALIDATE_OTLP 1 posts the run’s OTLP files to a Collector, above SIMCLUSTER_SIM_EXTRA_VALUES simulator values files, space separated, after the generated ones; scenario.sh sets it for simulator.set SIMCLUSTER_SCENARIOS 1 makes make simcluster-smoke also run the smoke scenario on its cluster after TestSimclusterE2E, into the smoke run’s scenario-smoke/ simscenario simscenario validate <file> [-repo DIR] simscenario plan <file> -out RUNDIR [-repo DIR] [-workloadgen BIN] simscenario run -variant-dir DIR [-kubeconfig FILE] simscenario evaluate DIR simscenario summarize RUNDIR Exit codes: 0 success, 1 a failed assertion or comparison of severity fail, 2 a usage error, an invalid scenario, or a run that could not be carried out.
CI .github/workflows/simcluster-nightly.yml runs the library on a schedule, with permissions: contents: read, and never cancels a run in progress. Every job uploads its run directory, kept 14 days.
Monday to Saturday at 03:17 UTC: nightly-mixed (130 minute timeout) and deadlock-visible with the OTLP check, as separate jobs. Sunday at 03:17 UTC: weekly-compare, one variant per runner (150 minute timeout) into a run directory named once for all of them, then a job that plans the same directory, collects the variants and runs simscenario summarize. On demand (workflow_dispatch, which works once the file is on the default branch): nightly or weekly.

title: Workload Scenarios

body:
This page documents how Joulie generates realistic AI workload traces for the simulator.
It is separate from Workload Simulator:
this page explains how traces are generated, the workload-simulator page explains how those traces are consumed at runtime. Scope The current generator is designed to be realistic for:
AI-oriented Kubernetes clusters, CPU + GPU workloads, memory-pressure-sensitive jobs, multi-pod logical workloads such as distributed training and HPO-style experiments. The current generator does not explicitly model:
network bandwidth, disk IO throughput, exact framework-level communication protocols. Instead, distributed overhead is folded into workload structure and bottleneck signals such as:
gpuUtilization, memoryIntensity, cpuFeedIntensityGpu. Why the generator changed The original synthetic generator was intentionally simple: it sampled single jobs with coarse CPU/GPU classes. That was fine for basic scheduler and power-loop testing, but it was too weak for realistic AI experiments.
The current generator now reflects the main public observations from production GPU clusters:
many jobs are single-GPU, a smaller fraction of multi-GPU jobs dominates GPU-time, job durations are heavy-tailed, arrivals follow a daily pattern, multi-pod logical workloads are common, and accelerator jobs often have lower host CPU compute utilisation than their CPU requests would suggest. Evidence base The current defaults are grounded in the following public sources.
Production traces and workload studies HeliosData repository (SenseTime traces) Characterization and Prediction of Deep Learning Workloads in Large-Scale GPU Datacenters, SC'21 Philly traces repository Analysis of Large-Scale Multi-Tenant GPU Clusters for DNN Training Workloads, USENIX ATC'19 Alibaba cluster-trace-gpu-v2020 README Modelling and scheduler references Roofline: an insightful visual performance model for multicore architectures Blox: A Modular Toolkit for Scheduling and Optimizing DAG-based Workflows in ML Clusters Kubernetes-native multi-pod workload references Kubeflow Trainer distributed training reference Kubeflow PyTorchJob guide Kubeflow Trainer job scheduling with Volcano Kueue introduction Kubeflow Katib overview Katib experiment configuration guide Trace format The generator now emits two kinds of JSONL records:
type=workload: logical workload metadata type=job: pod-expanded runnable records consumed by the simulator The simulator currently consumes the type=job records directly and ignores type=workload metadata records. The workload metadata is still useful for inspection, debugging, and future calibration tooling.
In benchmark experiments, there can also be a post-generation retargeting step. For example, experiment 02 keeps the canonical logical trace produced by workloadgen, then rewrites only the pod-level placement constraints so the runnable jobs land on concrete heterogeneous KWOK nodes present in the benchmark cluster. That retargeting does not change the logical workload shape, work units, or submission timing; it only makes the generated jobs hardware-aware for that specific cluster instance.
Schema versions --schema-version selects the trace schema. Every record carries it as schemaVersion.
v3 (default) v2 sensitivity on job records absent, so the simulator reads 1 (a cap slows the job in full); --cpu-sensitivity and --gpu-sensitivity write the keys they name on every job always present: {"cpu":0,"gpu":0} in default mode, 0.5 on performance jobs in diurnal mode power-profile affinity none; the class is declared only by intentClass, which the simulator turns into its placement intent: a NotIn [eco] affinity on joulie.io/power-profile in the legacy workload model, the joulie.io/workload-class annotation in v1 performance jobs carry NotIn [eco] on joulie.io/power-profile work units every pod’s ideal runtime equals its workload’s durationSec (see How work units are derived) scaled by utilisation, role and rate flags diurnal GPU class gpu.compute_bound, which the physics model knows gpu.compute, which the physics model treats as gpu.mixed --arrival-window-sec, --max-duration-sec available rejected --peer-transfer-intensity available rejected v2 is the schema experiments 01 to 03 were measured with. With --schema-version v2 the output is byte for byte what the generator wrote before v3, and every legacy caller pins it: the experiment scripts 04_run_one.py and 05_sweep.py, scripts/standalone_sweep.py and example 10. A contract test (TestWorkloadgenCallersPinSchemaVersion) fails when one of these callers runs workloadgen without --schema-version v2 as the first flag after the package. Other callers may build or install workloadgen and rely on the default v3. Golden traces in simulator/cmd/workloadgen/testdata, and the SHA-256 of the traces written with the legacy callers’ flags, guard the v2 bytes in both modes.
Each schema rejects the flags that only shape the other: v2 rejects --cpu-sensitivity, --gpu-sensitivity, --arrival-window-sec, --max-duration-sec and --peer-transfer-intensity; v3 rejects --cpu-work-rate-per-core, --gpu-work-rate-per-gpu and --work-scale, which would break its ideal runtime.
Logical workload record Example:
{"type":"workload","schemaVersion":"v3","workloadId":"workload-000001","submitTimeOffsetSec":12.4,"namespace":"default","workloadType":"distributed_training","gang":true,"durationSec":14400,"workloadClass":{"cpu":"cpu.mixed","gpu":"gpu.compute_bound"},"sharedIntensityProfile":{"cpuUtilization":0.28,"gpuUtilization":0.47,"memoryIntensity":0.58,"ioIntensity":0.08,"cpuFeedIntensityGpu":0.56},"pods":[{"role":"launcher","replicas":1,"requests":{"cpu":"2","memory":"4Gi"},"gang":true},{"role":"worker","replicas":4,"requests":{"cpu":"4","memory":"12Gi","nvidia.com/gpu":"1"},"gang":true}]} Pod-expanded job record Example (v3, base speed 1.0: the worker runs for the workload’s 14400 s on its 4 cores and its GPU):
{"type":"job","schemaVersion":"v3","jobId":"workload-000001-worker-01","workloadId":"workload-000001","workloadType":"distributed_training","podRole":"worker","gang":true,"submitTimeOffsetSec":12.4,"namespace":"default","intentClass":"performance","podTemplate":{"requests":{"cpu":"4","memory":"12Gi","nvidia.com/gpu":"1"}},"work":{"cpuUnits":57600,"gpuUnits":14400},"workloadClass":{"cpu":"cpu.mixed","gpu":"gpu.compute_bound"},"workloadProfile":{"cpuUtilization":0.28,"gpuUtilization":0.47,"memoryIntensity":0.58,"ioIntensity":0.08,"cpuFeedIntensityGpu":0.56}} Statistical model The generator follows a hierarchical sampling path:
sample arrival time, sample workload family, sample GPU footprint, sample duration, sample shared workload profile, sample pod structure and per-role resource requests, expand the logical workload into runnable pod-level jobs. When a benchmark or integration harness needs to bind those jobs to a specific synthetic cluster inventory, it can add an eighth step:
retarget pod-level placement to the concrete nodes or hardware families available in the current test cluster. Arrival model Joulie now uses a simple NHPP-like day-shaped arrival process with an hourly rate multiplier and optional bursts.
The current built-in hourly prior reflects Helios-style behavior:
lower rate at night (00:00-08:00), visible lunch/dinner dips, higher submission activity during working hours. Current built-in multipliers:
00:00-07:59: 0.70 12:00: 0.85 18:00: 0.85 09:00-11:59: 1.20 13:00-17:59: 1.15 20:00-22:59: 1.00 remaining hours: 0.95 Inter-arrival is sampled as:
delta ~ Exp(mean_inter_arrival / hourly_multiplier) Optional burst behavior is also supported:
--burst-day-probability --burst-multiplier --burst-mean-jobs This is intentionally lightweight, but it captures the key point from Helios and Blox-style evaluation work: realistic clusters are not homogeneous Poisson streams with a single flat rate.
Workload families The current generator samples from these workload families.
GPU-backed logical workloads Conditional on --gpu-ratio, the generator currently uses:
debug_eval: 45% single_gpu_training: 25% distributed_training: 14% parameter_server_training: 7% hpo_experiment: 9% CPU-only logical workloads For non-GPU logical workloads:
cpu_preprocess: 75% cpu_analytics: 25% These are not claimed to be universal production truth. They are the current HEP-friendly prior inspired by the public traces:
many short exploratory jobs, many single-GPU runs, fewer but more expensive multi-GPU jobs, some multi-pod training and HPO structure. GPU-count distribution The current default categorical prior is:
P(G=1) = 0.80 P(G=2) = 0.10 P(G=4) = 0.07 P(G=8) = 0.03 This follows the key shape reported in Helios:
single-GPU jobs dominate job count, but larger jobs dominate GPU-time. For small debug benchmarks, the generator distribution is usually combined with a family-aware retargeting pass so at least the major GPU families in the synthetic cluster are exercised, even when the total job count is intentionally small.
Duration model Durations are heavy-tailed and workload-family-specific.
Current built-in approximations:
debug_eval: lognormal around Helios-like short-job behavior, clamped to 30s .. 1000s single_gpu_training: long-tail lognormal, clamped to 15min .. 7d distributed_training: longer-tail lognormal, clamped to 20min .. 14d parameter_server_training: clamped to 15min .. 7d hpo_experiment: clamped to 20min .. 3d cpu_preprocess: clamped to 2min .. 8h cpu_analytics: clamped to 5min .. 24h This is meant to preserve the public observation that AI job durations are not well represented by a narrow bell curve.
Utilisation and bottleneck priors The generator explicitly separates:
requested resources, used for placement, utilisation/intensity profile, used for slowdown and power. That separation matters because ATC'19 reports that many training jobs underutilise GPU cycles, and also that host CPU cycles are often underutilised even when CPU and memory are allocated proportionally to requested GPUs.
GPU utilisation prior The built-in gpuUtilization prior is seeded from the ATC'19 Philly means by total GPU count:
1 GPU: 0.5238 4 GPUs: 0.4518 8 GPUs: 0.5899 16 GPUs: 0.4039 The generator interpolates this into a practical small-cluster prior:
1 GPU: 0.5238 2 GPUs: 0.50 4 GPUs: 0.4518 8 GPUs: 0.5899 Then it adjusts by workload type:
debug_eval: lower effective GPU utilisation distributed_training: lower effective GPU utilisation because coordination overhead is folded into the shared profile parameter_server_training: similar reduction CPU utilisation prior CPU utilisation is sampled independently from CPU requests.
Examples from the current generator:
cpu_preprocess: 0.50 .. 0.75 cpu_analytics: 0.75 .. 0.95 debug_eval: 0.20 .. 0.40 single_gpu_training: 0.20 .. 0.45 distributed_training: 0.15 .. 0.35 This reflects the public observation that many accelerator-heavy jobs are not CPU-compute-bound even when they still consume CPU and memory resources.
Memory / IO / CPU-feed intensities The shared profile also samples:
memoryIntensity ioIntensity cpuFeedIntensityGpu Examples:
parameter_server_training: high memoryIntensity distributed_training: moderate-to-high cpuFeedIntensityGpu cpu_preprocess: high memoryIntensity, low-to-moderate ioIntensity debug_eval: more memory-heavy and less GPU-saturated than long training These fields are what connect the workload generator to the physical model documented in Hardware Modeling.
Multi-pod workload structures The generator now emits realistic pod structures instead of only single pods.
single_gpu_training 1 worker pod all GPUs requested by that pod distributed_training 1 launcher pod (CPU-only) G worker pods, typically 1 GPU each gang=true parameter_server_training G worker pods (1 GPU each) 1-2 CPU-only parameter-server pods gang=true hpo_experiment 1 controller pod K trial pods each trial usually requests 1 GPU not gang-coupled by default in the current simulator path This is a good fit for the report requirement that a single logical workload may span multiple pods while preserving a shared performance and power profile.
How work units are derived The simulator still runs on abstract work units, so the generator maps duration into work.
In v3, in both modes, every pod of a workload gets:
CPUUnits = duration_sec * cpu_request * base_speed_per_core GPUUnits = duration_sec * gpu_request * base_speed_per_core At full speed the simulator does request * base_speed_per_core units per second (SIM_BASE_SPEED_PER_CORE, default 1.0), so a pod’s ideal runtime, with no cap and no contention, is exactly its workload’s durationSec. --base-speed-per-core defaults to 1.0 in v3; a trace generated with another value must run on a simulator set to the same speed. The CPU request is taken as written to the trace (two decimals), so the simulator reads back the request the units were sized with. Utilisation and intensity stay in the profile, where they drive power and slowdown, not the amount of work.
v2 keeps the earlier mapping:
default mode: CPUUnits ~= duration_sec * cpu_request * cpu_utilization * cpu_work_rate_per_core GPUUnits ~= duration_sec * gpu_request * gpu_utilization * gpu_work_rate_per_gpu diurnal mode: CPUUnits ~= duration_sec * cpu_request * cpu_utilization * base_speed_per_core * work_scale GPUUnits ~= duration_sec * gpu_request * gpu_utilization * base_speed_per_core * work_scale with utilisation floored at 0.10, --base-speed-per-core defaulting to 2.0, and, in default mode, small role-specific scaling factors for launchers, controllers, parameter servers, workers and trials.
This is not a trace-replay of exact instruction counts. It is a practical way to make requested duration, requested resources, and throttling line up inside the simulator.
Fitting a trace into a run Two v3 flags shape a trace for a run of fixed length:
--arrival-window-sec S scales every submit offset linearly so the last arrival is at S seconds. The arrival pattern keeps its shape; a window past the last arrival changes nothing. --max-duration-sec D clamps each workload’s durationSec to D before its work is sized, so no pod’s ideal runtime exceeds D. Both default to 0, which keeps the sampled offsets and durations.
Gang semantics in the simulator The generator now marks distributed and parameter-server workloads with gang=true.
The simulator uses that metadata to avoid advancing workload progress until all pods in the gang are running. This makes multi-pod workloads behave more like real distributed jobs rather than a bag of unrelated pods.
CLI summary The main generator remains:
go run ./simulator/cmd/workloadgen --out trace.jsonl This writes a v3 trace. A script that depends on the earlier traces passes --schema-version v2.
Useful knobs:
--schema-version (v3 or v2) --mode (default or diurnal) --jobs --mean-inter-arrival-sec --seed --gpu-ratio --perf-ratio --burst-day-probability --burst-multiplier --burst-mean-jobs --emit-workload-records --base-speed-per-core (both modes in v3, default 1.0; diurnal mode only in v2, default 2.0) --cpu-sensitivity, --gpu-sensitivity (v3 only) --arrival-window-sec, --max-duration-sec (v3 only) --peer-transfer-intensity (v3 only): workloadProfile.peerTransferIntensity, in [0, 1], on every job that requests two or more GPUs, the share of its GPU time spent copying between its GPUs (see Peer transfers) --cpu-work-rate-per-core, --gpu-work-rate-per-gpu, --work-scale (v2 only) What is still intentionally simplified A few things are still simplified compared with a full production-trace replay system:
no direct fitting from Helios / Philly / Alibaba traces inside the generator yet no explicit network model no explicit storage-bandwidth model no phased time-series profile yet; profiles are currently shared averages per logical workload no manifest renderer yet for PyTorchJob, MPIJob, or Katib Experiment That said, the current implementation is a large step up from a toy generator:
arrivals are no longer flat, job sizes are no longer uniform, durations are no longer narrow, multi-pod AI workloads are first-class, and utilisation/bottleneck priors are tied to public workload studies. References Trace datasets and workload studies [WG1] HeliosData repository (SenseTime traces)
https://github.com/S-Lab-System-Group/HeliosData [WG2] Tianwei Zhang et al., Characterization and Prediction of Deep Learning Workloads in Large-Scale GPU Datacenters (SC'21)
https://tianweiz07.github.io/Papers/21-sc.pdf [WG3] Philly traces repository
https://github.com/msr-fiddle/philly-traces [WG4] Myeongjae Jeon et al., Analysis of Large-Scale Multi-Tenant GPU Clusters for DNN Training Workloads (USENIX ATC'19)
https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc19-jeon.pdf [WG5] Alibaba cluster-trace-gpu-v2020 README
https://github.com/alibaba/clusterdata/blob/master/cluster-trace-gpu-v2020/README.md Modelling references [WG6] Samuel Williams et al., Roofline: an insightful visual performance model for multicore architectures
https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1498765.1498785 [WG7] Blox workflow/scheduler evaluation reference used for burst-style arrival thinking
https://arxiv.org/html/2312.12621v1 Kubernetes multi-pod AI workload references [WG8] Kubeflow Trainer distributed training reference
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/trainer/legacy-v1/reference/distributed-training/ [WG9] Kubeflow PyTorchJob guide
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/trainer/legacy-v1/user-guides/pytorch/ [WG10] Kubeflow Trainer scheduling with Volcano
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/trainer/operator-guides/job-scheduling/volcano/ [WG11] Kueue introduction
https://kubernetes.io/blog/2022/10/04/introducing-kueue/ [WG12] Kubeflow Katib overview
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/katib/overview/ [WG13] Katib experiment configuration guide
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/katib/user-guides/hp-tuning/configure-experiment/ These references support the current Joulie workload generator in four ways:
trace-shaped arrival and duration priors, realistic GPU-count skew and utilisation priors, multi-pod workload structure, and Kubernetes-native execution patterns for distributed training and HPO. Gap analysis against the workload-generation report The current implementation covers the core generator/runtime path described in the workload report:
realistic AI-oriented workload families daily arrival shaping with bursts heavy-tailed durations GPU-count skew multi-pod logical workloads gang-style progress for distributed/PS workloads explicit utilization and bottleneck priors However, a few report items are still not implemented and should be read as future work, not current behavior:
direct fitting from Helios / Philly / Alibaba traces inside workloadgen profile-bundle import/export for fitted priors phase/time-series intensity profiles instead of only shared averages direct manifest rendering for Kubeflow / Katib objects calibration-mode telemetry ingestion loop So the implementation is now clearly beyond a toy generator, but it is not yet the full end-state envisioned by the report.

body:
This page documents the statistical distributions and priors behind the current workload generator.
Use it together with:
Workload Generation Workload Simulator Hardware Modeling What this page is for The generator is no longer just a flat random-job emitter. It now uses explicit priors for:
arrival timing, GPU-count skew, duration shape, utilization, memory pressure, multi-pod workload structure. This page makes those priors visible and explains why they are reasonable.
1. Arrival model The current implementation uses a lightweight NHPP-like process:
a baseline exponential inter-arrival sampler, modulated by an hourly multiplier, with optional burst windows. That is not yet a full trace-fit pipeline, but it is designed to capture the main structure reported in Helios and in scheduler-evaluation work:
workday-heavy submission activity, visible midday dips, lower submission activity overnight, and occasional bursty periods. Current hourly multipliers 00:00-07:59: 0.70 09:00-11:59: 1.20 12:00: 0.85 13:00-17:59: 1.15 18:00: 0.85 20:00-22:59: 1.00 other hours: 0.95 Burst overlay Optional burst parameters:
--burst-day-probability --burst-multiplier --burst-mean-jobs This is inspired by Blox-style simulator methodology, where trace-derived rates are combined with controlled spikes for stress testing.
2. GPU-count prior The generator follows the trace-backed pattern that:
single-GPU jobs dominate job count, larger jobs dominate GPU-time. Current default categorical prior P(G=1) = 0.80 P(G=2) = 0.10 P(G=4) = 0.07 P(G=8) = 0.03 This is a practical HEP-oriented prior derived from the shape reported in Helios rather than a literal replay of one production cluster.
3. Duration model The generator uses heavy-tailed duration priors, because public AI cluster traces consistently show that durations are not well represented by narrow or symmetric distributions.
Current family-level approximations debug_eval short-biased lognormal clamped to 30s .. 1000s single_gpu_training long-tail lognormal clamped to 15min .. 7d distributed_training longer-tail lognormal clamped to 20min .. 14d parameter_server_training clamped to 15min .. 7d hpo_experiment clamped to 20min .. 3d cpu_preprocess clamped to 2min .. 8h cpu_analytics clamped to 5min .. 24h These choices are intended to preserve the Helios-style pattern:
many short exploratory/evaluation jobs, fewer long-running training jobs, a strong long tail extending far beyond the median. 4. Requested resources vs used resources One of the most important modeling choices in the generator is that it separates:
requested resources used by the scheduler, used resources / intensity profile used by the physical model. This separation matters because public studies report that:
CPU and memory are often requested proportionally to GPUs, but host CPU compute utilization can still be low, while memory pressure can remain high, and GPU utilization is often substantially below 100% in production training clusters. 5. GPU utilization prior The current implementation seeds GPU utilization from the ATC'19 Philly mean GPU-utilization values by GPU count.
Reference points used in the current generator 1 GPU: 0.5238 4 GPUs: 0.4518 8 GPUs: 0.5899 16 GPUs: 0.4039 The generator then interpolates this into a small-cluster prior and adjusts by workload family:
debug_eval: lower effective GPU utilization distributed_training: lower effective GPU utilization than single-GPU training parameter_server_training: similar downward adjustment This is meant to reflect the well-known difference between:
GPU allocation, GPU utilization, and actual useful throughput. 6. CPU utilization prior The generator samples CPU utilization independently from CPU request size.
Examples from the current implementation:
cpu_preprocess: 0.50 .. 0.75 cpu_analytics: 0.75 .. 0.95 debug_eval: 0.20 .. 0.40 single_gpu_training: 0.20 .. 0.45 distributed_training: 0.15 .. 0.35 parameter_server_training: 0.20 .. 0.40 This reflects the observed pattern that many accelerator-heavy jobs are not CPU-compute-bound even though they still require host CPU resources.
7. Memory / IO / CPU-feed priors The current generator samples three explicit bottleneck signals:
memoryIntensity ioIntensity cpuFeedIntensityGpu These are the bridge from workload generation into the throttling model.
Interpretation high memoryIntensity more memory-dominated behavior softer slowdown under CPU throttling high ioIntensity even softer CPU-side slowdown high cpuFeedIntensityGpu GPU throughput becomes more sensitive to CPU throttling This is deliberately aligned with the more realistic class-aware slowdown semantics described in Hardware Modeling.
8. Structure prior The current generator samples a logical workload family first, then derives pod structure from it.
This is directly motivated by the Alibaba PAI trace and Kubernetes-native ML systems, where a single logical workload may span multiple pods.
Structure classes used today single-pod GPU job distributed training parameter-server style training HPO experiment CPU-only preprocessing / analytics jobs Current expansion behavior distributed_training launcher + worker pods gang=true parameter_server_training parameter-server pods + worker pods gang=true hpo_experiment controller + multiple trial pods no gang requirement by default in the current simulator path 9. Throttling-sensitivity motivation The workload report does not just motivate arrival and resource distributions; it also motivates class-aware slowdown.
That is why Joulie models compute-bound, memory-bound, and mixed regimes rather than using a single slowdown curve for every job.
The core literature-backed idea is:
compute-bound workloads should slow down more under reduced compute roof, memory-bound workloads should often slow down less, but the exact attenuation depends on how bandwidth, clocks, and control surfaces interact. The workload generator therefore emits priors that support this model rather than fighting it.
10. What is implemented vs not yet implemented Implemented today day-shaped arrivals with bursts heavy-tailed durations GPU-count skew workload-family-based generation multi-pod logical workloads gang metadata for distributed/PS workloads shared workload intensity profiles explicit resource-vs-utilization separation Not yet implemented direct fitting from Helios / Philly / Alibaba traces inside workloadgen profile-bundle loading from a fitted YAML/JSON file phased time-series workload profiles explicit network and disk models calibrated per-framework workload templates So the current implementation is research-informed and structure-aware, but not yet a full trace-fitting platform.
References [WD1] HeliosData repository
https://github.com/S-Lab-System-Group/HeliosData [WD2] Tianwei Zhang et al., Characterization and Prediction of Deep Learning Workloads in Large-Scale GPU Datacenters (SC'21)
https://tianweiz07.github.io/Papers/21-sc.pdf [WD3] Philly traces repository
https://github.com/msr-fiddle/philly-traces [WD4] Myeongjae Jeon et al., Analysis of Large-Scale Multi-Tenant GPU Clusters for DNN Training Workloads (USENIX ATC'19)
https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc19-jeon.pdf [WD5] Alibaba cluster-trace-gpu-v2020 README
https://github.com/alibaba/clusterdata/blob/master/cluster-trace-gpu-v2020/README.md [WD6] Samuel Williams et al., Roofline: an insightful visual performance model for multicore architectures
https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1498765.1498785 [WD7] Blox arrival/burst evaluation reference
https://arxiv.org/html/2312.12621v1 [WD8] David Meisner et al., Memory Performance at Reduced CPU Clock Speeds, HotPower'12
https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/hotpower12/hotpower12-final21.pdf [WD9] Characterizing the Impact of GPU Power Management on HPC Applications, PMBS 2025 preprint used in the workload report
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16371 [WD10] Tapasya Patki et al., Comparing GPU Power and Frequency Capping for Energy Savings in Scientific Applications, SC Workshops 2019
https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8944989

body:
This page explains how the logical workload structures used by Joulie map onto common Kubernetes-native AI workload patterns.
It is mainly a documentation page today. The current simulator generator emits the structure metadata and pod-expanded jobs, but it does not yet render PyTorchJob, MPIJob, or Katib Experiment manifests directly.
Why this page exists The workload-generation report makes an important point:
realistic AI workloads are often not single pods, and a single logical workload may map to: a launcher + workers, parameter servers + workers, or a controller + many HPO trial pods. That distinction matters even in a simulator, because power and slowdown should often be understood at the logical workload level, not only at the pod level.
Current Joulie mapping The current generator emits:
a logical type=workload record, and one or more type=job records derived from it. The simulator consumes the expanded pod-level records, while keeping workload-level metadata such as:
workloadId workloadType podRole gang Distributed training Current Joulie representation one launcher pod G worker pods gang=true This is meant to approximate the common pattern used by:
PyTorch distributed training, Kubeflow Trainer / Training Operator, MPI-style worker sets. Why gang semantics matter A distributed job is not realistically represented as “some workers are running, so useful progress should continue normally.”
That is why the simulator now treats gang=true workloads specially:
workload progress waits until all pods in the gang are running. This is a practical approximation of real distributed-training startup and co-scheduling behavior.
Parameter-server training Current Joulie representation 1-2 CPU-only ps pods G GPU worker pods shared workload profile gang=true This is inspired by Alibaba PAI-style role hierarchy and older TF-style parameter-server deployments.
Hyperparameter optimisation Current Joulie representation one controller pod multiple trial pods shared workload-level prior no gang requirement by default This is meant to capture the idea that one logical HPO experiment can fan out into several trial pods while still being one experiment-level workload.
What Joulie does not do yet The current implementation does not yet include:
direct manifest rendering to PyTorchJob direct manifest rendering to MPIJob direct manifest rendering to Katib Experiment integration with Volcano / Kueue objects So this page is partly architectural guidance for the next step, not a claim that those rendering paths already exist.
Why these references still matter now Even before manifest rendering exists, these references are useful because they justify the logical structures already present in the generator:
multi-worker distributed training, role-based pod sets, gang-like startup semantics, HPO as one experiment with many trial pods. References [KW1] Kubeflow Trainer distributed training reference
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/trainer/legacy-v1/reference/distributed-training/ [KW2] Kubeflow PyTorchJob guide
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/trainer/legacy-v1/user-guides/pytorch/ [KW3] Kubeflow Trainer scheduling with Volcano
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/trainer/operator-guides/job-scheduling/volcano/ [KW4] Kubeflow legacy job scheduling guide
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/trainer/legacy-v1/user-guides/job-scheduling/ [KW5] Kueue introduction
https://kubernetes.io/blog/2022/10/04/introducing-kueue/ [KW6] Kubeflow Katib overview
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/katib/overview/ [KW7] Katib experiment configuration guide
https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/katib/user-guides/hp-tuning/configure-experiment/ [KW8] Alibaba cluster-trace-gpu-v2020 README
