This page describes the simulator runtime mechanics (control/state/energy paths).
The canonical physical model, provenance, and hardware assumptions are documented in:
Hardware Modeling For workload progression semantics:
Workload Simulator Scope The power simulator runtime is responsible for:
keeping per-node control state (CPU cap, DVFS throttle, GPU cap), applying control actions from /control/{node}, updating dynamics with settling/ramp behavior, exposing power telemetry on /otlp/telemetry/{node} and /telemetry/{node} (OTLP JSON; /telemetry/{node}?format=legacy serves the deprecated legacy JSON until v0.4.0), integrating energy over time (/debug/energy). The physics step A modelled node (any node outside the emulate-mode cluster spec) advances only in a physics step, in simulated time, never when it is read:
Mode What steps the nodes Step Longest substep Kubernetes (KWOK) the physics tick, every SIM_PHYSICS_TICK (default 1s) the wall time since the last tick 100 ms Emulate mode the emulator’s tick (SIM_EMULATE_TICK), for the nodes outside the spec the time between two snapshots 100 ms Standalone each standalone tick SIM_SA_DT seconds of virtual time SIM_SA_SUBSTEP (default SIM_SA_DT) A control sets targets only: its response, and every read until the next step, show the cap and the power the last step left. The telemetry routes, /state/{node} and the per-node gauges report the node as the last step left it, so reading a node more or less often never changes its behaviour. Each node carries simTime in /state/{node}: the simulated time its physics has reached. The energy in /debug/energy and in the timeseries is the integral of each node’s instantaneous CPU and GPU power over the substeps, not of the averaged telemetry signal. The order of the work inside a substep and the lag equations are in Hardware Modeling, section 5.5.
Runtime state and controls Main node state includes:
CPU: target/applied cap utilization effective frequency scale throttle target/current saturation flag instantaneous and averaged power temperature and thermal-throttle fraction GPU: per-device cap/target per-device instantaneous and averaged power per-device temperature and thermal-throttle fraction aggregate utilization effective performance multiplier workload-model inputs aggregated from running jobs: memoryIntensity ioIntensity cpuFeedIntensity Supported control actions:
rapl.set_power_cap_watts dvfs.set_throttle_pct gpu.set_power_cap_watts Telemetry contract actually exposed by the simulator The simulator serves each node’s power in two formats, computed from one snapshot of the node:
GET /otlp/telemetry/{node}: one OTLP JSON ExportMetricsServiceRequest, the HTTP input format that the agent’s and the controller manager’s http sources read. Its resource carries k8s.node.name. It holds hw.power gauges for the CPU (hw.id=cpu, hw.type=cpu) and for each GPU (hw.id=gpu<index>, hw.type=gpu, hw.name the product), and hw.host.power (hw.id=host) for their sum. The values are the averaged powers, or the instantaneous ones while the average is still 0, unrounded. An emulated node answers instead with its part of the emulate-mode export: energy counters and power gauges per CPU package, DRAM zone and GPU. GET /telemetry/{node}: the same OTLP JSON by default. With ?format=legacy it serves the legacy JSON, a compact node-level view and richer subsystem views, deprecated and removed in v0.4.0; the first such read logs one warning per process. Any other format than otlp or legacy answers 400. Important top-level fields of the legacy JSON:
packagePowerWatts exported averaged node power instantPackagePowerWatts internal instantaneous node power used by the model Important CPU fields:
cpu.packagePowerWatts cpu.instantPowerWatts cpu.utilization cpu.memoryIntensity cpu.ioIntensity cpu.freqScale cpu.temperatureC cpu.thermalThrottlePct Important GPU fields:
gpu.powerWattsTotal gpu.avgPowerWattsTotal gpu.utilization gpu.memoryIntensity gpu.cpuFeedIntensity gpu.capWattsPerGpuApplied gpu.capWattsPerGpuTarget gpu.devices[] This distinction matters because the simulator is now intentionally modeling the difference between:
internal fast-changing device power exported averaged telemetry seen by the controller Hardware identity and overrides The simulator runtime no longer depends primarily on pre-enumerated node classes.
Today the intended precedence is:
node labels define simulated hardware identity shared inventory resolves that identity into a CPU/GPU model optional SIM_NODE_CLASS_CONFIG overrides refine or override profile parameters So SIM_NODE_CLASS_CONFIG is still useful, but it is now an override layer rather than the main source of hardware truth.
Model source of truth This page intentionally avoids duplicating formulas and hardware assumptions. Use Hardware Modeling as source of truth for:
measured vs proxy curves, CPU/GPU workload-class behavior, heterogeneous-node normalization semantics, vendor/API-specific constraints and references. Operational note When formulas and this page diverge, simulator behavior and hardware-modeling.md are authoritative; update this page only for runtime flow and interfaces.

body:
The Joulie simulator lets you evaluate energy management policies without physical hardware. It provides a controlled, reproducible environment for benchmarking power savings and scheduling strategies.
The simulator keeps scheduling behavior real while simulating telemetry, control dynamics, and workload progression.
The simulator mirrors the real Joulie architecture. The controller manager, agent, and scheduler extender are the real components running against simulated hardware:
the real controller manager computes desired state (NodeTwin.spec, NodeTwin.status), the real agent (pool mode) realizes caps via HTTP against the simulator, the real scheduler extender reads NodeTwin.status and applies workload-class-aware scoring, workloads carry trace-defined fields (criticality, cap sensitivity), facility stress model (simulator/pkg/facility) provides PSU and cooling stress signals. The heterogeneous benchmark (experiments/02-heterogeneous-benchmark/) demonstrates the full architecture across three baselines: no Joulie, static partition, and queue-aware policy with scheduler extender steering.
Use simulator docs after you are familiar with the core controller manager/agent control loop in Getting Started + Architecture.
Read in this order Installation – deploy the simulator stack locally or in CI Workload and Power Simulator – architecture overview and how simulated components interact Workload Generation – trace-driven job creation and replay Workload Distributions – arrival rates, duration profiles, resource demand curves Kubernetes AI Workloads – GPU-heavy training and inference workload models Workload Simulator – per-pod lifecycle simulation and utilization dynamics Power Simulator – node-level power draw and thermal response modeling Hardware Modeling – CPU/GPU power curves used by the simulator Simulator Metrics – Prometheus metrics exported by simulated nodes Model Changes – every change that moves the numbers the simulator produces, and how far; read it before comparing with results from an older simulator Simulator architecture diagram See detailed explanation in:
Workload and Power Simulator

The digital twin is Joulie’s core predictive engine. It is a lightweight O(1) parametric model that predicts the impact of scheduling and power-cap decisions on node thermal and power state, without running a full simulation for each scheduling decision.
What the digital twin computes For each managed node, the twin produces three scores stored in NodeTwin.status:
Signal Range Meaning Power headroom up to 100, can go negative Fraction of the node’s capped power budget still unused. Higher is better for new workload placement. Negative means the node already draws more than its budget. CoolingStress 0-100 Measured node power as a fraction of node TDP, scaled by an ambient temperature multiplier. High values indicate the node is near its thermal limit. PSUStress 0-100 Rack power draw (or cluster power draw when no rack is known) as a fraction of a reference rack capacity. Computed and published, but not read by the scheduler today. The twin also computes:
SchedulableClass: performance, eco, or draining (transition state). The scheduler extender uses this to filter and score nodes. EstimatedPUE: derived from cooling stress, between 1.05 and 1.40. Published for observability; not read by the scheduler today. PowerMeasurement: a block of measured and derived power values consumed directly by the scheduler for projected headroom scoring. Every power-derived score starts from one number: measuredNodePowerW. The twin is not a cap-based estimator. It reads what the node is drawing and compares it against budgets it derives from hardware.
PowerMeasurement output The powerMeasurement block in NodeTwin.status provides the scheduler with the real-time power data it needs for projected headroom scoring:
Field Unit Description source string Where the power reading came from (see below) measuredNodePowerW watts Current total node power draw cpuCappedPowerW watts CPU power budget (CPU TDP x cap percentage) gpuCappedPowerW watts GPU power budget (GPU TDP x cap percentage) nodeCappedPowerW watts Total node power budget (CPU + GPU capped power) cpuTdpW watts CPU thermal design power (max watts per socket x sockets) gpuTdpW watts GPU thermal design power (max watts per GPU x GPU count, 0 when no GPU is present) nodeTdpW watts Total node TDP (CPU + GPU) powerTrendWPerMin watts/min Rolling derivative of node power draw over a 5 minute window. Positive = rising, negative = falling. The scheduler uses measuredNodePowerW + pod marginal power to compute projected headroom relative to nodeCappedPowerW. The powerTrendWPerMin feeds the trend bonus, capped at 25 points in either direction. See Scheduler Extender for details.
Where the power reading comes from The controller manager resolves measuredNodePowerW before calling the twin. NODE_POWER_SOURCE selects the source:
NODE_POWER_SOURCE Behaviour source written prometheus (chart default) Runs one grouped query per reconcile against NODE_POWER_PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS (default PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS) and reads every node from the answer. The default preset otel reads the OpenTelemetry metrics hw.energy (as a rate) and hw.power of the CPU packages and GPUs, keyed by k8s.node.name; NODE_POWER_PRESET selects Kepler or a custom query instead. See Input metrics (OpenTelemetry). prometheus, or prometheus-no-data when there is no address, the query fails, or the answer has no positive reading for the node http GETs NODE_POWER_HTTP_ENDPOINT (with {node} substituted) and reads one OTLP JSON document with the same rules, such as the simulator’s /otlp/telemetry/{node}. The legacy packagePowerWatts JSON is read until v0.4.0. http, http-error, or http-no-endpoint static (code default) Returns 0 watts. static NODE_POWER_SCOPE sets what the reading covers. The default, components, is the CPU packages plus the GPUs: the same boundary as nodeTdpW (CPU TDP plus GPU TDP), so headroom and cooling stress compare like with like. host reads the whole host’s wall power instead, which includes memory, fans and the platform and exceeds nodeTdpW under load.
Without the chart, the code default is static, and an unconfigured controller manager reports 0 watts for every node: headroom reads 100 and cooling stress reads 0 everywhere. Configure a source before treating the scores as a ranking signal.
kepler and utilization are reserved source values; no component writes them yet. When a reading exceeds twice the node’s TDP the controller manager logs a one-shot warning, because that is the signature of a cumulative joules counter being read as watts.
Node TDP and the capped budget Both power formulas need the node’s hardware limits, derived from NodeHardware.status:
cpuTdp = cpuMaxWattsPerSocket * sockets gpuTdp = gpuMaxWatts * gpuCount (0 when no GPU is present) nodeTdp = cpuTdp + gpuTdp cpuCappedPower = cpuTdp * cpuCapPct/100 gpuCappedPower = gpuTdp * gpuCapPct/100 nodeCappedPower = cpuCappedPower + gpuCappedPower cpuCapPct and gpuCapPct come from the resolved NodeTwin.spec intent, defaulting to 100 when unset or non-positive.
When the socket count is unknown but a per-socket maximum is known, the twin assumes a single socket. A zero socket count would multiply the per-socket maximum down to zero, and a zero budget reads as unlimited headroom further down, so a busy node would look like the emptiest one in the cluster. Assuming one socket underestimates the budget on a multi-socket machine, which is the safe direction: the node looks fuller than it is rather than infinitely free.
Reference node used in the examples below A node with two AMD EPYC 9654 sockets (360 W per socket) and four NVIDIA H100 NVL GPUs (400 W each), running eco at a 60% cap on both CPU and GPU:
cpuTdpW = 360 * 2 = 720 W gpuTdpW = 400 * 4 = 1600 W nodeTdpW = 2320 W cpuCappedPowerW = 720 * 0.6 = 432 W gpuCappedPowerW = 1600 * 0.6 = 960 W nodeCappedPowerW = 1392 W CoolingStress formula CoolingStress is a per-node metric. It answers: “how close is this node to its cooling limit?”
tempMultiplier = 1 / max(0.5, 1 - (ambientTempC - 20) * 0.02) coolingStress = clamp((measuredPower / nodeTdp) * tempMultiplier * 100, 0, 100) Stress is normalized against uncapped TDP, not against the capped budget, because the cooling system is sized for the hardware that is installed, not for the cap currently applied to it. Capping a node lowers its measured power and so lowers its cooling stress, which is the intended behaviour.
Term Rationale measuredPower / nodeTdp Fraction of the node’s installed thermal capacity actually in use. A node drawing its full TDP scores 100 at 20C ambient. (ambientTempC - 20) * 0.02 Each degree above a 20C baseline shrinks the denominator by 0.02, so warm air makes the same watts cost more cooling effort. Below 20C the denominator grows and the multiplier drops below 1. max(0.5, ...) Floors the denominator, capping the multiplier at 2.0. The cap is reached at 45C ambient and holds for anything hotter. If nodeTdp is 0 (no hardware information) the score is 0: the twin emits no stress signal rather than a fabricated one. The ambient temperature is the most local one the facility inputs read: the node’s inlet, then its cooling zone’s, then the outdoor ambient (see Facility metrics). Any reading counts, 0C and below included. With no reading the ambient is unknown and the multiplier is 1.0. Facility metrics are off by default (ENABLE_FACILITY_METRICS=false), so an unknown ambient is the common case.
The multiplier at a few ambient temperatures:
Ambient Multiplier unknown (no reading) 1.000 15C 0.909 20C 1.000 25C 1.111 30C 1.250 40C 1.667 45C and above 2.000 Example: the reference node drawing a measured 1160 W at 25C ambient:
measuredPower / nodeTdp = 1160 / 2320 = 0.5 tempMultiplier = 1 / max(0.5, 1 - (25 - 20) * 0.02) = 1 / 0.9 = 1.111 coolingStress = 0.5 * 1.111 * 100 = 55.6 The same node with an unknown ambient temperature scores 0.5 * 1.0 * 100 = 50.0.
Why this model It is an algebraic proxy. It avoids CFD or thermal RC simulation and runs in O(1) per node. It is deliberately conservative (it overestimates stress relative to real cooling capacity) because its job is to provide a ranking signal for the scheduler, not an exact thermal prediction.
Power headroom Power headroom is the fraction of the node’s capped power budget that is still unused:
headroom = min(100, (nodeCappedPower - measuredPower) / nodeCappedPower * 100) It is clamped at 100 at the top but not at the bottom: a node drawing more than its budget scores negative, which ranks it below an idle node instead of tying with one. If nodeCappedPower is 0 (unknown hardware) the score is 100, a neutral value that avoids penalizing nodes the twin knows nothing about.
Example: the reference node (1392 W capped budget) drawing a measured 1160 W:
headroom = (1392 - 1160) / 1392 * 100 = 16.7 Example: the same node drawing 1600 W, over its eco budget:
headroom = (1392 - 1600) / 1392 * 100 = -14.9 The scheduler prefers its own projected headroom, computed from powerMeasurement plus the candidate pod’s marginal watts, and falls back to this predictedPowerHeadroomScore only for a node with no powerMeasurement block.
PSUStress formula PSUStress answers: “how close is this rack to its power supply limit?”
rackPower = rackTotalPowerW, or clusterTotalPowerW when no rack total is known psuStress = clamp(rackPower / 50000 * 100, 0, 100) Term Rationale rackTotalPowerW Sum of estimated power for every node carrying the same joulie.io/rack label. Set only when rack topology is available. clusterTotalPowerW Fallback: total cluster IT power from the facility metrics poller. Used when no rack total is known. 50000 W (50 kW) Reference rack capacity, a shared constant. In a real deployment this would come from per-rack facility data. When neither power figure is available the score is 0. Both come from the facility metrics poller, which is disabled by default, so PSU stress is 0 on a default install.
PSUStress is per-rack when rack topology is available and cluster-wide otherwise. In the cluster-wide case every node reports the same score, which is intentional: a PDU brownout affects every node behind it, not just the one drawing the most power.
The scheduler does not read this score today. It is published for observability and reserved for rack-topology-aware placement.
Example: a rack drawing 30 kW:
psuStress = 30000 / 50000 * 100 = 60 Estimated PUE estimatedPUE = 1.05 + (coolingStress / 100) * 0.35 A node at zero cooling stress reports 1.05 (best-case datacenter overhead) and one at full stress reports 1.40 (stressed cooling, high overhead). It is a restatement of cooling stress on a PUE scale, not an independent measurement, and the scheduler does not read it.
Example: the reference node at cooling stress 55.6 reports 1.05 + 0.556 * 0.35 = 1.24.
How it feeds the scheduler The twin controller runs in the controller manager on each reconcile tick (~1 minute) and writes NodeTwin.status per managed node. The scheduler extender caches these NodeTwin CRs with a 30-second TTL and uses them in its filter and score logic:
twin controller (controller manager) → writes NodeTwin.status → scheduler extender cache (30s TTL) → filter: rejects eco and draining nodes for performance pods → score: headroomScore*0.7 + (100-coolingStress)*0.15 + trendBonus + profileBonus + pressureRelief Of the twin’s outputs, the scheduler reads schedulableClass, predictedCoolingStressScore, the whole powerMeasurement block, and predictedPowerHeadroomScore as a fallback. predictedPsuStressScore and estimatedPUE are not part of the score.
This keeps scheduling decisions lightweight (one cache lookup per node per scheduling attempt) while reflecting the latest thermal and power state of the cluster.
How it feeds the controller manager The twin also drives controller manager decisions:
Transition guard: when a node is transitioning from performance to eco, the twin sets schedulableClass to draining until all performance pods have completed or been drained. Governor fields A governor is a dimension of its own, separate from caps: one vendor-neutral preset per component, which the agent maps to the native settings of the node’s cpufreq driver or GPU family. Only pkg/governor turns a preset into a native word; every other component speaks presets, listed in pkg/api/governor.go.
Field Type Owner Description spec.cpu.governor.preset performance, balanced, efficiency Controller manager the CPU governor of every cpufreq policy: highest frequency at any load, demand-driven with a quick ramp, or demand-driven with an energy bias spec.cpu.governor.boost on, off, optional Controller manager frequency boost (turbo); absent leaves it as it is spec.gpu.governor.preset auto, sustained, efficient, low, peak Controller manager the GPU clock governor of every GPU: vendor default, data-path clocks held at their maximum with idle gating kept, compute clock under a ceiling, every clock at its minimum, every clock at its maximum with idle gating off spec.gpu.governor.computeClockCeilingPctOfMax number in (0, 100] Controller manager the compute clock ceiling of efficient, in percent of the maximum compute clock status.controlStatus.cpuGovernor, status.controlStatus.gpuGovernor ControlResult Agent outcome of the last governor write: backend (cpufreq, amdgpu-sysfs, nvidia-smi), result, message, and applied, the native setting in effect NodeHardware.status.cpu.governor object Agent driver, driverMode, current, available, epp, boost (state on or off; scope global for cpufreq/boost, per-cpu for each policy’s boost, no-turbo for the inverted intel_pstate/no_turbo), presets (each with the result it gives, applied or equivalent), baseline, writable NodeHardware.status.gpu.governor object Agent mechanism, current, presets, clockRangesMHz (graphics, memory, fabric), baseline (per GPU, keyed by PCI bus id), writable, uniform A preset a node cannot express is left out of its presets. Beside the governor block the agent publishes the cpufreq frequency landmarks in NodeHardware.status.cpu.landmarks (minFreqMHz, nominalFreqMHz, maxBoostMHz).
kubectl get nodetwins shows the presets in the columns CPU-Gov and GPU-Gov; an empty column means no preset, so the agent changes nothing there, or puts back its baseline if it changed something earlier.
The controller manager writes the presets only with GOVERNOR_CONTROL on, and the agent writes the native settings only with GOVERNOR_WRITES on; both are off by default (see Governor presets and Governor control). When a preset disappears, or writes are turned off, the agent puts back the baseline it recorded and reports restored.
The result values are applied, applied-unverified, equivalent, unsupported, not-applied, refused, drift, contended, disabled, restored and error. ControlResult is shared with the cap results, so the CRD does not enumerate them.
The twin reads none of these fields: a governor moves measured power, which the twin already reads through measuredNodePowerW.
Implementation The twin is implemented in pkg/controller/twin/twin.go. Key types and functions:
Input: everything needed to compute twin state for one node (hardware, profile, cap percentages, measured power, power trend, facility and topology signals). Output: the computed NodeTwin.status fields. Compute(Input) Output: the main computation function. Derives TDP and capped budgets, then calls the helpers below. computePowerHeadroom, computeCoolingStress, computePSUStress: the three score formulas. There is no cooling model interface and no alternative cooling implementation. Cooling stress is the single closed-form expression above; replacing it with a higher-fidelity thermal model means changing computeCoolingStress.
What to read next Scheduler Extender Joulie Controller Manager CRD and Policy Model Hardware Modeling: reference power profiles used by NodeHardware and the twin’s TDP derivation

hwcalib fit (simulator/cmd/hwcalib, package simulator/pkg/calib) fits the physics of a hardware profile to a sweep measured on one of your nodes, and writes the result as a local profile the simulator loads from SIM_PROFILES_DIR. The builtin profiles keep vendor figures and placeholders; a calibrated profile replaces them with what your machine draws. hwcalib sweep records such a sweep on the node itself (see Recording on the node).
Recording a sweep A sweep holds the node at a series of setpoints and records, at every sample, the node’s readings and the setpoints it held. Each setpoint should last long enough to settle: the fit drops the start of every setpoint (see Segments and steady windows) and needs at least 5 samples after that, so with a 2 s sample period a setpoint of 22 s or more is enough.
The readings use the names the simulator emits (see Simulator Metrics):
What Name Used for CPU package and DRAM power hw.energy (preferred) or hw.power, with hw.id cpu<socket> or memory<socket> and hw.type CPU and DRAM fit GPU power and load hw.energy or hw.power with hw.type=gpu, hw.gpu.utilization GPU fit Host power hw.host.energy or hw.host.power platform power CPU frequency hw.cpu.speed and hw.cpu.speed.limit with hw.limit_type=max CPU fit, frequency ramp Power limits joulie.hw.power.limit, points requested and enforced capped samples, limit settling CPU load system.cpu.utilization{cpu.mode=idle}, per logical CPU with cpu.logical_number or for the whole host CPU fit Setpoints joulie.calibration.setpoint, one point per knob segments No common exporter emits hw.energy{hw.type=cpu} from RAPL today, so the sweep comes from a collector on the node that reads powercap energy_uj (which needs root, as the file is mode 0400), such as hwcalib sweep, or from a converter of another exporter’s output.
Utilization is one minus the idle share. Per logical CPU, it is mapped to packages by the profile’s topology (socket-major-smt-last: CPU k sits on package (k mod sockets x cores) / cores). Without system.cpu.utilization, the cpu.utilization setpoint stands in for it.
Setpoints joulie.calibration.setpoint carries one point per knob the sweep holds, at every sample. Its unit is {setpoint}, because each knob has its own:
joulie.calibration.knob Value cpu.utilization busy fraction of every logical CPU, 0 to 1 cpu.frequency.max scaling_max_freq written to every cpufreq policy, in Hz cpu.power.limit package limit written to every package (RAPL PL1 or the HSMP socket cap), in W gpu.utilization busy fraction of every GPU, 0 to 1 gpu.power.limit limit written to every GPU, in W A utilization knob also carries joulie.calibration.class, the class of the load as the simulator’s power models name it (such as cpu.compute_bound or gpu.memory_bound; empty for the default weights), and joulie.calibration.memory_intensity, 0 to 1. The GPU fit inverts the model at that class, so record it.
File formats The default input is OTLP JSON Lines: one MetricsData object per line, as the OpenTelemetry file exporter writes them. Int64 values and times may be strings or numbers, sums may be cumulative or delta, and a counter that falls or restarts its series is a reset whose interval is dropped. The resource names the node in k8s.node.name or host.name; -node picks it when the file holds several.
-format csv reads one node with the same names: a header row, then one row per point. The columns are time_unix_nano, metric, value (required), unit and start_time_unix_nano (optional), and every other column is a point attribute named by its header: hw.id, hw.type, hw.limit_type, cpu.logical_number, cpu.mode, joulie.calibration.knob, joulie.calibration.class, joulie.calibration.memory_intensity, and joulie.hw.limit.state when the sweep has limit points. An empty cell is an absent attribute. A value must be a finite number; NaN or Inf is an error naming its line, so leave out a reading the collector missed rather than write it as NaN. Counters are the metrics the name table registers as counters, with cumulative values.
Recording on the node with hwcalib sweep hwcalib sweep holds the node’s CPUs at each setpoint of a grid and writes the sweep as OTLP JSON Lines that hwcalib fit reads as they are. Run it on the node, as root, with nothing else running there (drain the node first): reading energy_uj needs root since Linux commit 949dd0104c49 made it mode 0400, writing limits needs root, and other work would disturb both the load and the readings.
go build -o hwcalib ./simulator/cmd/hwcalib sudo ./hwcalib sweep -node <node> -write-limits -freq-max-mhz 2400,1900,1500 -out sweep.jsonl ./hwcalib fit -profile amd-epyc-2s-energy-only -node <node> sweep.jsonl The load is one thread per logical CPU that /proc/stat lists, each locked to its OS thread and pinned to its CPU (sched_setaffinity), busy for the setpoint’s share of every -duty-period and asleep for the rest. It spins on registers with no memory traffic, so the setpoint records no joulie.calibration.class (the models’ default weights) and memory intensity 0. The grid nests power limits outermost, then frequency ceilings, then loads; each setpoint lasts -hold and is sampled every -period, the first sample one period in.
It writes to the host only with -write-limits: scaling_max_freq of every cpufreq policy for -freq-max-mhz, and for -power-limit-w the limit of every package, the HSMP power1_cap of each socket when the amd_hsmp_hwmon devices are present, else the long_term constraint of each RAPL package zone. Without -write-limits, either list is a usage error. Every file it wrote is put back as it was found when the sweep ends, also on an error, SIGINT, SIGTERM or SIGHUP, so a dropped SSH session does not leave the node capped. Under nohup a hangup stays ignored and the sweep goes on.
Reading Read from Written as Package energy energy_uj of each package-N zone of the intel-rapl control type (its package-N-die-M zones summed when it has no package zone), a wrap at max_energy_range_uj counted hw.energy{hw.id=cpuN, hw.type=cpu}, cumulative from the sweep’s start DRAM energy energy_uj of the dram child of each package zone hw.energy{hw.id=memoryN, hw.type=memory, hw.parent=cpuN} Socket power power1_input of each amd_hsmp_hwmon device, socket by socket in hwmon order hw.power{hw.id=cpuN, hw.type=cpu} Package limit HSMP power1_cap, or the RAPL long_term power_limit_uw of an enabled zone joulie.hw.power.limit, point enforced, and requested once the sweep wrote a limit Frequency scaling_cur_freq, scaling_max_freq and cpuinfo_max_freq of the policies of each package hw.cpu.speed, hw.cpu.speed.limit points throttled and max CPU load the idle share of each cpuN line of /proc/stat system.cpu.utilization{cpu.mode=idle} with cpu.logical_number Setpoints the setpoint held joulie.calibration.setpoint A CPU’s package is its topology/physical_package_id, else the physical id of /proc/cpuinfo, which also gives hw.vendor and hw.model. Core, uncore and psys zones are never read, since none is a package or DRAM. GPUs are not swept: the load is CPU only. Host power is not read either, since no kernel file measures the whole host; the platform fit needs hw.host.energy or hw.host.power, which a converter can add from a BMC or a metered PDU. The resource has service.name=hwcalib, service.namespace=joulie, and service.instance.id and host.name set to -node; the scope is github.com/matbun/joulie/simulator/pkg/calib, and both carry the pinned schemaUrl.
Flag Default Meaning -node the host name the node name in the resource, which hwcalib fit -node picks -util 0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,1 the loads, busy fractions of every CPU -freq-max-mhz (none) the scaling_max_freq ceilings, in MHz; needs -write-limits -power-limit-w (none) the package power limits, in W; needs -write-limits -write-limits false allow writing frequency ceilings and power limits -hold 30s how long each setpoint lasts -period 2s the sample period -duty-period 100ms the period of the duty-cycled load -sys-root, -proc-root /sys, /proc the trees to read and write; the load still runs on this machine’s CPUs -out - the file to write, - for standard output; an existing file is never replaced It exits 0 when the sweep completes, 1 when the host cannot be read, a file cannot be written or the sweep is interrupted (the lines written so far stay whole, and a file with no sample is removed), and 2 on a usage error. The tests run it over an emulated node’s tree, with the emulated node in place of the load, and fit the result back to the profile (CB11).
Running a fit go build -o hwcalib ./simulator/cmd/hwcalib export SIM_PROFILES_DIR=/srv/joulie/profiles # outside any clone of this repository ./hwcalib fit -profile amd-epyc-2s-energy-only -node <node> sweep.jsonl Flag Default Meaning -profile (required) the profile the node is described by: a builtin, or a local one in SIM_PROFILES_DIR. It gives the topology, the settling times that size the steady windows, and the value of every parameter the sweep cannot fit -node (the only node) the node whose resource to read -format otlp otlp or csv -out-dir SIM_PROFILES_DIR where to write the fitted profile -name <profile>-measured the fitted profile’s name and file name -substep 0 the fixed physics substep of a simulated source, such as 100ms; 0 for hardware The input file may be - for standard input. The command prints one row per parameter (base value, fitted value, method, samples behind it, or why it was not fitted), then notes on what it assumed. It exits 0 on success, 1 when the sweep cannot be read or fitted or the profile cannot be written, and 2 on a usage error.
What is fitted Parameter Method physics.cpu.idlePkgW mean package power below 2 % utilization physics.cpu.maxPkgW, alphaUtil, betaFreq least squares of ln(P - idle) on [1, ln(U x activity), ln F] for the analytic model P = idle + (max - idle) (U x activity)^alpha F^beta, where F is hw.cpu.speed over the hardware maximum and activity the model’s memory intensity factor; packages are pooled physics.dram.wattsPerSocket mean DRAM power per socket physics.platform.otherW mean of host power minus every component over the idle segments (every package and GPU below 2 %); unmeasured DRAM counts with the base value physics.gpu.idleW mean GPU power below 2 % utilization physics.gpu.naturalMaxW the board model inverted at the recorded class and memory intensity: P - idle = (max - idle) x shape(U), least squares through the origin physics.cpu.freqRampMS, physics.hsmp.settleTauMS, physics.gpu.capSettleTauMS the decay of hw.cpu.speed and of the enforced joulie.hw.power.limit after setpoint steps Beta is not fitted when the sweep held one frequency (var(ln F) near 0, as under acpi-cpufreq powersave) or when frequency followed load (|corr(ln U, ln F)| > 0.95, as under intel_pstate powersave): the two exponents cannot be told apart, so the base beta stands (a base beta of 0 counts as 1, as in the model) and the fit solves alpha and the maximum with it. Sweep cpu.frequency.max under the performance governor to fit beta. Alpha and beta must lie in (0.3, 3). Samples drawing 98 % or more of their enforced limit are capped and left out of the CPU and GPU fits.
The GPU inversion matters: a full-load gpu.compute_bound GPU at memory intensity 0 draws only idle + 0.958 of its range (weights 0.88 compute and 0.12 memory, the memory curve reaching 0.65), so the raw full-load mean understates the natural maximum. A profile fitted to a CPU model other than analytic switches to analytic, since the fitted facts describe that model.
RAPL PL1 settling is reported but never written, because physics.rapl.settleTau is a plain setting without provenance.
Segments and steady windows The sweep is split where any setpoint changes: knob, value, class or memory intensity. Each segment drops max(10 s, 3 x the base profile’s largest settling time) after its first sample, per domain (frequency ramp, HSMP and RAPL windows for the CPU; limit settling and the telemetry window for the GPU), and is used only when at least 5 samples remain. Counters give the mean power over that window from their increments; gauges their mean.
Settling times and the substep correction A settling time comes from the samples after a setpoint change: ln|v - final| falls on a line of slope -1/tau_eff, fitted until the response comes within 0.1 % of the step. The samples must be faster than the settling time; a step that settles within one or two samples is not fitted.
The simulator moves a limit or a frequency by one Euler step (target - v) x h/tau per substep h, which decays like exp(-t/tau_eff) with exp(-h/tau_eff) = 1 - h/tau. For such a source, -substep applies tau = h / (1 - exp(-h/tau_eff)): a GPU limit of tau 150 ms under the 100 ms substep shows tau_eff = 91 ms. Hardware settles continuously; leave -substep at 0 there.
The fitted profile The fit is written as <name>.yaml, a local profile that extends the base and holds only what the sweep measured: a source sweep of kind measured, whose ref names the input file and node, and each fitted fact with the provenance measured:sweep#<fit>, where <fit> is cpu-idle, cpu-ols, dram-mean, platform-idle, gpu-idle, gpu-inversion, cpu-frequency-step, cpu-limit-step or gpu-limit-step. Powers are rounded to 0.01 W, exponents to 0.001 and settling times to whole milliseconds.
Outside the repository only. A directory inside this repository (any directory under a go.mod of module github.com/matbun/joulie, by its own path or through a link) is refused before the fit starts, and there is no override: a measured profile may name the machine it was measured on, and it belongs to your site, in SIM_PROFILES_DIR. Never replaced. An existing file of that name is an error; remove it or pick another -name. Checked. The profile is loaded back with the others of its directory (hwemu.LoadProfileSet) and removed when it does not load. A local base profile must therefore live in the output directory too. Point the simulator at the directory with SIM_PROFILES_DIR and name the profile in a cluster spec pool, as for any local profile (see Configuration Reference).

body:
This page documents the controller policy algorithms implemented in pkg/controller/policy/.
Use this page after:
CRD and Policy Model Joulie Controller Manager Classification Input Policy demand classification is derived from the joulie.io/workload-class pod annotation:
performance: pod carries joulie.io/workload-class: performance. standard (default): no annotation or joulie.io/workload-class: standard. Shared Reconcile Flow Each reconcile tick:
Select eligible nodes from NODE_SELECTOR, excluding reserved and unschedulable nodes. Build a hardware view from NodeHardware when available, otherwise from node labels/inventory fallback. Build a desired plan with the selected policy. Apply downgrade guard (sets NodeTwin.status.schedulableClass to draining while blocking pods still run). Write NodeTwin.spec and update the joulie.io/power-profile node label. In other words, static_partition and queue_aware_v1 decide how many nodes stay in performance, and the per-family split below decides which nodes those are.
Performance Node Selection static_partition and queue_aware_v1 compute a performance slot count hp_count and pass it to policy.PerformanceSet:
Group the eligible nodes into hardware families (policy.NodeFamily): gpu:<model> when the node has GPUs, otherwise cpu:<model>. Raise hp_count to the number of families and cap it at the number of nodes. Give every family one slot. Each further slot goes to the family with the largest size / (2 * slots + 1), ties to the smaller family key (the Sainte-Lague divisor method). A family never gets more slots than it has nodes. Within a family, fill the slots with nodes whose current joulie.io/power-profile label is performance first, then by node name. Properties:
every family keeps performance capacity in proportion to its size, and at least one node, house monotone: when hp_count changes by one, exactly one node changes profile, a reconcile at constant demand moves no node, because nodes already in performance are kept first, the result does not depend on the order of the input node list. Example: the exp02 5k inventory (experiments/02-heterogeneous-benchmark/configs/cluster-nodes-5k.yaml, 5000 nodes in 8 families) with 1000 performance slots (STATIC_HP_FRAC=0.2) keeps a fifth of every family in performance:
Family Nodes Performance h100-nvl 1450 290 h100-sxm 730 146 l40s 850 170 mi300x 240 48 w7900 730 146 cpu-highcore 250 50 cpu-highfreq 250 50 cpu-intensive 500 100 TestPerformanceSetMatchesDocumentedExp02Split in pkg/controller/policy/policy_test.go pins this split. The standalone simulator calls the same policy.PerformanceSet.
The controller manager exports the split after the downgrade guard as joulie_policy_family_nodes{family} and joulie_policy_family_performance_nodes{family}, so a draining node counts as not performance.
static_partition Goal: deterministic fixed HP/LP split.
Inputs:
N: number of eligible nodes. STATIC_HP_FRAC: target fraction of high-performance nodes. Algorithm:
hp_count = round(N * STATIC_HP_FRAC). Pick the performance nodes with the per-family split, which raises hp_count to the number of families and caps it at N. Remaining nodes -> eco. Properties:
deterministic, stable over time unless node set changes. keeps about STATIC_HP_FRAC of every hardware family in performance, and at least one node per family. This policy is exercised in the CPU-Only Benchmark and Heterogeneous GPU Cluster Benchmark.
queue_aware_v1 Goal: adapt HP count to current performance-only pressure.
Inputs:
N: number of eligible nodes. P: count of performance-sensitive pods cluster-wide that are running or pending, so performance pods still waiting for a node raise the demand. Every Pending performance pod counts, including one that more performance nodes would not help (an unsatisfiable constraint, an image pull); QUEUE_HP_MAX bounds the effect. The downgrade guard counts running pods only. QUEUE_HP_BASE_FRAC QUEUE_HP_MIN QUEUE_HP_MAX QUEUE_PERF_PER_HP_NODE Algorithm:
base = round(N * QUEUE_HP_BASE_FRAC). need = ceil(P / QUEUE_PERF_PER_HP_NODE). hp_count = max(base, need). Clamp hp_count to [QUEUE_HP_MIN, QUEUE_HP_MAX]. Pick the performance nodes with the per-family split, which raises hp_count to the number of families and caps it at N. Remaining nodes -> eco. Properties:
deterministic for a fixed (N, P) and the current profile labels, monotonic in pressure P, bounded by min/max limits, except that every family keeps at least one performance node, heterogeneous-aware because slots follow family size, and a change of hp_count by one moves exactly one node. This policy is exercised in the CPU-Only Benchmark and Heterogeneous GPU Cluster Benchmark.
rule_swap_v1 (debug policy) Goal: force visible state transitions for debugging.
Algorithm:
Compute phase from wall-clock and RECONCILE_INTERVAL. Alternate which of the first two eligible nodes, in node-name order, is assigned eco. Others remain performance. This policy is intended for debugging only, not as default production behavior.
Downgrade Guard When the planned profile of a node is eco:
Count active performance pods on that node. If count > 0: keep desired profile as eco, set NodeTwin.status.schedulableClass to draining, write the performance caps in NodeTwin.spec until those pods finish, so they are not throttled; this holds for a node leaving performance and for one already in eco that runs a performance pod, record transition as deferred in controller manager FSM/metrics. If count == 0: keep desired profile eco, set NodeTwin.status.schedulableClass to eco. The scheduler extender reads schedulableClass and filters draining nodes out for performance pods, as it does eco nodes, so no new performance work lands on a node during the transition. Standard pods are not filtered.

body:
Joulie ships a scheduler extender that steers workloads toward appropriate nodes based on power profile, thermal stress, and hardware capabilities.
How a pod gets scheduled (end-to-end) When a new pod is created in the cluster, the following sequence occurs:
1. Pod created (e.g., kubectl apply, Job controller, Deployment rollout) | 2. kube-scheduler picks up the unscheduled pod | 3. kube-scheduler runs its default filters (resource fits, taints, affinity) | 4. kube-scheduler calls Joulie's /filter endpoint | - Sends: pod spec + candidate node list | - Joulie reads pod annotation joulie.io/workload-class | - Performance pods: reject nodes with schedulableClass = eco or draining | - Standard pods: pass all nodes | - Returns: filtered node list + rejection reasons | 5. kube-scheduler calls Joulie's /prioritize endpoint | - Sends: pod spec + surviving node list | - Joulie reads NodeTwin CRs (cached, 30s TTL) for power state | - Joulie reads NodeHardware CRs (cached, 30s TTL) for hardware specs | - Joulie extracts pod CPU/GPU requests for marginal power estimation | - Joulie scores each node 0-100 using the scoring formula | - Returns: list of (node, score) pairs | 6. kube-scheduler combines Joulie scores with its own plugin scores | 7. Pod is bound to the highest-scoring node The extender participates in steps 4 and 5 only. It does not replace the Kubernetes scheduler; it extends it with energy-aware filter and scoring logic.
What the extender reads Source CRD What it provides Cache TTL Digital twin output NodeTwin.status schedulableClass, headroom, cooling stress, power measurement (measured/capped/TDP/trend) 30s Hardware discovery NodeHardware.status CPU cores, CPU max watts, GPU count, GPU max watts, memory 30s Pod spec (from kube-scheduler request) joulie.io/workload-class annotation, container CPU/GPU resource requests per-request What the extender does NOT do It does not execute a full digital twin simulation per scheduling decision. It does not perform live pod migration or eviction. It does not override Kubernetes resource fits; it only participates in the extender filter/prioritize hooks. It does not make admission decisions for already-running pods. Decisions are lightweight: one cache lookup per node per scheduling attempt.
Why a scheduler component is needed Kubernetes scheduling decisions are made before a pod is running. That is the right place to enforce Joulie’s power-profile intent, because:
placing a performance workload on an eco (capped) node defeats energy savings and violates workload SLOs, placing any workload on a node under heavy thermal stress increases the risk of throttling and headroom violations, the joulie.io/workload-class annotation is the single source of truth for placement intent; the extender enforces it without requiring users to write complex scheduling rules. What Joulie implements: scheduler extender Joulie implements an HTTP-based scheduler extender, not an in-tree plugin.
The extender registers with kube-scheduler through a KubeSchedulerConfiguration extender block. The scheduler calls the extender’s HTTP endpoints as part of the normal scheduling cycle:
filter (POST /filter): rejects nodes that are incompatible with the pod, prioritize (POST /prioritize): ranks remaining nodes by suitability. The extender does not replace the Kubernetes scheduler. It runs as a lightweight HTTP service and participates in the existing scheduling cycle.
The scheduler extender is always deployed as part of Joulie. Without it, pods run anywhere and get standard Kubernetes scheduling.
Filter logic (step 4) The extender applies one hard rule: performance pods are rejected from eco and draining nodes.
A pod is treated as performance if it carries joulie.io/workload-class: performance.
For such pods, the extender rejects any node whose NodeTwin.status has schedulableClass set to "eco" or "draining". A label-based fallback also rejects nodes with joulie.io/power-profile: eco when no NodeTwin status is present.
Standard pods (the default, or joulie.io/workload-class: standard) pass the filter unconditionally. Unknown nodes (no NodeTwin state) are allowed for all pod classes.
Score logic (step 5) After filtering, the extender scores remaining nodes. Each node receives a score from 0 to 100. Higher scores are better. kube-scheduler uses these scores (combined with its own plugin scores) to pick the winning node.
Scoring inputs per node For each candidate node, the extender gathers:
Power measurement from NodeTwin.status.powerMeasurement:
measuredNodePowerW: measured node power draw, the CPU packages plus the GPUs by default, which the controller manager reads from Prometheus (OpenTelemetry hw.* metrics or Kepler) or an HTTP endpoint, or 0 with NODE_POWER_SOURCE=static (see Digital Twin) nodeCappedPowerW: the node’s current power budget (sum of CPU + GPU caps) nodeTdpW: thermal design power (maximum possible draw) powerTrendWPerMin: rolling derivative of power draw (watts/minute, positive = rising) Twin-computed scores from NodeTwin.status:
predictedPowerHeadroomScore: fallback headroom if no power measurement is available predictedCoolingStressScore: thermal stress (0 = cool, 100 = at cooling limit) schedulableClass: performance, eco, or draining Pod resource demand extracted from the pod’s container specs:
CPU cores requested (summed across all containers) GPU count requested (from nvidia.com/gpu or amd.com/gpu limits) Node hardware from NodeHardware.status:
CPU model, total cores, max watts per socket GPU model, count, max watts per GPU Marginal power estimation Before scoring, the extender estimates how many additional watts this specific pod will add to the node. This makes the score pod-specific: the same node scores differently for a lightweight 2-core pod vs. an 8-GPU training pod.
The estimation uses powerest.EstimateMarginalImpact:
podMarginalW = CPUUtilCoeff * (podCPUCores / nodeTotalCores) * nodeMaxCPUWatts + GPUUtilCoeff * (podGPUCount / nodeGPUCount) * nodeMaxGPUWatts Coefficients are tunable via environment variables (MARGINAL_CPU_UTIL_COEFF, MARGINAL_GPU_UTIL_COEFF_STANDARD, MARGINAL_GPU_UTIL_COEFF_PERFORMANCE). GPU coefficients differ by workload class because performance workloads typically drive GPUs harder.
Scoring formula projectedPower = measuredPower + podMarginalPower headroomScore = (cappedPower - projectedPower) / cappedPower * 100 coolingStress = from NodeTwin.status.predictedCoolingStressScore (0-100) clusterTrend = sum of all per-node powerTrend (W/min) trendScale = 2.0 if |clusterTrend| > 500 else 6.0 trendBonus = -clamp(powerTrend / trendScale, -25, 25) score = headroomScore * 0.7 + (100 - coolingStress) * 0.15 + trendBonus + profileBonus + pressureRelief Each component explained:
Component Weight Range What it does headroomScore * 0.7 70% can go negative to +70 Favors nodes with room in their power budget after this pod is placed. Can go negative if the pod would exceed the budget, so the node is penalized, not just zeroed. (100 - coolingStress) * 0.15 15% 0 to +15 Penalizes thermally stressed nodes. At coolingStress=0 (cool), contributes 15 points. At coolingStress=100, contributes 0. trendBonus ±25 pts -25 to +25 Rewards nodes whose power draw is falling (trend < 0), penalizes nodes whose power is rising (trend > 0). Uses adaptive scaling: trendScale=6.0 at steady state (amplifies signal), trendScale=2.0 during cluster-wide bursts (|clusterTrend| > 500 W/min). profileBonus +10 pts 0 or +10 Standard pods on eco nodes get +10, steering non-critical work toward energy-saving nodes. pressureRelief up to -30 pts -30 to 0 Standard pods on performance nodes are penalized when performance nodes are congested (see below). Example: A node with 600W capped power, 300W measured, pod adds 50W, cooling stress 20, power trend flat:
headroomScore = (600 - 350) / 600 * 100 = 41.7 score = 41.7 0.7 + (100 - 20) 0.15 + 0 = 29.2 + 12.0 = 41.2 Example: An ideal node (empty, fully uncapped, cool, standard pod on eco):
headroomScore = 100, coolingStress = 0, trendBonus = 0, profileBonus = 10 score = 100 0.7 + 100 0.15 + 0 + 10 = 70 + 15 + 10 = 95 Projected headroom (the key innovation) Unlike simple utilization-based scheduling, Joulie computes headroom relative to the node’s capped power budget (not TDP or max capacity), and it subtracts the pod’s estimated marginal power before scoring:
projectedPower = measuredPower + podMarginalPower headroomScore = (cappedPower - projectedPower) / cappedPower * 100 This means:
Eco nodes (capped at, say, 60%) have a lower cappedPower, so they run out of headroom sooner and are naturally deprioritized for heavy workloads. GPU-heavy pods consume more marginal watts, so nodes near their cap are penalized more for GPU pods than CPU-only pods. headroomScore can go negative: if the pod would push the node over its cap, the score goes below zero. After the formula is applied and clamped to [0, 100], such nodes get score 0 and are effectively last-choice. If power measurement data is unavailable (no powerMeasurement in NodeTwin status), the extender falls back to the twin-computed predictedPowerHeadroomScore.
Stale twin fallback If the NodeTwin’s lastUpdated timestamp is older than 5 minutes (configurable via TWIN_STALENESS_THRESHOLD), the node receives a neutral score of 50. This prevents stale data from a controller manager that may have stopped updating from influencing placement. Nodes with no lastUpdated timestamp at all are also treated as stale. Nodes with no NodeTwin state at all also receive 50.
Adaptive performance pressure relief For standard pods on performance nodes, a pressure penalty is applied:
if workloadClass == "standard" AND schedulableClass == "performance": score -= perfPressure * 0.3 Where perfPressure is computed once per scoring batch as the average congestion across all performance nodes:
perfPressure = average(100 - headroom) across all non-stale performance nodes At full saturation (perfPressure = 100), this subtracts up to 30 points from the score on performance nodes. The effect steers standard pods toward eco nodes when performance nodes are congested, preserving performance capacity for performance-class workloads.
When performance nodes are idle (perfPressure = 0), there is no penalty and standard pods spread normally.
Experimental validation The scoring formula was validated in Experiment 04: Scoring Formula Validation across 2,500 nodes and 8 random seeds, confirming 6.4% IT energy reduction and 13% fewer dropped jobs versus standard Kubernetes bin-packing.
Score clamping All scores are clamped to [0, 100] before being returned to kube-scheduler.
PUE The scheduler extender does not weight marginal power by PUE. NodeTwin.status.estimatedPUE is derived from the node’s predicted cooling stress (1.05 at no stress, 1.40 at full stress), is reserved for future use, and no score reads it. Facility metrics (ENABLE_FACILITY_METRICS=true on the controller manager) reach the score through the cooling stress term instead: the twin scales cooling stress with the most local ambient temperature it reads, so a node in a warm zone scores lower for the same power. The measured PUE, (IT power + cooling power) / IT power, is logged by the controller manager and can be plotted from joulie_twin_facility_*.
Summary Condition Effect Performance pod + eco/draining node Hard reject (filter) Standard pod + any node Allowed (no filter) Unknown node (no NodeTwin) + any pod Allowed, neutral score (50) High headroom, low cooling stress, falling power trend High score Low headroom (pod would exceed cap) Low score (headroomScore goes negative) Standard pod + eco node +10 bonus (profile steering) Standard pod + performance node under pressure Score penalty up to -30 via pressureRelief Stale or missing NodeTwin Neutral score (50) Heavy pod (high CPU/GPU) on nearly-full node Low score (marginal power eats headroom) Light pod on same node Higher score (less marginal power) Environment variables Variable Default Purpose EXTENDER_ADDR :9876 HTTP listen address CACHE_TTL 30s Minimum interval between rebuilding the scoring maps from the informer cache TWIN_STALENESS_THRESHOLD 5m Max age of NodeTwin data before treating as stale MARGINAL_CPU_UTIL_COEFF (from powerest.DefaultCoefficients) CPU marginal power coefficient MARGINAL_GPU_UTIL_COEFF_STANDARD (from powerest.DefaultCoefficients) GPU marginal power coefficient for standard pods MARGINAL_GPU_UTIL_COEFF_PERFORMANCE (from powerest.DefaultCoefficients) GPU marginal power coefficient for performance pods Debug endpoint The extender exposes GET /debug/scoring which returns the current scoring state for all nodes as JSON:
{ "coefficients": {"cpuUtilCoeff": 0.8, "gpuUtilCoeffStandard": 0.6, "gpuUtilCoeffPerformance": 0.9}, "nodes": [ { "nodeName": "node-0", "schedulableClass": "performance", "headroom": 72.5, "coolingStress": 31.3, "measuredPowerW": 450.0, "cappedPowerW": 1200.0, "nodeTdpW": 2000.0, "powerTrendWPerMin": -5.2, "baseScore": 60.0, "cpuTotalCores": 128, "cpuMaxWattsTotal": 700.0, "gpuCount": 8, "gpuMaxWattsPerGpu": 400.0, "hasGpu": true, "stale": false } ] } This endpoint is useful for debugging scoring decisions without needing to trigger an actual scheduling event.
How to deploy The scheduler extender is deployed as part of the Joulie Helm chart.
KubeSchedulerConfiguration extender block apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1 kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration profiles: - schedulerName: default-scheduler extenders: - urlPrefix: "http://joulie-scheduler-extender.joulie-system.svc.cluster.local:9876" filterVerb: "filter" prioritizeVerb: "prioritize" weight: 1 enableHTTPS: false nodeCacheCapable: false ignorable: true Setting ignorable: true means the scheduler proceeds normally if the extender is temporarily unreachable.
Testing The extender exposes a /healthz endpoint.
To verify filter decisions without a running scheduler:
curl -s -X POST \ http://localhost:9876/filter \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"pod": {...}, "nodes": {"items": [...]}}' What to read next Digital Twin Pod Compatibility Joulie Controller Manager

body:
The simulator publishes three kinds of telemetry:
Prometheus metrics about itself at /metrics (joulie_sim_*), for Prometheus to scrape. OpenTelemetry metrics and events about the emulated nodes and the facility, in emulate mode only. Metrics are pushed as OTLP JSON over HTTP; events are written to events.jsonl and pushed when a logs endpoint is set. Compatibility exporters, in emulate mode only: the Prometheus formats of real exporters (Kepler, dcgm-exporter) at /exporters/<name>/metrics, opt-in. The OpenTelemetry names are spelled once, in pkg/otel/semconv, and the controller manager reads the same names back from Prometheus. Their Prometheus spelling is computed by pkg/otel/promname. A contract test (tests/contracts/otel_docs_test.go) fails when this page misses a name of that table, names one the table does not define, or gives a name another unit, instrument, attribute list, severity or Prometheus spelling than the table.
Prometheus metrics at /metrics Endpoint:
path: /metrics address: simulator HTTP listen address (SIM_ADDR, default :18080) Related debug endpoints (non-Prometheus):
/debug/nodes /debug/events /debug/energy /debug/emulate (emulate mode): the latest snapshot of every emulated node and the facility, the values the OpenTelemetry export and the compatibility exporters are computed from HTTP/request metrics joulie_sim_requests_total{route,method,status} (counter) total HTTP requests by route/method/status joulie_sim_request_duration_seconds{route,method} (histogram) request latency Control-path metrics joulie_sim_controls_total{node,action} (counter) received control actions by node/action joulie_sim_control_actions_total{node,action,result} (counter) control action outcomes result: applied|blocked|error Per-node simulated state metrics joulie_sim_node_cap_watts{node} (gauge) current simulated effective cap joulie_sim_node_rapl_cap_watts{node} (gauge) simulated RAPL cap value joulie_sim_node_throttle_pct{node} (gauge) simulated DVFS throttle percent joulie_sim_node_power_watts{node} (gauge) simulated exported node power joulie_sim_node_cpu_util{node} (gauge) simulated CPU utilization joulie_sim_node_freq_scale{node} (gauge) simulated frequency scale joulie_sim_node_running_pods{node} (gauge) running pods observed on the node joulie_sim_node_class_info{node,class} (gauge) class assignment marker (1 on active class) In emulate mode the per-node gauges of an emulated node are set from its snapshot at every tick.
Workload/job metrics joulie_sim_job_submitted_total{class} (counter) jobs submitted by class joulie_sim_job_completed_total{class,node} (counter) jobs completed by class and node joulie_sim_job_completion_seconds (histogram) job completion latency distribution Emulate mode and export metrics joulie_sim_emulate_nodes (gauge) emulated nodes, one per cluster spec member joulie_sim_emulate_tick_duration_seconds (histogram) time one tick takes to step every emulated node joulie_sim_emulate_tick_overruns_total (counter) ticks that took longer than the tick interval; the next tick advances to wall time joulie_sim_emulate_node_step_errors_total{node} (counter) failed steps of one emulated node joulie_sim_otlp_requests_total{signal,result} (counter) OTLP exports by signal (metrics, logs) and result result: success|partial|error|dropped (partial: the receiver rejected some points; dropped: the logs queue was full) joulie_sim_otlp_points_total{signal} (counter) data points and log records the receiver accepted joulie_sim_otlp_dropped_points_total{signal} (counter) values left out of the export because they were NaN, infinite or out of the int64 range joulie_sim_events_total{event} (counter) events emitted, by eventName Notes Prometheus metrics capture online simulator state and request/control behavior. Integrated node/cluster energy totals of the label-modelled nodes are exposed through /debug/energy (JSON), not as Prometheus time series. Emulated nodes export their energy as OpenTelemetry counters (below). Richer thermal and averaged-vs-instantaneous details are currently exposed through the HTTP telemetry/debug endpoints rather than as separate Prometheus gauges. In particular, fields such as instantPackagePowerWatts, cpu.temperatureC, cpu.thermalThrottlePct, and per-device GPU averaged power live in the legacy JSON of /telemetry/{node}?format=legacy (until v0.4.0) and in /debug/nodes. OpenTelemetry metrics (emulate mode) The names follow the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions v1.44.0, and every resource and scope carries schemaUrl: https://opentelemetry.io/schemas/1.44.0. Every hw.* name is at Development stability upstream and may be renamed there; the pin makes such a rename a deliberate change in Joulie. Names no convention covers use the prefix joulie.. Points are cumulative, so Prometheus accepts them without otlp-deltatocumulative. Every pushed point carries the time of the export that sends it, with the values of the newest emulation step, as an OpenTelemetry SDK’s periodic reader stamps the time it collects; a step that has not changed since the last export is sent again at the later time, and counters keep their ledger’s start as startTimeUnixNano. A point stamped with the step’s time would reach Prometheus up to a step old, and rate() would read low (see the pitfalls). The per-node /otlp/telemetry/{node} route keeps the step’s time instead, because its reader derives power from the change between two reads. How they are sent is described under Simulator telemetry export.
Resources Each emulated node is one resource:
Attribute Value service.name OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, default joulie-simulator service.namespace joulie service.instance.id, k8s.node.name, host.name the node name host.id hwemu- followed by the first 32 hex characters of sha256(node name) k8s.cluster.name the cluster spec’s name service.version the simulator’s module version The facility is a resource of its own, with service.instance.id facility and k8s.cluster.name. OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES adds attributes but never overrides service.instance.id, k8s.node.name or host.name. In Prometheus a node’s series get job="joulie/joulie-simulator" and instance="<node>".
Metrics Prometheus names are those of the default translation strategy (UnderscoreEscapingWithSuffixes).
OTel name Unit Instrument Emitted for Point attributes Prometheus name hw.host.energy J Counter (int) a measured host hw.id=host hw_host_energy_joules_total hw.host.power W Gauge a measured host hw.id=host hw_host_power_watts hw.host.ambient_temperature Cel Gauge a measured host: the inlet, which is its cooling zone’s temperature hw.id=host hw_host_ambient_temperature_celsius hw.energy J Counter measured CPU packages, DRAM zones and GPUs hw.id, hw.type, hw.name, hw.parent (memory only) hw_energy_joules_total hw.power W Gauge the same hw.id, hw.type, hw.name, hw.parent (memory only) hw_power_watts hw.cpu.speed Hz Gauge (int) CPU packages with cpufreq hw.id, hw.name, hw.vendor, hw.model hw_cpu_speed_hertz hw.cpu.speed.limit Hz Gauge (int), one point per hw.limit_type: max and throttled the same hw.id, hw.name, hw.vendor, hw.model, hw.limit_type hw_cpu_speed_limit_hertz hw.gpu.utilization 1 Gauge GPUs hw.id, hw.name, hw.vendor, hw.model, hw.gpu.task=general hw_gpu_utilization_ratio joulie.hw.power.limit W Gauge, one point per joulie.hw.limit.state: requested and enforced components with a power limit hw.id, hw.type, joulie.hw.limit.state joulie_hw_power_limit_watts hw.gpu.io By Counter (int), one point per network.io.direction and joulie.hw.gpu.io.path GPUs, on the peer path only: the bytes a GPU received from and sent to the other GPUs of its node. The emulator models no host or network interface bytes, so host and nic have no point. The counters come from the node’s ledger and start at its start hw.id, hw.name, hw.vendor, hw.model, network.io.direction (receive, transmit), joulie.hw.gpu.io.path (peer, host, nic) hw_gpu_io_bytes_total joulie.hw.gpu.speed Hz Gauge (int), one point per joulie.hw.clock.domain GPUs with a clock model, every GPU of the builtin profiles: graphics and memory on NVIDIA, plus fabric and soc on an AMD family whose profile has fclk and socclk tables hw.id, hw.vendor, hw.model, joulie.hw.clock.domain (graphics, memory, fabric, soc) joulie_hw_gpu_speed_hertz joulie.hw.gpu.speed.limit Hz Gauge (int), one point per joulie.hw.clock.domain and hw.limit_type: max and throttled the GPUs and domains of joulie.hw.gpu.speed: max is the domain’s hardware maximum (the top of its pp_dpm_* table, NVML’s maximum clock), throttled the maximum in effect, the clock a busy GPU reaches under the present performance level, overdrive range or clock lock (on NVIDIA at most the sustained maximum) hw.id, hw.vendor, hw.model, joulie.hw.clock.domain, hw.limit_type joulie_hw_gpu_speed_limit_hertz joulie.hw.governor 1 UpDownCounter (int): 1 for the state a component is in, 0 for the one it left CPU packages and GPUs with a governor state: 1 for the state, and 0 for the state the component was in before, sent with every export until the state changes again and dropped by a simulator restart. joulie.hw.governor.preset is empty when no single preset maps to the native state hw.id, hw.type, joulie.hw.governor.preset, joulie.hw.governor.native joulie_hw_governor joulie.facility.ambient_temperature Cel Gauge the facility joulie_facility_ambient_temperature_celsius joulie.facility.it.energy J Counter the facility joulie_facility_it_energy_joules_total joulie.facility.it.power W Gauge the facility joulie_facility_it_power_watts joulie.facility.cooling.energy J Counter the facility joulie_facility_cooling_energy_joules_total joulie.facility.cooling.power W Gauge the facility joulie_facility_cooling_power_watts joulie.facility.pue 1 Gauge the facility; for dashboards, since the controller manager derives PUE itself joulie_facility_pue_ratio joulie.cooling_zone.ambient_temperature Cel Gauge each cooling zone joulie.cooling_zone.name joulie_cooling_zone_ambient_temperature_celsius joulie.rack.energy J Counter each rack joulie.rack.name joulie_rack_energy_joules_total joulie.rack.power W Gauge each rack joulie.rack.name joulie_rack_power_watts The point attributes become the labels hw_id, hw_type, hw_name, hw_parent, hw_vendor, hw_model, hw_limit_type, joulie_hw_limit_state, network_io_direction, joulie_hw_gpu_io_path, joulie_hw_clock_domain, joulie_hw_governor_preset, joulie_hw_governor_native, joulie_cooling_zone_name and joulie_rack_name. The resource attributes k8s_node_name and host_name are always on target_info, and on the data series only when Prometheus promotes them (below).
Components Component hw.id hw.type hw.name Also CPU package cpu<socket> cpu package-<socket> hw.vendor (Intel or AMD) and hw.model on the CPU metrics DRAM zone memory<socket> memory dram hw.parent=cpu<socket> GPU gpu<index> gpu the product name hw.vendor and hw.model on the GPU metrics Host host none Producer rules Whole-host energy is reported only as hw.host.energy, never as hw.energy, so a sum over hw.energy never counts the host twice. hw.host.* points carry no hw.type. One cpu component per package. RAPL core, uncore and psys zones are never cpu. DRAM is memory; Joulie does not count it as node power. Host power is the packages, the DRAM zones, the platform remainder and the GPUs together. Power supply losses are not included. Only readings a real collector could measure are emitted: package and DRAM energy_uj, NVML total energy, amdgpu power. A node whose profile is a virtual machine gets no hw.* metric at all, and a CPU without a DRAM zone gets no memory component. Exported counters never decrease, not even across a simulator restart: they continue from a ledger kept in the tree root, the GPU bytes of hw.gpu.io as well as the energies. While the simulator is down no energy accrues, so a restart shows as a gap in the rate, never as a reset. A counter’s start time is the ledger’s start. Prometheus A Prometheus started with --web.enable-otlp-receiver accepts the push at /api/v1/otlp/v1/metrics. Promote the node identity onto the data series:
otlp: promote_resource_attributes: [k8s.node.name, host.name] translation_strategy: UnderscoreEscapingWithSuffixes storage: tsdb: out_of_order_time_window: 30m Prometheus promotes no attribute by default. Without the promotion a query joins target_info for the node name, which is what the controller manager’s auto mode falls back to; group target_info first, so that a restarted simulator’s second target_info series does not fail the join:
sum by (k8s_node_name) ( rate(hw_energy_joules_total{hw_type=~"cpu|gpu"}[5m]) * on (job, instance) group_left (k8s_node_name) max by (job, instance, k8s_node_name) (target_info) ) instance="<node>" is a convenience of the default setup, not part of the contract; select nodes by k8s_node_name.
rate() under-reads a series younger than its window, so a rate window should cover at least 4 export intervals. Under the other translation strategies the names change:
OTel UnderscoreEscapingWithSuffixes (default) NoUTF8EscapingWithSuffixes UnderscoreEscapingWithoutSuffixes NoTranslation hw.energy (J, counter) hw_energy_joules_total hw.energy_joules_total hw_energy hw.energy hw.host.power (W, gauge) hw_host_power_watts hw.host.power_watts hw_host_power hw.host.power hw.gpu.utilization (1, gauge) hw_gpu_utilization_ratio hw.gpu.utilization_ratio hw_gpu_utilization hw.gpu.utilization label k8s.node.name k8s_node_name "k8s.node.name" k8s_node_name "k8s.node.name" The full table for every name is pkg/otel/promname/testdata/prometheus-names.tsv.
Events (emulate mode) Events are OpenTelemetry log records with an eventName. timeUnixNano is when the change happened in the emulated node, observedTimeUnixNano when the simulator emitted it. The body is only a display string; read the attributes. A record is emitted on its node’s resource, so the node is not an attribute.
They are always appended to events.jsonl in SIM_OTEL_FILE_DIR, one LogsData object per line, and pushed only when a logs endpoint is set. /debug/events and events.ndjson keep their previous format.
eventName Severity When Attributes joulie.sim.node.ready 9 INFO an emulated node’s tree is in place and its first step ran, once per node per start joulie.sim.profile, joulie.sim.pool, joulie.sim.tree.resumed, joulie.sim.tree.added joulie.sim.node.mismatch 13 WARN the Kubernetes Node of a spec node is missing or names another profile; once per change, not once per poll error.type (node_missing, profile_mismatch), joulie.sim.profile, joulie.sim.node.profile joulie.sim.cap.applied 9 INFO a power limit written to a node file took effect, possibly quantized or clamped hw.id, hw.type, joulie.sim.file, joulie.sim.outcome, joulie.sim.value.written, joulie.sim.value.effective joulie.sim.setting.applied 9 INFO another setting took effect, such as a frequency bound or a governor the same joulie.sim.cap.reset 13 WARN a GPU limit went back to its default: persistence mode off and no client the same, with hw.type=gpu; written is the old limit, effective the default joulie.sim.write.rejected 13 WARN a write was reverted the same, and error.type (reverted_out_of_range, parse_error, restored, einval, eopnotsupp, ebusy) joulie.sim.outcome is the emulator’s own name for what happened to the write, such as accepted, clamped, rejected or reset-persistence-off. restored means a file only the emulator writes was overwritten and put back. einval, eopnotsupp and ebusy mean the real driver refuses the value with that errno (outcome rejected): a file tree cannot fail the write itself, so the emulator reverts the value at its next step, and a reader sees its write not applied.
Workload run and scenario names A v1 workload run in emulate mode writes the joulie.sim.* names below to its run directory, <SIM_RUNS_DIR>/<runId>/otlp/ (simulator.metrics.jsonl, a cumulative snapshot every SIM_OTLP_FILE_INTERVAL and one at the end; simulator.logs.jsonl, the run’s and its jobs’ events, with copies of the emulated nodes’ hardware events). The scenario runner writes the joulie.capture.* and joulie.scenario.* names to harness.metrics.jsonl and harness.logs.jsonl next to them. Both are OTLP JSON Lines, one MetricsData or LogsData object per line, in the format of the OpenTelemetry Collector’s file exporter; neither is pushed to the OTLP endpoint, and the joulie_sim_* Prometheus series above are a different set. Every resource of a run carries joulie.sim.run.id. See Workload Scenarios.
OTel name Unit Instrument Point attributes Prometheus name joulie.sim.workload.jobs.submitted {job} Counter (int) joulie.workload.class joulie_sim_workload_jobs_submitted_total joulie.sim.workload.jobs.finished {job} Counter (int) joulie.workload.class, joulie.sim.job.outcome joulie_sim_workload_jobs_finished_total joulie.sim.workload.jobs.active {job} UpDownCounter (int) joulie.workload.class, joulie.sim.job.state joulie_sim_workload_jobs_active joulie.sim.workload.job.duration s Histogram joulie.workload.class joulie_sim_workload_job_duration_seconds joulie.sim.workload.job.queue_wait s Histogram joulie.workload.class joulie_sim_workload_job_queue_wait_seconds joulie.sim.workload.job.slowdown 1 Histogram joulie.workload.class joulie_sim_workload_job_slowdown joulie.sim.workload.work {unit} Counter joulie.workload.class, joulie.sim.work.kind joulie_sim_workload_work_total joulie.sim.workload.energy J Counter joulie.workload.class, hw.type, k8s.node.name, joulie.sim.profile joulie_sim_workload_energy_joules_total joulie.capture.nodetwin.measured_power W Gauge k8s.node.name, joulie.nodetwin.power_source joulie_capture_nodetwin_measured_power_watts joulie.capture.nodetwin.schedulable_class 1 UpDownCounter (int) k8s.node.name, joulie.node.schedulable_class joulie_capture_nodetwin_schedulable_class joulie.capture.nodetwin.control_result 1 UpDownCounter (int) k8s.node.name, hw.type, joulie.nodetwin.control.backend, joulie.nodetwin.control.result joulie_capture_nodetwin_control_result joulie.scenario.assertion.value {value} Gauge joulie.assertion.name, joulie.assertion.source joulie_scenario_assertion_value eventName Severity joulie.sim.run.started, joulie.sim.run.finished, joulie.sim.run.resumed 9 INFO joulie.sim.run.stalled 13 WARN joulie.sim.job.submitted, joulie.sim.job.scheduled, joulie.sim.job.started, joulie.sim.job.resumed, joulie.sim.job.completed 9 INFO joulie.sim.job.adopted, joulie.sim.job.stalled, joulie.sim.job.incomplete 13 WARN joulie.sim.job.failed 17 ERROR joulie.scenario.started, joulie.scenario.variant.started, joulie.scenario.finished 9 INFO joulie.scenario.assertion.evaluated 9 INFO, or 17 ERROR with error.type=assertion_failed for a failed check Calibration sweep names A calibration sweep records these two names beside the hardware metrics above, and hwcalib fit reads them back. Neither the simulator nor any Joulie component emits them. See Hardware Calibration.
OTel name Unit Instrument Point attributes Prometheus name system.cpu.utilization 1 Gauge cpu.mode, cpu.logical_number (opt-in) system_cpu_utilization_ratio joulie.calibration.setpoint {setpoint} Gauge joulie.calibration.knob, joulie.calibration.class, joulie.calibration.memory_intensity joulie_calibration_setpoint Compatibility exporters (emulate mode) SIM_EXPORTERS turns on exporters that reproduce the Prometheus format of a pinned release of a real exporter, at /exporters/<name>/metrics. They are computed from the same counters the agent and the fake GPU tools read, so a query written for the real exporter reads the emulated nodes. They exist to test Joulie’s kepler and kepler-legacy input presets and Collector bridges; the OpenTelemetry export above is the default. With the chart, the ServiceMonitor scrapes each listed exporter with honorLabels: false.

GPU series for NVIDIA GPUs only, source="NVML"; the others source="rapl-sysfs". platform is the host energy, and other the platform energy not counted in package, DRAM and GPU. Idle is the energy of the lowest-load interval seen so far, an approximation of Kepler’s rule. A node without RAPL emits nothing. kepler-0.12 Kepler v0.12.0 kepler_node_cpu_{joules_total,watts} and kepler_node_cpu_{active,idle}_{joules_total,watts} with zone, path and the constant label node_name; for NVIDIA GPUs kepler_node_gpu_{,active_,idle_}{joules_total,watts} with gpu, gpu_uuid, gpu_name, vendor Zones package, and dram when present; a 2-socket node aggregates each zone with path="aggregated-<zone>". The energy is the GPU’s NVML total energy counter. amd-dme-1.5.2 ROCm device-metrics-exporter v1.5.2 gpu_package_power and gpu_power_usage (whole W), gpu_energy_consumed (uJ), gpu_gfx_activity (%) per AMD GPU, all typed gauge as upstream does The fourteen labels upstream always sets: gpu_id (the index), hostname (the node), card_model (the product name here), serial_number (synthetic, stable per node and index), gpu_partition_id="0", gpu_compute_partition_type="spx", gpu_memory_partition_type="nps1", deployment_mode="baremetal", and pod, namespace, container, job_id, job_user, job_partition, which stay empty. The energy is the GPU’s energy ledger. A power or energy reading of 0, or of a GPU without a power sensor, is left out, as upstream exports nothing for a field it reads as 0. Upstream has no power cap metric at v1.5.2, so none is served. The exporters keep their counters in memory, so they restart from zero with the simulator, as the real exporters do. Counters that are hardware counters upstream (Kepler 0.12 totals, the DCGM energy, the AMD GPU energy) report the node’s ledger or device counter instead, which continues across a restart.
