body:
Joulie’s scheduler extender makes placement decisions informed by real-time energy telemetry, workload characteristics, and facility-level power conditions. This page describes the full pipeline from metrics collection through scoring and optional rescheduling.
End-to-end pipeline The energy-aware scheduling pipeline has five stages:
RAPL/NVML readings as OpenTelemetry metrics (or Kepler) -> Prometheus (OTLP receiver, or scrape) -> Digital twin (NodeTwin.status) -> Scheduler extender (filter + score) -> Placement decision Each stage runs independently and communicates through Kubernetes CRDs or Prometheus queries. There is no monolithic scheduling engine; each component does one thing and feeds the next.
Stage 1: Telemetry collection The twin’s measured power comes from the hardware energy interfaces (Intel and AMD RAPL for CPU packages, NVML or ROCm SMI for GPUs), published per component as the OpenTelemetry hardware metrics hw.energy and hw.power and pushed over OTLP to Prometheus. The simulator in emulate mode publishes them this way, and an OpenTelemetry Collector can translate other exporters into them. The input contract lists every name.
Kepler is the other supported source. It instruments the Linux kernel via eBPF, reads the same hardware interfaces and attributes energy to individual containers using kernel tracepoints. The controller manager reads its node counters with NODE_POWER_PRESET=kepler (Kepler 0.10 and later) or kepler-legacy (0.7 to 0.9). Kepler reports node GPU energy only from 0.12, behind an experimental feature that is off by default.
The agent also reads RAPL and NVML directly on its node, for cap enforcement.
Together, these produce three categories of signal:
Source Granularity Metrics OpenTelemetry producer Per component (CPU package, GPU) and host hw.energy, hw.power, hw.host.energy, hw.host.power (hw_energy_joules_total and so on in Prometheus) Kepler Per node and per container kepler_node_cpu_joules_total, kepler_node_gpu_joules_total (0.10 and later), kepler_node_package_joules_total (0.7 to 0.9), kepler_container_*_joules_total RAPL, NVML/DCGM on the node Per socket, per GPU CPU package power for the agent’s caps; GPU power draw, temperature, utilization Stage 2: Prometheus aggregation OpenTelemetry producers push into Prometheus’ OTLP receiver, and exporters such as Kepler are scraped into the same store. The controller manager queries it with one grouped query per input every reconcile, over a rate() window of 5 minutes by default (PROMETHEUS_RATE_WINDOW). This decouples data collection from decision-making and lets each consumer query at its own cadence.
Stage 3: Digital twin computation The controller manager’s twin controller ingests NodeHardware (static capabilities) and Prometheus telemetry to compute three scores per node, written to NodeTwin.status:
Power headroom (0-100): remaining power budget before hitting thermal or PSU limits. CoolingStress (0-100): predicted fraction of cooling capacity in use. PSUStress (0-100): predicted fraction of rack power capacity in use (tracked but reserved for future use in scoring). Stage 4: Scheduler filter and scoring When kube-scheduler has a pending pod, it calls the Joulie extender at two endpoints:
Filter (POST /filter): The extender reads the pod’s joulie.io/workload-class annotation. Performance pods are rejected from nodes whose NodeTwin.status.schedulableClass is eco or draining. Standard pods pass all nodes. This is a hard constraint: rejected nodes are excluded from scoring.
Prioritize (POST /prioritize): The extender scores each surviving node 0-100. The score is pod-specific: it accounts for the power this particular pod would add to the node:
projectedPower = measuredPower + podMarginalPower headroomScore = (cappedPower - projectedPower) / cappedPower * 100 clusterTrend = sum of all per-node powerTrend (W/min) trendScale = 2.0 if |clusterTrend| > 500 else 6.0 trendBonus = -clamp(powerTrend / trendScale, -25, 25) score = headroomScore * 0.7 + (100 - coolingStress) * 0.15 + trendBonus + profileBonus (+10 for standard pods on eco nodes) + pressureRelief (up to -30 for standard pods on congested perf nodes) Key properties:
Headroom is relative to capped power, not TDP. Eco nodes (capped lower) run out of headroom sooner. Pod marginal power is estimated from the pod’s CPU/GPU requests and the node’s hardware profile. A GPU-heavy pod reduces headroom more than a CPU-only pod. headroomScore can go negative if the pod would exceed the node’s cap; such nodes get score 0. Trend bonus uses adaptive scaling (±25 pts): trendScale=6.0 at steady state, trendScale=2.0 during cluster-wide bursts (|clusterTrend| > 500 W/min). This provides strong smoothing during normal operation while avoiding over-reaction during coordinated ramps. See Scheduler Extender for the full scoring logic, worked examples, and environment variable reference.
Stage 5: Placement The Kubernetes scheduler combines the extender’s scores with its own resource-fit checks (CPU/memory requests, taints, affinity) and places the pod on the highest-scoring node. The extender never overrides Kubernetes resource accounting; it only participates in the filter and prioritize hooks.
PUE-weighted marginal scoring Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) measures the ratio of total facility power to IT equipment power. A PUE of 1.4 means the facility consumes 40% overhead for cooling, power distribution, and lighting. Joulie’s scoring accounts for this overhead.
Why PUE matters for scheduling Two nodes drawing identical IT power can have different total energy costs if one is in a rack with worse cooling efficiency. Scheduling purely on IT power ignores the facility multiplier and can lead to suboptimal placement.
How Joulie incorporates PUE The CoolingStress score in NodeTwin.status serves as a proxy for marginal PUE impact. When cooling stress is high on a node, placing additional workloads there increases the cooling system’s marginal power draw disproportionately. The scoring formula penalizes high cooling stress:
coolingPenalty = (100 - coolingStress) * 0.15 At coolingStress = 80, this contributes only 3 points (vs. 15 at coolingStress = 0). The effect is that nodes near their cooling capacity become less attractive even if they have spare compute headroom. This steers workloads toward nodes where the marginal PUE impact is lower.
The cooling stress term (0.15 weight) provides a facility-level energy efficiency signal, while headroom relative to the capped power budget dominates scoring at 70% weight. PSU stress is tracked but reserved for future use in scoring. A trend bonus (up to ±10 points) rewards nodes whose power draw is falling and penalizes nodes whose power is rising, improving responsiveness to dynamic workloads.
State of the art Joulie’s energy-aware scheduling builds on several lines of research. This section places the design in context and identifies the relevant prior work.
Energy measurement Kepler (Amaral et al., 2023) provides the per-container energy attribution that underpins Joulie’s classification pipeline. By attaching eBPF probes to kernel scheduling events and reading hardware energy counters, Kepler disaggregates node-level power into per-container contributions without requiring hardware modifications or hypervisor-level instrumentation.
RAPL (David et al., 2010) is the Intel hardware interface for reading and capping CPU and DRAM energy consumption. RAPL’s Running Average Power Limit model exposes per-socket energy counters and power capping through MSRs. Joulie’s agent reads RAPL for node-level telemetry and writes RAPL power limits for cap enforcement.
H. David, E. Gorbatov, U.R. Hanebutte, R. Khanna, and C. Le. “RAPL: Memory Power Estimation and Capping.” Proceedings of the International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), 2010.
M. Amaral et al. “Kepler: A Framework for Energy-Efficient Kubernetes Clusters.” Proceedings of the ACM/SPEC International Conference on Performance Engineering, 2023.
Data center energy modeling PUE modeling has been studied extensively in the data center literature. Dayarathna et al. (2016) survey energy consumption models for data centers, covering thermal models, workload-dependent cooling, and facility-level power distribution. Joulie’s CoolingStress and PSUStress scores are simplified parametric models in this tradition, designed for O(1) per-node evaluation rather than full CFD simulation.
M. Dayarathna, Y. Wen, and R. Fan. “Data Center Energy Consumption Modeling: A Survey.” IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials, vol. 18, no. 1, pp. 732-794, 2016.
Energy-proportional computing Barroso and Holzle (2007) argued that servers should consume power proportional to their utilization, noting that real servers are far from energy-proportional: an idle server still draws 50-60% of peak power. This observation motivates Joulie’s approach of consolidating workloads onto fewer, more-utilized nodes and capping idle nodes, rather than spreading load uniformly.
L.A. Barroso and U. Holzle. “The Case for Energy-Proportional Computing.” IEEE Computer, vol. 40, no. 12, pp. 33-37, 2007.
Power-aware scheduling Fan, Weber, and Barroso (2007) demonstrated that aggregate power consumption in warehouse-scale computers can be managed through power budgeting at the cluster level. Their work on power provisioning showed that statistical multiplexing of power across many machines allows significant oversubscription of power capacity. Joulie’s PSUStress scoring applies a similar principle: it penalizes nodes that would push rack power consumption toward the provisioned limit.
X. Fan, W.-D. Weber, and L.A. Barroso. “Power Provisioning for a Warehouse-Sized Computer.” Proceedings of the International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), 2007.
Digital twin for data centers The concept of a digital twin for thermal-aware provisioning was introduced by Patel, Bash, and Sharma (2003), who proposed using thermal models to guide server placement in data centers. Joulie extends this idea to Kubernetes: the digital twin is a lightweight parametric model embedded in the controller manager, continuously updated from telemetry, and consumed by the scheduler in real time.
C.D. Patel, C.E. Bash, and R. Sharma. “Thermal Considerations in Cooling Large Scale High Compute Density Data Centers.” Proceedings of the International Symposium on High Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA), 2003.
Kubernetes scheduling Burns et al. (2016) trace the evolution from Borg through Omega to Kubernetes, describing how scheduling evolved from a monolithic model to an extensible, API-driven architecture. Joulie’s scheduler extender leverages this extensibility: it participates in the standard scheduling cycle through HTTP hooks without forking or replacing the Kubernetes scheduler.
B. Burns, B. Grant, D. Oppenheimer, E. Brewer, and J. Wilkes. “Borg, Omega, and Kubernetes.” ACM Queue, vol. 14, no. 1, 2016.
What Joulie adds Prior work has addressed energy measurement, power-aware scheduling, and data center thermal modeling independently. Joulie’s contribution is integrating these into a single Kubernetes-native feedback loop:
RAPL and NVML telemetry as OpenTelemetry metrics, or through Kepler, provides node-level power measurement, and Kepler adds per-container attribution. A digital twin predicts the facility-level impact (cooling, PSU) of placement decisions, not just IT power. PUE-weighted scoring makes the scheduler aware of marginal facility energy cost, not just compute availability. No existing Kubernetes scheduler plugin combines real-time eBPF energy telemetry, a digital twin with facility-stress modeling, and workload classification into a single scheduling pipeline.
For production-scale validation of this pipeline, see Scoring Formula Validation.
What to read next Scheduler Extender Digital Twin

This page lists every change since Joulie v0.2.3 that moves the numbers the simulator produces for its modelled nodes (standalone mode, and Kubernetes mode without emulation), and how far each one moved them. A result produced with an older simulator holds for the model it ran; read it together with this table. Emulated nodes (SIM_EMULATE) run the physics of simulator/pkg/hwemu and are not covered here.
The reports of experiments 01 to 03 in experiments/ were produced before every change below and have not been rerun; each carries a dated note that says which of its model statements did not hold.
Two yardsticks The reference scenario lives in simulator/cmd/simulator/testdata/reference/: eight inventory entries (nine nodes), one for each way the simulator resolves a node’s model (a SPECpower curve, the same CPU on one socket, a second curve, a proxy CPU, an Intel CPU with official figures only, catalog GPUs on an Intel and on an EPYC host, GPUs the catalog does not know), and 40 jobs over 2 h. It runs in standalone mode under baselines A, B and C with SIM_SA_WORKERS=1, SIM_SA_DT=5, SIM_SA_TIMEOUT=7200, the code defaults and the embedded catalog. TestReferenceScenarioStandalone compares the run with reference.golden.json (energy as hw.energy by hw.type and by node, job statistics as joulie.sim.*) and fails on any key that moves by more than a relative 1e-9, printing a table of what moved.
The debug runs are each experiment’s configs/benchmark-debug.yaml through the standalone sweep: one seed, 800 jobs (01) or 600 (02 and 03), 300 s of simulated time, all three baselines.
PATH=$HOME/.local/go/bin:$PATH python3 scripts/standalone_sweep.py \ --config experiments/02-heterogeneous-benchmark/configs/benchmark-debug.yaml \ --simulator <simulator binary> --results-dir <directory> Energy in the tables is the integral of the power a run reports: the sum over the rows of timeseries.csv of cpu_power_w + gpu_power_w, times the 5 s step. From the stepNode change on it equals the golden’s hw.energy total to within 0.001 %. The saving of B or C is 1 minus its energy over A’s. Every simulator binary ran the same trace of each experiment.
How each change was measured. From the stepNode change on, each one compares the tree just before it with the tree just after it. The earlier changes were measured on the v0.2.3 simulator, with the old and the new behaviour selected through its inputs: the thermal thresholds through SIM_{CPU,GPU}_THERMAL_THROTTLE_{START,FULL}_C, the catalog corrections and the generated catalog through SIM_HARDWARE_CATALOG_PATH. With all of them selected, v0.2.3 gives the same energy as the tree just before the stepNode change: identical on the reference scenario, and within 0.03 % on the debug runs, less than two identical runs of that simulator differ on GPU nodes (up to 0.05 %). The other changes in between (the curve cap solver among them, and the emulate mode, workload and OpenTelemetry work) therefore moved neither yardstick.
Changes Change What changed Reference scenario Debug runs Thermal throttling is opt-in SIM_{CPU,GPU}_THERMAL_THROTTLE_{START,FULL}_C default to 0, which means off; they were 85 and 97 °C for CPUs, 82 and 92 °C for GPUs. A 2x EPYC 9654 node at full load on its SPECpower curve headed for 126 °C, throttled fully at 97 °C, dropped to 141 W with throughput 0, cooled and swung back. Guards: TestCurveNodeIsNotThermallyThrottledByDefault, TestGPUIsNotThermallyThrottledByDefault A +0.2 %, B and C +1.1 %; B and C complete 30 jobs instead of 29 under 0.02 %, within the run-to-run spread A curve node throttles under its cap (D13) Above its RAPL cap, a node on a measured curve now lowers its frequency on its own curve (phys.SolveFreqScaleForCap). Before, the curve clamped its power to the cap, so the solver never saw the excess and the node kept full frequency and full throughput. This change leaves the analytic model’s power unchanged (TestAnalyticCPUPowerUnchangedByF2); its cap solver changed later, see the row on memory traffic. Guards: TestCatalogEPYC9655CurveIsSPECResult01457, TestCatalogGPUMinimumsHavePublicSources A -1.3 %, B and C -1.7 %, all on the EPYC 9655 node none at the time: the experiments read a generated catalog The experiments read the embedded catalog The sweep and the installers no longer generate a catalog from the inventory (it gave every CPU a 300 W TDP and no curve, so every CPU ran the analytic model at 80 W idle and 420 W peak) and clear SIM_HARDWARE_CATALOG_PATH. Guard: TestExperimentInventoriesMatchTheEmbeddedCatalog none: it always read the embedded catalog A +108 % (01), +12 % (02), +19 % (03); the saving of C falls from 31.2 to 17.0 % (01), 31.8 to 30.4 % (02), 34.5 to 33.6 % (03) stepNode The physics of a modelled node advances only in stepNode, in simulated time and in substeps (SIM_SA_SUBSTEP in standalone mode, 100 ms on the physics tick SIM_PHYSICS_TICK otherwise); HTTP reads and gauges no longer advance it, and energy is the integral of the instantaneous power. Guards: TestIdlePowerDoesNotDependOnThrottleTarget, TestP03GPUPowerNeverBelowIdle, TestCapBelowFloorReportsFloorPower A unchanged, B and C +0.2 % (the curve nodes) A unchanged; B +0.6, +3.1, +4.5 % and C +0.9, +4.6, +6.4 % (01, 02, 03); the saving of C falls from 17.0 to 16.3 % (01), 30.4 to 27.2 % (02), 33.6 to 29.4 % (03) A GPU cap slows a job once A GPU cap slows a GPU job by what the capped board model says it costs. The legacy progress formula charged it a second time, by the cap over the board maximum weighted by the job’s GPU sensitivity. Guard: TestGPUCapSlowsAGPUJobOnce none none: no job with a GPU sensitivity ran on a capped GPU Catalog facts reach the model With no environment or class value, a node takes from the catalog its GPU maximum and lowest cap per board (they were 300 and 80 W unless an environment variable or a class set them), its CPU socket cap range (TDP down to the lowest cTDP, else 0.55 x TDP) and, without a curve, a peak of sockets x TDP (was 420 W); node2S curves scale with the socket count. SIM_POD_W, SIM_DVFS_DROP_W_PER_PCT, SIM_GPU_ALPHA_UTIL and SIM_GPU_BETA_CAP are removed and warn once. Guards: TestCatalogGPUCapsReachTheModelWhenEnvIsUnset, TestNode2SCurveScalesWithSocketCount, TestProxyCPUPeakFollowsTDP, TestRemovedModelKnobsWarnOnce A +61 %, B and C +63 %: GPU energy x2.07; CPU energy of A -5 %, mostly the one-socket node, whose curve now halves A +4.2 % (01), +32 % (02), +20 % (03); the saving of C rises from 16.3 to 17.3 % (01), 27.2 to 30.5 % (02), 29.4 to 32.6 % (03) Standalone runs hwemu profiles An inventory entry may name an hwemu profile; legacy entries honour gpu_min_cap_watts and gpu_max_cap_watts; eco on a profile node with a writable PL1 is a CPU power cap. Guards: TestStandaloneHonoursInventoryGPUCapRange, TestStandaloneInventoryProfileKey, TestStandaloneEcoOnRAPLProfileIsAPowerCap none none: no profile nodes, and the inventories’ GPU cap ranges equal the catalog’s The analytic cap solver counts memory traffic phys.SolveFreqScaleForCap on the analytic model now inverts the power formula with the memory and IO activity factor that the power it then computes applies. Before, a capped node with memory or IO intensity above 0 drew below its cap (262.5 W under a 300 W cap). 20 of the 548 cases in testdata/physics/analytic-cpu-power.golden.json moved, all capped with memory or IO traffic; no saturation flag changed. Guards: TestFC04CappedAnalyticNodeWithMemoryTrafficDrawsItsCap, H15 none: no CPU cap binds in the reference scenario not rerun An unknown GPU takes its labelled count A node whose GPU the catalog does not know takes its device count from the joulie.io/hw.gpu-count label (the inventory’s gpu_count in standalone mode). Before, it got 0 GPUs and drew no GPU power. Guard: TestFC03UnknownGPUTakesTheLabelCount ref-gpu-unknown now draws power for its 4 GPUs: its energy in baseline A rose from about 1.09 MJ to 8.44 MJ; only the GPU and ref-gpu-unknown energy keys moved, in A, B and C not rerun Cap ranges stay ordered An explicit SIM_CPU_SOCKET_CAP_MIN_W or SIM_GPU_MIN_CAP_WATTS_PER_GPU above the maximum the catalog fills in is lowered to that maximum, with a warning. Before, the range came out inverted (200 to 165 W on a Xeon Platinum 8260). Guard: TestFC02ExplicitCapMinimumAboveTheCatalogueMaximumIsOrdered none: the reference scenario sets no explicit minimum none, for the same reason Clock suffix in CPU names Catalog matching drops a trailing clock token and the cpu before it, so the label-safe form of a full cpuinfo name such as Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8260 CPU @ 2.40GHz matches its catalog entry instead of falling back to the generic model. Guard: TestFC07LabelSafeCPUInfoSpellingMatchesThe8260 none: the reference inventory spells its models without the suffix not rerun Eco GPU nodes keep their CPU uncapped The controller manager wrote spec.cpu.packagePowerCapWatts at ECO_CAP_WATTS (120 W by default) on eco GPU nodes, and the agent applied it, although a GPU node is meant to get GPU caps only; the CPU of a GPU node now gets PERFORMANCE_CAP_WATTS whatever the profile, as on a performance GPU node. Only Kubernetes mode, where the controller manager drives the agents, moves: CPU power and job speed on eco GPU nodes. Standalone mode does not run the controller manager and still scales the CPU frequency of eco GPU nodes, so the two modes differ there until it follows. Guard: TestEcoGPUNodeCPUIsNotCapped none: standalone mode none, standalone mode; Kubernetes mode not rerun Governor and clock physics in emulate mode An emulated node whose profile has the governor facts, every builtin profile, runs its cpufreq governor as the kernel does (phys.GovernorStep: schedutil, ondemand, conservative, userspace, and the EPP-driven powersave of intel_pstate with HWP and amd-pstate-epp), counts work in cycles, so a governor that holds a lower frequency shows the same work as a busier CPU in power and utilization, and measures CPU job speed against performance at cpuinfo_max_freq with the profile’s boost instead of against the governor’s own frequency, which made a governor cost nothing by construction. GPU clock locks, levels and overdrive ceilings, forced data-path levels and idle gating off reach GPU power and speed (phys.GPUPowerWithClock, phys.GPUThroughputWithClock), and peer transfers are counted per GPU. What moved, in emulate mode only: CPU power and job speed under every governor but performance, for example a fully loaded 2x Xeon 8260 under its shipped powersave with EPP balance_performance runs at 3.32 of 3.9 GHz, 140.6 W per package instead of 165 W, and a cpu.compute_bound job at 0.87 of the reference speed instead of 1; an AMD GPU under auto draws dataPathHoldW (10 W, assumed) more while its data path holds after its own memory-active work. Unchanged: every node under performance, every GPU without a lock or a forced level, and every profile without the governor facts. Guards: TestCG13PowersaveCostsThroughputAgainstTheReference, TestCG14PerformanceUncappedGivesThroughputOne, TestCG15SchedutilAtLightLoadSitsAtTheLowestEntryAndRunsBusier, TestXF10IdlePowerOfHeldDataPathAndGatingOff none: standalone mode does not run hwemu nodes none, for the same reason Standalone eco GPU nodes keep their CPU at full frequency Standalone mode now follows the controller manager (the row above): the CPU of an eco GPU node runs as on a performance node, at frequency scale 1 under the performance cap, and only its GPUs take the eco cap. Before, standalone scaled the CPU frequency of an eco GPU node to SIM_SA_CPU_ECO_PCT (60 % by default and in the debug runs), or capped its PL1 at that share of the maximum on a profile with a writable PL1. Guard: TestStandaloneEcoGPUNodeCPURunsAsOnAPerformanceNode none: each GPU family of the reference scenario has one node, and every family keeps one performance node 01 none (no GPU node); energy of B +0.59 % and C +0.66 % (02), B +0.42 % and C +0.63 % (03), all of it CPU energy of eco GPU nodes; the saving of B falls from 21.4 to 21.0 % (02) and 22.5 to 22.1 % (03), of C from 30.5 to 30.0 % (02) and 32.6 to 32.2 % (03) GPU clock model: a lower cap or clock never raises power or throughput The cap and the governor are two limits on one clock (phys.GPUPowerWithClock, phys.GPUThroughputWithClock). The GPU runs at the lower of the governor’s clock and the cap-implied clock, (cap / natural)^ComputeGamma; its compute share is that clock, its memory share the lower of the capped board’s memory scale and the memory knee at the governor’s clock, and its power the capped board power, its dynamic part scaled by (clock / cap-implied clock)^ClockBeta below the cap-implied clock, but never more than the governor’s clock draws without a cap, idle + (P_natural - idle) x r^ClockBeta. With ComputeGamma x ClockBeta x (1 - IdleW / MaxW) <= 1 that bound never binds and the power is as before: a lock at the cap-implied clock draws the cap, and a lock above it changes nothing. Beyond it, a lock at or above the cap-implied clock draws the lower of the cap and its uncapped power, at the cap’s compute share. Before, the memory share of a locked GPU was relative to the knee at the cap-implied clock, so below the knee a lower cap raised it (the throughput of a memory-bound GPU locked at 0.3 of its maximum clock rose from 0.32 to 0.55 as the cap came down, test parameters), and beyond the bound a cap raised a locked GPU’s power above its uncapped power (202 W under a cap against 134 W without one). At the maximum clock both still equal the capped board model. Guards: TestGP13LoweringTheCapOrTheClockNeverRaisesPowerOrThroughput, TestGP14LoweringTheCapNeverRaisesALockedGPU, TestGP09LockAndCapActThroughOneClock none: the clock model runs on emulated nodes only none, for the same reason The efficient GPU preset defaults to 80 % governor.DefaultCeilingPctOfMax, the compute clock ceiling of efficient when neither the NodeTwin nor GPU_GOVERNOR_ECO_CEILING_PCT_OF_MAX names one, is 80 % of the maximum compute clock (was 75 %). In the Tier A sweep of the governor exploration, eco GPU work at 75 % had a p95 slowdown of +22.5 % for -13.2 % energy, above the 20 % the eco class allows, and at 80 % +17.3 % for -10.7 %. The value is provisional: the saving rests on the assumed clockBeta and memoryKneeFrac (sensitivity, Q5), which a clock sweep on each GPU family must measure. What moves: eco GPU nodes under governor control (GOVERNOR_CONTROL gpu or all, off by default), which in the simulator only emulated nodes model. Guards: TestGC17DefaultGPUPresetsAndTheModelMap, TestGC07CeilingOnlyWithEfficientAndOutOfRangeFallsBack, TestHwemuA27MI300XEfficientOverdrive none: standalone mode writes no governor none, for the same reason No change moved the number of completed jobs of the debug runs.
Energy after each change The reference scenario (energy in MJ):
After A B C A: CPU, GPU Completed jobs A, B, C v0.2.3 39.63 38.81 38.81 16.52, 23.11 33, 29, 29 thermal throttling opt-in 39.71 39.22 39.22 16.60, 23.11 33, 30, 30 catalog corrections 39.20 38.57 38.57 16.09, 23.11 33, 30, 30 stepNode 39.20 38.57 38.57 16.09, 23.11 33, 30, 30 artifact removals 39.20 38.65 38.65 16.09, 23.11 33, 30, 30 catalog facts 63.18 63.05 63.05 15.29, 47.89 33, 30, 30 The debug runs (energy of A in MJ, saving of B and of C against A):
After 01: A 01: B, C 02: A 02: B, C 03: A 03: B, C v0.2.3, generated catalog 2.63 23.4 %, 31.2 % 9.02 22.7 %, 31.8 % 10.96 24.1 %, 34.5 % embedded catalog 5.48 10.9 %, 17.0 % 10.11 21.6 %, 30.4 % 13.03 23.6 %, 33.6 % stepNode 5.48 10.9 %, 17.0 % 10.11 21.7 %, 30.4 % 13.03 23.7 %, 33.6 % artifact removals 5.48 10.3 %, 16.3 % 10.11 19.2 %, 27.2 % 13.03 20.3 %, 29.4 % catalog facts 5.71 11.2 %, 17.3 % 13.36 21.4 %, 30.5 % 15.68 22.5 %, 32.6 % standalone eco GPU node CPU 5.71 11.2 %, 17.3 % 13.36 21.0 %, 30.0 % 15.68 22.1 %, 32.2 % The changes the tables leave out moved neither yardstick by more than 0.03 %. A 300 s debug run says how a change moves an experiment, not what the experiment’s 60 h result would be.
Adding a change A change that moves a number of a modelled node (physics in nodephys.go, model resolution in modelresolve.go, job speed, the catalog, the standalone policy) adds a row here in the same pull request:
Run go test ./simulator/cmd/simulator/ -run ReferenceScenario on the change; the failure prints the keys that moved. Review them, then rewrite the golden with -update and commit it. Build the simulator before and after the change and run the three debug configurations with each binary on the same traces: the sweep reuses the trace it finds in <results-dir>/traces/, so copy that directory from the first run into the second run’s results directory. Add the row: what changed, the guard test, the reference and debug-run deltas. A change that moves neither yardstick but changes another mode (Kubernetes mode caps, emulate mode) still gets a row that says so. Add a dated note to the reports of any experiment whose description the change makes untrue.

title: Model Changes

body:
Complete reference for all Joulie environment variables. These are set via Helm values or directly in the Deployment/DaemonSet manifests.
Defaults listed below are the code defaults. The Helm chart (charts/joulie/values.yaml) overrides some of them: notably, the controller manager NODE_SELECTOR defaults to joulie.io/managed=true in the chart even though the code default is node-role.kubernetes.io/worker.
Images The chart values agent.image.tag, controllerManager.image.tag and schedulerExtender.image.tag (and image.tag in the simulator chart) default to empty, which pulls the chart’s appVersion. A chart installed from oci://registry.cern.ch/joulie carries the version it was released with, so it runs the images of that release. A chart installed from a checkout has appVersion: latest and runs the newest stable release. Set a tag only to run other images, for example your own build.
Pre-releases (a GitHub pre-release, or a version such as 0.2.0-rc0) are published under their version only and never move latest.
Agent Variable Default Description AGENT_MODE daemonset daemonset (one agent per node) or pool (shared agents with sharding) NODE_NAME (required in daemonset mode) Name of the node this agent manages RECONCILE_INTERVAL 20s How often the agent reconciles desired state METRICS_ADDR :8080 Address for the Prometheus metrics endpoint SPEC_READ_TIMEOUT 5m How long the agent tolerates failed reads of its NodeTwin spec, leaving the node as it is. Past it the agent relaxes every cap and puts the governor baseline back, as when the spec is gone, until a read succeeds. A Go duration such as 90s; a value it cannot parse keeps 5m SIMULATE_ONLY false If true, agent discovers hardware but does not apply power caps or governors (governor result disabled) HARDWARE_CATALOG_PATH (empty: the catalog embedded in the binary) Path to a hardware inventory catalog YAML that replaces the embedded one KUBE_CLIENT_QPS 50 Queries per second the agent’s Kubernetes client may send KUBE_CLIENT_BURST 100 Burst above KUBE_CLIENT_QPS the agent’s Kubernetes client may send Agent pool mode Variable Default Description POOL_NODE_SELECTOR joulie.io/managed=true Label selector for nodes managed by pool agents POOL_SHARDS 1 Total number of shards for pool mode partitioning POOL_SHARD_ID (from pod ordinal) Shard ID for this agent instance Agent DVFS control Variable Default Description DVFS_EMA_ALPHA 0.3 Exponential moving average smoothing factor for power tracking DVFS_HIGH_MARGIN_W 10.0 Power above cap (watts) to trigger frequency reduction DVFS_LOW_MARGIN_W 15.0 Power below cap (watts) to trigger frequency increase DVFS_STEP_PCT 10 Frequency throttle step size (%) DVFS_COOLDOWN 20s Minimum duration between DVFS adjustments DVFS_TRIP_COUNT 2 Consecutive samples outside margin before acting DVFS_MIN_FREQ_KHZ 1500000 Floor frequency for DVFS throttling (kHz) Agent governor control The agent always discovers the CPU and GPU governors of its node and publishes them in NodeHardware (see Governor discovery). It writes the presets of its NodeTwin, spec.cpu.governor and spec.gpu.governor, only with GOVERNOR_WRITES true; the controller manager writes those fields only with its own GOVERNOR_CONTROL on (see “Governor control” under Controller manager). Before its first write the agent records the baseline in NodeHardware, and it puts it back when a field disappears or GOVERNOR_WRITES is turned off.
Variable Default Chart Description GOVERNOR_WRITES false false Write the governor presets. false reports disabled for a preset and writes no preset. An agent started with false after an earlier run changed the node puts the baseline back once (result restored), its only write, and then reports disabled. GOVERNOR_RESTORE_ON_EXIT true true On SIGTERM or SIGINT, put the baseline back before the agent exits, for every component it changed. A rolling update of the agent therefore restores the baseline and the new agent applies the preset again. SIGKILL and OOM kills restore nothing. Writes use the agent’s existing /host-sys mount, root user and privileges, the ones the DVFS fallback uses; the pod spec does not change. Without them the result is refused and NodeHardware shows writable: false. NVIDIA presets run nvidia-smi -i <pci bus id> -lgc or -lmc, so they need nvidia-smi in the agent (see “Agent GPU tools”); without it the result is error, as for caps. In the HTTP control mode (TELEMETRY_CPU_CONTROL or TELEMETRY_GPU_CONTROL http) and in pool mode the agent writes no governor and reports unsupported. What each preset becomes on each CPU driver and GPU family is in CPU support and GPU support. The results, their retries and the restore rules are in Governor control. Check them with: kubectl get nodetwins -o custom-columns=NODE:.spec.nodeName,CPU-GOV:.status.controlStatus.cpuGovernor.result,CPU-NATIVE:.status.controlStatus.cpuGovernor.applied,GPU-GOV:.status.controlStatus.gpuGovernor.result,GPU-NATIVE:.status.controlStatus.gpuGovernor.applied Agent telemetry and control backends Variable Default Description TELEMETRY_CPU_SOURCE host CPU telemetry source: host (the node’s RAPL files), http (TELEMETRY_CPU_HTTP_ENDPOINT), none TELEMETRY_CPU_CONTROL host CPU control backend: host, http, none TELEMETRY_GPU_CONTROL host GPU control backend: host, http, none TELEMETRY_CPU_HTTP_ENDPOINT (empty) HTTP endpoint for CPU telemetry, {node} replaced with the node name (e.g., http://sim:18080/otlp/telemetry/{node}). Each answer is one OTLP JSON ExportMetricsServiceRequest: the agent sums the hw.type=cpu components, from the rate of hw.energy or else the hw.power gauge, of the resource whose k8s.node.name is the node (a resource without it is read too). See HTTP input format. The legacy packagePowerWatts JSON is still read, with one warning per endpoint and node, until v0.4.0. TELEMETRY_CPU_CONTROL_HTTP_ENDPOINT (empty) HTTP endpoint for CPU control (e.g., http://sim:18080/control/{node}) TELEMETRY_CPU_CONTROL_MODE (empty) CPU control mode override TELEMETRY_GPU_CONTROL_HTTP_ENDPOINT (empty) HTTP endpoint for GPU control (e.g., http://sim:18080/control/{node}) TELEMETRY_GPU_CONTROL_MODE (empty) GPU control mode override TELEMETRY_HTTP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 2 HTTP client timeout for telemetry/control requests, in whole seconds Agent chart values Helm values of charts/joulie that shape the agent pods. The DaemonSet and the emulated agents share one pod spec (joulie.agentPodSpec in templates/_helpers.tpl), so agent.tolerations, agent.runtimeClassName and the agent.extra* hooks apply to both; the pool StatefulSet takes none of them. Emulated agents ignore agent.hostNetwork and agent.privileged.
Value Default Effect agent.mode daemonset daemonset: one agent per node matching agent.daemonset.nodeSelector. pool: the StatefulSet joulie-agent-pool (see “Agent pool mode”). emulated: one Deployment per agent.emulated.nodes entry, for the simulated cluster. none: no agent. agent.tolerations nvidia.com/gpu and amd.com/gpu, operator Exists, effect NoSchedule Tolerations of the agent pods. GPU nodes usually carry their vendor’s NoSchedule taint; an agent that does not tolerate it never runs there, and the caps the controller manager plans for those nodes are never enforced. Add any other taint your managed nodes carry; [] tolerates none. agent.runtimeClassName "" RuntimeClass of the agent pods, for example the one of the NVIDIA container runtime, which puts the node’s driver tools into the container. agent.extraEnv [] EnvVar entries added after the chart’s own. agent.extraVolumes [] Volume entries added after the chart’s own. agent.extraVolumeMounts [] VolumeMount entries added to the agent container after the chart’s own. agent.emulated.root /var/lib/joulie-hwemu The simulator’s SIM_HWEMU_ROOT. Each emulated agent mounts its node’s tree from there: sys at /host-sys, cpuinfo over /proc/cpuinfo (read-only), state at /emu/state, bin at /emu/bin (read-only), <root>/lib at /emu/lib (read-only), and dev/nvidiactl at /dev/nvidiactl for an entry with devNvidiactl. agent.emulated.hostNodeSelector joulie.io/hwemu-host: "true" Node selector of the emulated agents: the node that holds the trees and runs the simulator. agent.emulated.path /emu/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin PATH of the emulated agents, so the emulated GPU tools come first. agent.emulated.nodes [] One entry per emulated node, as simcluster agents writes them: name (the Node, also the literal NODE_NAME), profile, devNvidiactl, extraVolumes, extraVolumeMounts. Entry i becomes the Deployment joulie-agent-emu-<i>, with strategy Recreate, no host network and no privileges. A name that is not a Node name, or is listed twice, fails the render. Emulated agents are what the simulated cluster runs: one per node the DaemonSet would reach, judged from the DaemonSet’s own render.
Agent GPU tools The agent reads and caps GPUs by running nvidia-smi or rocm-smi from its PATH; it never runs amd-smi. The agent image (gcr.io/distroless/static) ships neither, and has no C library, no ELF loader and no Python, so mounting the host’s tool alone is not enough: nvidia-smi is dynamically linked (file $(command -v nvidia-smi) on a GPU node shows it) and also needs the loader and the NVML library (libnvidia-ml.so.1), and rocm-smi is a Python script that needs /usr/bin/env and python3. The hooks above are where these come in: agent.runtimeClassName for a container runtime that injects the driver’s tools and libraries, such as the NVIDIA one, or agent.extraVolumes and agent.extraVolumeMounts for a host directory, with agent.extraEnv.
Which combination works on a real GPU node is an open question: no recipe has been verified yet. After installing, check the GPU control status of every GPU node:
kubectl get nodetwins -o custom-columns=NODE:.spec.nodeName,GPU:.status.controlStatus.gpu.result,MESSAGE:.status.controlStatus.gpu.message A tool that cannot run shows as error with a message starting gpu inventory failed, or as blocked with no supported GPU backend detected when the vendor cannot be told either; the GPUs then keep their limits. The simulated cluster reproduces both sides: fakesmi fails as the real tool does when something it needs is missing (HWEMU_ROOTFS under Simulator hardware emulation), and the harness either mounts those files (toolDelivery: mounted) or not (toolDelivery: none).
Controller manager Variable Default Description RECONCILE_INTERVAL 1m How often the controller manager reconciles cluster state METRICS_ADDR :8081 Address for the Prometheus metrics endpoint LEADER_ELECT false Run the reconcile loop only on the leader of a coordination.k8s.io lease. Required before running more than one controller manager replica. Helm: controllerManager.leaderElection.enabled, which also creates the lease Role. POD_NAMESPACE joulie-system Namespace of the leader election lease. The chart sets it from the downward API. HARDWARE_CATALOG_PATH (empty: the catalog embedded in the binary) Path to a hardware inventory catalog YAML that replaces the embedded one NODE_SELECTOR node-role.kubernetes.io/worker Label selector for managed nodes RESERVED_LABEL_KEY joulie.io/reserved Label key for nodes excluded from policy decisions POWER_PROFILE_LABEL joulie.io/power-profile Node label key for the active power profile KUBE_CLIENT_QPS 50 Queries per second the controller manager’s Kubernetes client may send KUBE_CLIENT_BURST 100 Burst above KUBE_CLIENT_QPS the controller manager’s Kubernetes client may send Measured node power The controller manager writes each node’s measured power to NodeTwin.status.powerMeasurement.measuredNodePowerW. With NODE_POWER_SOURCE=prometheus, which the chart sets, it runs one grouped PromQL query per reconcile (GET <address>/api/v1/query) and reads every node from the answer; with http it reads one OTLP JSON document per node. The default preset otel reads the OpenTelemetry hardware metrics that producers push to Prometheus’ OTLP receiver: the rate of hw.energy, or the hw.power gauge, of the cpu and gpu components, keyed by the resource attribute k8s.node.name. Input metrics (OpenTelemetry) has the contract, every preset query and the Prometheus settings it needs.
The Chart column is what charts/joulie/values.yaml sets; “unset” means the code default applies.
Variable Default Chart Description PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS (empty) http://prometheus-operated.monitoring:9090 Prometheus the measured inputs are read from. The default of NODE_POWER_PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS and FACILITY_PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS. PROMETHEUS_NAME_TRANSLATION UnderscoreEscapingWithSuffixes unset Prometheus’ otlp.translation_strategy, which the controller manager must match: UnderscoreEscapingWithSuffixes, NoUTF8EscapingWithSuffixes, UnderscoreEscapingWithoutSuffixes or NoTranslation, case-insensitive. It spells the metric and label names of the otel presets, and under every facility preset the key labels of the zone, rack and node inputs, which are translated the same way. PROMETHEUS_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES auto unset Where the otel node power preset finds k8s.node.name. labels: on every series, which needs k8s.node.name in Prometheus’ otlp.promote_resource_attributes. target_info: joined from target_info on job and instance, which needs no promotion. auto: the labels form first, then the target_info form when the first returns nothing or a series lacks the node label; it keeps the form that works until that form returns nothing or fails, and logs every switch. PROMETHEUS_RATE_WINDOW 5m 5m Window of every rate() the inputs run, and the longest interval the http source measures an energy rate over. At least 10s, a whole number of seconds, and at least four export intervals of the producer, or rate() reads low. NODE_POWER_SOURCE static prometheus static (0 W), prometheus or http. An unknown value means static, with a warning. NODE_POWER_PRESET (empty: otel, or custom when NODE_POWER_PROMETHEUS_QUERY is set) unset The format the Prometheus query reads: otel, kepler (Kepler 0.10 and later), kepler-legacy (Kepler 0.7 to 0.9) or custom. A preset other than custom together with NODE_POWER_PROMETHEUS_QUERY stops the controller manager at start, so a query is never silently ignored. NODE_POWER_SCOPE components components components: the CPU packages plus the GPUs, the boundary of the twin’s budget (CPU TDP plus GPU TDP). host: the whole host (hw.host.energy and hw.host.power, or Kepler 0.7 platform energy), which exceeds the budget under load. kepler with host stops the controller manager at start. NODE_POWER_NODE_LABEL per preset: the translated k8s.node.name (k8s_node_name by default) for otel and custom, node_name for kepler, exported_instance for kepler-legacy unset The label that names the node in the query result. NODE_POWER_PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS unset Prometheus of the node power query only. NODE_POWER_PROMETHEUS_QUERY (empty) unset Your own PromQL, in watts, for the custom preset. With {node} it runs once per node with the node name filled in, and every series it returns is summed (a warning names a node whose query returns more than one). Without {node} it is summed by NODE_POWER_NODE_LABEL. NODE_POWER_HTTP_ENDPOINT (empty) unset With NODE_POWER_SOURCE=http: a URL with {node}, answering one OTLP JSON ExportMetricsServiceRequest per node, such as the simulator’s /otlp/telemetry/{node}. It is read with the rules of the otel preset under NODE_POWER_SCOPE; see HTTP input format. The legacy packagePowerWatts JSON, CPU packages only, is still read with a warning until v0.4.0. Deprecated aliases, removed in the next minor release: OPERATOR_NODE_POWER_SOURCE, OPERATOR_NODE_POWER_HTTP_ENDPOINT, OPERATOR_NODE_POWER_PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS, OPERATOR_NODE_POWER_PROMETHEUS_QUERY. They are read only when the new name is unset, and the controller manager logs a warning naming the replacement.
A custom query must return instantaneous power in watts. Energy exporters publish cumulative joules counters, which grow without bound, so they have to be converted with rate(); the presets already do:
rate(kepler_node_platform_joules_total{exported_instance="{node}"}[5m]) NODE_POWER_PRESET=kepler-legacy with NODE_POWER_SCOPE=host reads the same series without a custom query. Passing a counter directly makes measuredNodePowerW climb forever, which drives power headroom negative and cooling stress to 100% on every node. The controller manager logs a warning when a reading exceeds twice the node’s TDP.
Upgrading to v0.3.0.
The chart now sets NODE_POWER_SOURCE=prometheus. Set controllerManager.env.NODE_POWER_SOURCE=static to keep 0 W. NODE_POWER_SOURCE=prometheus without a query now runs the otel preset; before, it read nothing. KEPLER_AVAILABLE is removed: nothing read it, and an alias would have switched every install to Kepler. Use NODE_POWER_PRESET=kepler or kepler-legacy. The facility default is now the otel preset. The datacenter_* names need FACILITY_PRESET=legacy, which is deprecated and removed in v0.4.0. FACILITY_POLL_INTERVAL of 0 or less now stops the controller manager at start. FACILITY_ZONE_AMBIENT_METRIC_TEMPLATE and FACILITY_RACK_POWER_METRIC_TEMPLATE are removed: they were documented as planned and never read. Use FACILITY_ZONE_AMBIENT_TEMP_QUERY and FACILITY_RACK_POWER_QUERY. The chart no longer sets FACILITY_PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS; it defaults to PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS. Power cap configuration Variable Default Description PERFORMANCE_CAP_WATTS 5000 Absolute CPU power cap for performance nodes (watts). The CPU of a GPU node gets it whatever the node’s profile. ECO_CAP_WATTS 120 Absolute CPU power cap for eco CPU-only nodes (watts). A GPU node never gets it: capping the CPU of a GPU node slows the GPU data feed by more than it saves. Earlier releases wrote it on eco GPU nodes too. CPU_PERFORMANCE_CAP_PCT_OF_MAX 100 CPU cap as percentage of max for performance nodes CPU_ECO_CAP_PCT_OF_MAX 60 CPU cap as percentage of max for eco nodes CPU_WRITE_ABSOLUTE_CAPS false If true, write absolute watts instead of percentage GPU_PERFORMANCE_CAP_PCT_OF_MAX 100 GPU cap as percentage of max for performance nodes GPU_ECO_CAP_PCT_OF_MAX 60 GPU cap as percentage of max for eco nodes GPU_WRITE_ABSOLUTE_CAPS false If true, write absolute GPU watts instead of percentage GPU_MODEL_CAPS_JSON {} JSON map of GPU model name to {"minCapWatts": N, "maxCapWatts": M} GPU_PRODUCT_LABEL_KEYS joulie.io/gpu.product,nvidia.com/gpu.product,amd.com/gpu.product-name,beta.amd.com/gpu.product-name,amd.com/gpu.product,amd.com/gpu.family Comma-separated node label keys to read the GPU product name from, first match wins. The AMD node labeller names the board in amd.com/gpu.product-name (and beta.amd.com/gpu.product-name); amd.com/gpu.product is the older key, and the family code in amd.com/gpu.family (for example GC_11_0_0) names no board, so it comes last. When its GPU inventory fails, the agent reads these default labels, in this order; it does not read this variable. Policy configuration Variable Default Description POLICY_TYPE static_partition Policy algorithm: static_partition, queue_aware_v1, or rule_swap_v1 STATIC_HP_FRAC 0.50 Fraction of nodes allocated to performance in static_partition, split across hardware families in proportion to their size, at least one node per family QUEUE_HP_BASE_FRAC 0.60 Base fraction of performance nodes in queue_aware_v1. The resulting count is split across hardware families in proportion to their size, at least one node per family QUEUE_HP_MIN 1 Minimum performance nodes in queue_aware_v1 QUEUE_HP_MAX 1000000 Maximum performance nodes in queue_aware_v1 QUEUE_PERF_PER_HP_NODE 10 Running or pending performance pods per performance node in queue_aware_v1 The controller manager exports the split as joulie_policy_family_nodes{family} and joulie_policy_family_performance_nodes{family}, where family is gpu:<model> or cpu:<model>. See Metrics.
Governor control Off by default. With GOVERNOR_CONTROL on, the controller manager writes a vendor-neutral governor preset into each managed node’s NodeTwin, spec.cpu.governor and spec.gpu.governor, chosen by the profile the node runs at: a draining node keeps the performance presets until its performance pods finish, as it keeps the performance caps. The agent maps a preset to the node’s native governor, energy-performance preference, performance level or clock locks, and writes no preset unless its own GOVERNOR_WRITES is true (see “Agent governor control”).
A node gets only a preset its agent lists in NodeHardware status.cpu.governor.presets or status.gpu.governor.presets. Any other preset is not written and nothing replaces it, auto included, so a setting the node’s operator chose stays; the controller manager logs one warning per node. A node whose agent does not discover governors lists none and gets none. A GPU node gets no CPU governor unless CPU_GOVERNOR_ON_GPU_NODES is true, the rule the CPU cap follows. Only GPU nodes get a GPU governor. An empty preset writes none for that profile. Turning control off, for one component or both, removes the field in the next spec write; the agent then puts back the state it recorded before its first write. Nothing changes on a node until its agent also runs with GOVERNOR_WRITES true (see “Agent governor control”). A value the controller manager cannot use logs a warning and keeps the default; an unknown GOVERNOR_CONTROL means off. Variable Default Description GOVERNOR_CONTROL off off, cpu (CPU governors only), gpu (GPU governors only) or all. CPU_GOVERNOR_PERFORMANCE_PRESET performance CPU preset of performance nodes: performance (highest frequency at any load), balanced (demand-driven, quick ramp) or efficiency (demand-driven with an energy bias). CPU_GOVERNOR_ECO_PRESET efficiency CPU preset of eco nodes. CPU_GOVERNOR_ECO_BOOST empty on or off: frequency boost (turbo) with the eco preset, on nodes whose agent found a boost control (status.cpu.governor.boost). Empty leaves boost alone. CPU_GOVERNOR_ON_GPU_NODES false Write the CPU governor on GPU nodes too. GPU_GOVERNOR_PERFORMANCE_PRESET empty GPU preset of performance nodes: auto, sustained, efficient, low, peak, or empty for none. GPU_GOVERNOR_ECO_PRESET efficient GPU preset of eco nodes; set it to an empty value to write none. GPU_GOVERNOR_ECO_CEILING_PCT_OF_MAX 80 Compute clock ceiling of the efficient preset, in percent of the GPU’s maximum compute clock, in (0, 100]. Written only with efficient; a value out of range gives 80. The default is provisional: in the simulator’s governor exploration 75 slowed eco work past the eco class’s 20 % p95 limit and 80 did not (see Model changes). GPU_GOVERNOR_MODEL_PRESETS_JSON {} Presets per GPU model: {"<model>": {"performance": "<preset>", "eco": "<preset>", "ecoCeilingPctOfMax": <pct>}}. Keyed like GPU_MODEL_CAPS_JSON, by the GPU product label value, and also matched against the GPU model the agent reports. A field left out keeps the default above, "" writes none for that model, and an invalid field is dropped with a warning. GPU presets: auto is the vendor default. sustained holds the data-path clocks (memory, fabric) at their maximum and keeps idle gating, leaving the compute clock free to idle; a demand-driven governor sees only a GPU’s own kernels, so a GPU that receives a peer transfer can stay at low data-path clocks, and on families where those clocks bound the transfer, sustained removes that limit at some idle power. No default selects it: opt a model in through GPU_GOVERNOR_MODEL_PRESETS_JSON once a measurement on that model shows the gain. efficient puts the compute clock under the ceiling and leaves the data path dynamic. low and peak are for experiments; peak turns idle gating off on AMD GPUs. These defaults are provisional until measured. Hardware modeling says what each preset means, and the controller manager page which node gets which.
The overview dashboard’s “Agent: Governors” row plots the presets in effect (joulie_agent_governor_state) and the writes per result (joulie_agent_governor_writes_total).
Facility metrics The facility poller reads six inputs from Prometheus, each with one grouped query per poll. The outdoor ambient temperature, IT power and cooling power are one value each; the twin uses the IT power for PSU stress and the ambient temperature for cooling stress, and the controller manager logs PUE as (IT power + cooling power) / IT power. The zone, rack and node inputs return one series per cooling zone, rack or node (see “Node topology” below). An input whose query fails or returns nothing is unknown until a later poll reads it, never the value of an earlier poll. Every query is counted in joulie_twin_input_queries_total{input,result}, and the three single values are exported as joulie_twin_facility_* (Metrics).
Variable Default Chart Description ENABLE_FACILITY_METRICS false false Poll the facility inputs. The first poll runs at start. FACILITY_PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS, or http://prometheus-operated.monitoring:9090 when that is unset unset Prometheus of the facility queries only. FACILITY_POLL_INTERVAL 30s 30s How often the inputs are polled. 0 or less stops the controller manager at start. FACILITY_PRESET otel otel otel: the facility, cooling zone, rack and host metrics of the input contract, all six inputs. legacy: the datacenter_ambient_temperature_celsius, datacenter_total_it_power_watts and datacenter_cooling_power_watts names read before v0.3.0, the three single inputs only; deprecated, removed in v0.4.0. custom: only the inputs whose query is set below. FACILITY_AMBIENT_TEMP_QUERY from the preset unset Outdoor ambient temperature, one value in degrees Celsius. FACILITY_IT_POWER_QUERY from the preset unset Power of the IT equipment, one value in watts. FACILITY_COOLING_POWER_QUERY from the preset unset Power of the cooling, one value in watts. FACILITY_ZONE_AMBIENT_TEMP_QUERY from the preset unset Ambient temperature of each cooling zone, keyed by the translated joulie.cooling_zone.name label (joulie_cooling_zone_name by default), whose values are the nodes’ joulie.io/cooling-zone label values. FACILITY_RACK_POWER_QUERY from the preset unset Power of each rack in watts, keyed by the translated joulie.rack.name label (joulie_rack_name), whose values are the nodes’ joulie.io/rack label values. FACILITY_NODE_INLET_TEMP_QUERY from the preset unset Inlet temperature of each node, keyed by the translated k8s.node.name label (k8s_node_name). A query variable replaces its input’s query under any preset. A bare metric name is aggregated by the input’s key label, avg for a temperature and sum for a power, so FACILITY_IT_POWER_QUERY=ups_output_power_watts runs sum(ups_output_power_watts). Any other query is kept as written and must return one series, or for the zone, rack and node inputs one series per key carrying the key label.
Deprecated aliases, removed in v0.4.0: FACILITY_AMBIENT_TEMP_METRIC, FACILITY_IT_POWER_METRIC, FACILITY_COOLING_POWER_METRIC, the former names of the first three query variables. They are read only when the new name is unset, with a warning naming the replacement, and the bare metric name they hold keeps its meaning.
Node topology Joulie supports optional per-rack PSU stress and per-zone cooling stress. This is activated by adding standard node labels:
joulie.io/rack: physical rack identifier (e.g., rack-1) joulie.io/cooling-zone: cooling zone identifier (e.g., zone-a) When these labels are present, the controller manager computes PSU stress per rack instead of cluster-wide: the rack’s power is the facility’s rack power input (FACILITY_RACK_POWER_QUERY, keyed by the joulie.io/rack value) when it reads that rack, otherwise the sum of the estimated power of the rack’s nodes. The ambient temperature of a node’s twin is the most local one known: the node’s inlet temperature (FACILITY_NODE_INLET_TEMP_QUERY), then its cooling zone’s (FACILITY_ZONE_AMBIENT_TEMP_QUERY, keyed by the joulie.io/cooling-zone value), then the outdoor ambient. The twin model interfaces remain the same; topology just groups nodes for more accurate stress computation.
Nodes without topology labels fall back to cluster-wide stress computation, and still use their inlet temperature when the facility reads one.
Scheduler extender Variable Default Description EXTENDER_ADDR :9876 Bind address for the scheduler extender HTTP server METRICS_ADDR :9877 Address for the scheduler’s Prometheus metrics endpoint CACHE_TTL 30s Minimum interval between rebuilding the scoring maps from the informer cache. Reads no longer hit the API server; NodeTwin and NodeHardware are watched. TWIN_STALENESS_THRESHOLD 5m Duration after which NodeTwin data is considered stale With schedulerExtender.hostNetwork: true the chart deploys the extender with strategy Recreate: an old and a new pod cannot hold the host port on one node, so a rolling update would never finish. Pods are still scheduled while the extender restarts only if the scheduler configuration marks it ignorable: true; otherwise also set schedulerExtender.nodeName, so the new extender pod does not wait for the scheduler that waits for it.
Simulator This section covers the binaries under simulator/cmd. Each subsection names the binary that reads its variables.
Simulator thermal model The simulator (simulator/cmd/simulator) reads these variables at startup to build its base hardware profile. A node class in SIM_NODE_CLASS_CONFIG overrides one per node with the key in parentheses, under the class’s model:.
Temperature follows a first-order lag toward ambient plus power divided by the watts per degree, and is reported in the telemetry response. It reduces throughput only when thermal throttling is enabled, which it is not by default: both thresholds of a device are 0, which means off. Setting either variable of a pair turns throttling on for that device, and the other one takes the former default shown in its row. A node class key works differently: a threshold the class leaves unset comes from the base profile, which is 0 unless the environment sets the pair, so set both in a class, the full threshold above the start. A class full threshold alone is accepted and throttles linearly from 0 °C, so even an idle node is throttled. A class start threshold alone is rejected: every class in SIM_NODE_CLASS_CONFIG is ignored, with only a warning in the log, and all nodes run on the base profile. For a GPU start this happens only when the profile has GPUs, that is with SIM_GPU_COUNT or a class gpu.count above 0. With no GPU count it is accepted and GPU throttling stays off. See Hardware Modeling, sections 5.5 and 6.6, for why throttling is opt-in.
Variable Default Description SIM_CPU_AMBIENT_TEMP_C 24 CPU ambient temperature in °C (cpuAmbientTempC) SIM_CPU_THERMAL_TAU_MS 4000 CPU thermal time constant in milliseconds (cpuThermalTauMs) SIM_CPU_WATTS_PER_DELTA_C 8 CPU watts per °C above ambient at equilibrium (cpuWattsPerDeltaC) SIM_CPU_THERMAL_THROTTLE_START_C 0 (off) CPU temperature in °C where thermal throttling starts (cpuThermalThrottleStartC). 85 when only SIM_CPU_THERMAL_THROTTLE_FULL_C is set, the default before throttling became opt-in. SIM_CPU_THERMAL_THROTTLE_FULL_C 0 (off) CPU temperature in °C where thermal throttling reaches throughput 0 (cpuThermalThrottleFullC). 97 when only SIM_CPU_THERMAL_THROTTLE_START_C is set. SIM_GPU_AMBIENT_TEMP_C 24 GPU ambient temperature in °C (gpu.ambientTempC) SIM_GPU_THERMAL_TAU_MS 2500 GPU thermal time constant in milliseconds (gpu.thermalTauMs) SIM_GPU_WATTS_PER_DELTA_C 12 GPU watts per °C above ambient at equilibrium (gpu.wattsPerDeltaC) SIM_GPU_THERMAL_THROTTLE_START_C 0 (off) GPU temperature in °C where thermal throttling starts (gpu.thermalThrottleStartC). 82 when only SIM_GPU_THERMAL_THROTTLE_FULL_C is set. SIM_GPU_THERMAL_THROTTLE_FULL_C 0 (off) GPU temperature in °C where thermal throttling is full (gpu.thermalThrottleFullC). 92 when only SIM_GPU_THERMAL_THROTTLE_START_C is set. Simulator power limits The simulator (simulator/cmd/simulator) reads these variables at startup too. For a node whose labels match the hardware catalogue, a variable that is unset leaves the field to the catalogue; the built-in default applies only to hardware the catalogue does not know. A node class key (in parentheses) wins over both, and a value of 0 or less counts as unset. See Hardware Modeling, section 3.1.
Variable Default Description SIM_P_MAX_W sockets x catalogue TDP, else 420 Peak CPU power of the generic model, at full load and full frequency (pMaxW). A node with a measured curve uses the curve instead. SIM_CPU_SOCKET_CAP_MAX_W catalogue TDP, else 400 Upper end of the per-socket CPU cap: the node cap is split evenly over the sockets and clamped to this range (cpuSocketCapMaxW). SIM_CPU_SOCKET_CAP_MIN_W catalogue cTDP low end, else 0.55 x TDP, else 120 Lower end of the per-socket CPU cap (cpuSocketCapMinW). SIM_GPU_MAX_WATTS_PER_GPU catalogue maxBoardPowerW, else 300 Board power of one GPU at full load, and its highest cap (gpu.maxWattsPerGpu). SIM_GPU_MIN_CAP_WATTS_PER_GPU catalogue minBoardPowerW, else half the maximum, else 80 Lowest cap of one GPU (gpu.minCapWattsPerGpu). A catalogue minimum above a maximum set by a class or a variable is lowered to that maximum. A measured two-socket curve from the catalogue is scaled by sockets/2 on a node with another socket count.
Upgrading to v0.3.0.
A node the catalogue matches now takes the five values above from the catalogue: an H100 SXM caps between 300 and 700 W instead of 80 and 300 W, and two EPYC 9534 sockets peak at 560 W instead of 420 W. Set the variable, or the class key, to keep a value. A one-socket node with a measured curve now draws half the two-socket curve. SIM_POD_W, SIM_DVFS_DROP_W_PER_PCT, SIM_GPU_ALPHA_UTIL and SIM_GPU_BETA_CAP, and the node class keys podW, dvfsDropWPerPct, noiseStddevW and gpu.powerModel, are removed: nothing read them. The simulator still starts with them set and logs one warning per variable or key. Simulator physics step The simulator (simulator/cmd/simulator) advances the model of a node outside the emulate-mode cluster spec only in a physics step, in simulated time; a read or a control never advances it. A step splits its time into equal substeps, and the energy it books is the integral of the instantaneous power over them. See Power Simulator.
Variable Default Description SIM_POLL_INTERVAL 15s Kubernetes mode: how often the simulator lists pods and nodes. A value of 0 or less logs a warning and takes 15s. SIM_PHYSICS_TICK 1s Kubernetes mode without emulate mode: every modelled node is stepped by the wall time since the last tick, in substeps of at most 100 ms. A value of 0 or less logs a warning and takes 1s. In emulate mode SIM_EMULATE_TICK steps them instead, and standalone mode steps them on its own tick. SIM_SA_SUBSTEP SIM_SA_DT Standalone mode: the longest physics substep, in simulated seconds. Each SIM_SA_DT tick is split into equal substeps no longer than this; the default is one substep per tick. A shorter substep follows the cap, frequency and thermal lags more closely at the cost of run time. Simulator hardware emulation fakesmi (simulator/cmd/fakesmi) stands in for nvidia-smi, rocm-smi and amd-smi on an emulated node. It runs as the tool its name says, through a bin/<tool> link, and reads and writes the node’s emulated hardware files instead of a driver. The agent does not read these variables; only fakesmi does.
Variable Default Description HWEMU_SYS_ROOT /host-sys The emulated node’s sys/ directory, where the amdgpu PCI and hwmon attributes live. The default is where an emulated agent pod mounts it. HWEMU_STATE_ROOT /emu/state The emulated node’s state/ directory: tools.json, which lists the tools the node has and the variant each one emulates, the NVML state of NVIDIA GPUs, and the per-card AMD values sysfs has no text attribute for (amdgpu/card<N>/). The default is where an emulated agent pod mounts it. HWEMU_ROOTFS / The file system the real tool would run in, where fakesmi looks for what the tool needs before it runs (below). The default is the agent container’s own root. HWEMU_UNPRIVILEGED false Run the tools as a user without root would: 1, true or another word Go’s strconv.ParseBool reads as true; anything else, unset included, means root. A set then changes nothing: nvidia-smi -pl, -pm, -lgc, -lmc, -rgc and -rmc exit 4 with Insufficient Permissions; amd-smi set and reset fail with PermissionError: Command requires elevation; a rocm-smi set exits 0 with the failure only at --loglevel debug, and prints nothing at all on a family whose profile sets gpus.dpm.unprivilegedSetIsNoop. Reads work as with root. A tool that tools.json does not list exits 127 with fakesmi: <tool> is not installed on this emulated node.
A listed tool first checks the requirements of its tools.json entry, in order, under HWEMU_ROOTFS: each requirement is a list of paths, and one existing path meets it. The first requirement with none of its paths present ends the call, before any GPU state is read, with the exit code and message the real tool gives without that file. The requirements are profile data (gpus.tools[].requires); a tool without requirements always runs. The builtin profiles nvidia-h100-nvl-8gpu, nvidia-h100-sxm-8gpu, amd-instinct-mi300x-8gpu and amd-radeon-pro-w7900-4gpu list:
Tool Requirement (any one path) Exit Message nvidia-smi /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, the ELF loader 127 none: exec fails, which a shell reports as 127 nvidia-smi /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libnvidia-ml.so.1 or /usr/lib64/libnvidia-ml.so.1 12 NVIDIA-SMI couldn't find libnvidia-ml.so library in your system. ...; 12 is nvidia-smi’s “NVML Shared Library couldn’t be found or loaded” rocm-smi, amd-smi /usr/bin/env, from the scripts’ #!/usr/bin/env python3 127 none rocm-smi, amd-smi /usr/bin/python3 or /usr/local/bin/python3 127 /usr/bin/env: 'python3': No such file or directory An empty HWEMU_ROOTFS is the default, /. Only a caller of package simulator/pkg/hwemu/smi that builds its own Env with an empty RootFS skips the checks, as the in-process agent tests do.
Simulator emulate mode In emulate mode the simulator (simulator/cmd/simulator) emulates the bare-metal nodes a cluster spec lists: for each one it keeps a sysfs tree, /proc/cpuinfo and GPU tool state under SIM_HWEMU_ROOT/<node>/, and advances them on a fixed tick, so an unmodified agent pod that mounts them discovers and caps the node as it would a real one. Nodes the spec does not list keep the label-based model. /control/<node> answers 409 for an emulated node, whose limits are written to its files instead. See Emulate mode.
Variable Default Description SIM_EMULATE false Turn emulate mode on. The simulator refuses to start when SIM_STANDALONE is also set, or when SIM_CLUSTER_SPEC is empty. Workloads run on the v1 engine; SIM_WORKLOAD_MODEL=legacy is refused, since a legacy trace cannot drive emulated nodes (see Simulator workloads and scenarios). SIM_CLUSTER_SPEC (empty) Path of the cluster spec, a sim.joulie.io/v1alpha1 ClusterSpec such as tests/simcluster/specs/smoke.yaml. It names each node, its hardware profile, pool, rack and cooling zone, and the facility. SIM_HWEMU_ROOT /var/lib/joulie-hwemu Directory of the emulated trees: one <node>/ per spec node, lib/fakesmi and facility-ledger.json. One simulator holds it at a time; a second one fails to start. SIM_EMULATE_TICK 1s Physics tick: every spec node advances to wall time once per tick. A tick that runs late is counted and the next one catches up. The nodes outside the spec are stepped on the same tick (see “Simulator physics step”). SIM_GPU_RECEIVER_GATE profile The receiver gate of the peer links between the GPUs of a node, which bounds the copies into a GPU by that GPU’s data-path state: profile follows each hardware profile’s gpus.transfer.receiverGate.enabled, off in every builtin profile; off disables it everywhere; on enables it on every GPU profile with the profile’s fractions, for what-if runs (a profile that leaves a fraction unset lets the whole link through). Any other value logs a warning naming the variable and takes profile. A gated copy slows the v1 job that makes it (see peer transfers). SIM_EMULATE_WORKERS 0 Nodes stepped in parallel; 0 means GOMAXPROCS, at most 12. A step is mostly system calls on the node’s files, which contend past about 12 workers (see Tick cost); a set value is used as given. SIM_FAKESMI_SOURCE /usr/local/lib/joulie/fakesmi The fakesmi binary to install as SIM_HWEMU_ROOT/lib/fakesmi, where every node’s bin/nvidia-smi, bin/rocm-smi and bin/amd-smi link points. It is replaced by rename, and only when its sha256 changed. The simulator image ships it at the default path. Empty skips the copy, for a run outside the image. KUBECONFIG client-go loading rules The cluster the simulator watches, so it can also run on a workstation. Without a kubeconfig it uses the in-cluster configuration. The simulator logs the API server it uses. Hardware profiles are the builtin ones in simulator/pkg/hwemu/profiles/, plus local ones from SIM_PROFILES_DIR. The facility values come from the spec’s facility block and fall back to SIM_FACILITY_AMBIENT_TEMP_C, SIM_FACILITY_TEMP_AMPLITUDE_C and SIM_FACILITY_TEMP_PERIOD_H.
Restarts. An existing tree is resumed, not rendered again: energy counters, the limits agents wrote and NVML state continue from disk, and only missing files are put back, so nothing an agent pod holds open is replaced. Exported energy counters never decrease across a restart; they continue from a ledger in the tree. No energy accrues while the simulator is down, so a restart shows as a gap in the rate, never as a reset.
Recovery. A tree rendered for another profile, node or profile values, or one with an entry of the wrong kind (a file where a directory belongs), stops the start with an error that names the node. Make sure no agent pod mounts that node, remove SIM_HWEMU_ROOT/<node>, and start the simulator again: the node is rendered fresh, with its counters back at zero.

Simulator workloads and scenarios The simulator (simulator/cmd/simulator) drives a workload trace through the cluster with one of two engines, SIM_WORKLOAD_MODEL:
legacy, outside emulate mode: the engine experiments 01 to 03 were measured with. It creates bare pods and deletes each when its work is done, infers the class from the pod’s affinity, and completes a job by force after it stalls for SIM_WORKLOAD_STALL_FORCE_COMPLETE. v1, in emulate mode: each group of trace jobs becomes one batch/v1 Job (Indexed when larger than one, backoffLimit: 0), pods carry their class as the annotation joulie.io/workload-class, a finished pod is marked complete for KWOK instead of deleted, and nothing is completed by force: a job or a run that makes no progress is reported as stalled. Each job’s progress follows the throughput of the emulated hardware it runs on, energy is attributed from the emulated nodes’ energy ledgers, and the results are OTLP JSON Lines in the run’s directory. See Workload Scenarios. Variable Read by v1 default Legacy default Description SIM_WORKLOAD_MODEL both v1 with SIM_EMULATE=true legacy otherwise legacy or v1. v1 without emulate mode and legacy with it stop the start. SIM_WORKLOAD_TRACE_PATH both (empty) (empty) A trace file, or a directory of them, loaded at startup. Legacy replays it from startup. v1 starts it as an implicit run with id SIM_RUN_ID; a run that fails to start is logged and the run API stays open. The chart sets /etc/joulie-sim-trace/trace.jsonl outside emulate mode. SIM_WORKLOAD_TICK legacy 1s Period of the legacy workload loop. A value that does not parse as a duration, or of 0 or less, logs a warning and takes 1s. A v1 run advances once per emulator tick (SIM_EMULATE_TICK) and does not read it. SIM_WORKLOAD_IMAGE both registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9 the same Container image of every workload pod. SIM_BASE_SPEED_PER_CORE both 1 1 Work units one core, or one GPU, does per second at full speed. A v3 trace sizes work with it, so a job’s ideal runtime is its durationSec. A run request’s baseSpeedPerCore replaces it for that run. A value that does not parse as a number is ignored without a warning and takes 1. SIM_WORKLOAD_OWNER v1 job fixed pod job: one Job object per group; pod: bare pods. SIM_WORKLOAD_INTENT v1 annotation fixed affinity How a pod declares its class: annotation (joulie.io/workload-class), affinity (a performance pod gets NotIn [eco] on joulie.io/power-profile, ANDed into each required term of the trace’s affinity), both or none. SIM_WORKLOAD_COMPLETION v1 kwok fixed delete kwok: a finished pod is annotated sim.joulie.io/complete: "true" and the KWOK Stage pod-complete moves it to Succeeded; delete: the pod is deleted. SIM_WORKLOAD_NAMESPACE v1 (empty) Namespace of every pod; empty keeps each trace record’s. SIM_WORKLOAD_NODE_SELECTOR v1 sim.joulie.io/cluster=<spec name> fixed type=kwok key=value pairs, comma separated, added to every pod’s node selector where the trace does not set the key. The default keeps workload pods off every Node outside the cluster spec, such as the one running the simulator. SIM_WORKLOAD_TOLERATIONS v1 kwok.x-k8s.io/node=fake:NoSchedule fixed, the same A JSON list of tolerations added to every pod; [] adds none. Nothing adds a GPU vendor’s toleration for a GPU request unless the cluster runs the ExtendedResourceToleration admission plugin. SIM_WORKLOAD_JOB_TTL v1 10m ttlSecondsAfterFinished of the Job objects; 0 deletes them as they finish. SIM_WORKLOAD_MAX_CREATES_PER_TICK both -1 (no cap) 20 Pods or Job objects created per tick; a positive count or -1. SIM_WORKLOAD_MAX_DELETES_PER_TICK legacy 10 Finished pods deleted per tick; a positive count or -1. SIM_WORKLOAD_KUBE_QPS, SIM_WORKLOAD_KUBE_BURST both 100, 200 30, 50 Rate limits of the workload’s Kubernetes client. SIM_WORKLOAD_STALL_REPORT v1 5m How long a running job must make no progress before joulie.sim.job.stalled, and the whole run before joulie.sim.run.stalled: a submitted job not done, no progress, no pod becoming Running or Succeeded, and every Pending pod Unschedulable, all for this long. Jobs not yet due never count. SIM_WORKLOAD_STALL_FORCE_COMPLETE legacy 120s How long a legacy job may make no progress before it is completed by force; -1 disables it. SIM_RUNS_DIR v1 $SIM_HWEMU_ROOT/_runs Directory of the run directories, <SIM_RUNS_DIR>/<run id>/: trace.jsonl, and otlp/simulator.metrics.jsonl and otlp/simulator.logs.jsonl. SIM_RUN_ID v1 run-<UTC yyyymmdd-hhmmss> Id of the implicit run of SIM_WORKLOAD_TRACE_PATH; no slash, and not . or ... SIM_OTLP_FILE_INTERVAL v1 10s Period of the cumulative metrics snapshot in simulator.metrics.jsonl; one more is written when the run ends. An invalid value stops the start with an error naming the variable, except SIM_WORKLOAD_TICK and SIM_BASE_SPEED_PER_CORE, which fall back to their defaults (see their rows). A variable only the other model reads logs a warning naming it; under v1 that includes SIM_WORKLOAD_TICK. The legacy defaults are the constants of the simulator before these became settings, so a legacy run behaves as before, except for two loader fixes: a trace line longer than 64 KiB loads (up to 16 MiB), and two jobs whose pod names collide in one namespace (pods are named sim-<jobId>, sanitized and cut to 50 characters) both run, the later one with the lowest free -<n> suffix, instead of the second create failing and the job being completed by force.
Run API. In v1 emulate mode the simulator serves one run at a time on its HTTP port; in every other mode these paths answer 412.
Path Method Answer /sim/v1/runs POST Starts a run. Body: runId, optional trace (a path inside the simulator, default <SIM_RUNS_DIR>/<runId>/trace.jsonl), optional clusterName, and options overriding the settings above for this run (owner, intent, completion, namespace, jobTTL, nodeSelector, tolerations, maxCreatesPerTick, stallReport, baseSpeedPerCore; an empty nodeSelector or tolerations clears the default, null keeps it). 201 with runId, jobs, groups and startedAt; 400 for a bad request or trace, naming the trace line; 409 while a run is active, or when the run id already has results. /sim/v1/runs/current GET 200 with the active or last run’s status: phase (running, finished or aborted), elapsedSeconds, allSubmitted, the jobs per state and runStalled; 404 before the first run. /sim/v1/runs/current/finish POST Ends the run; jobs not done end incomplete. ?cleanup=true also deletes the run’s Job objects in the background. 200 with the final status once the run’s files are closed. Permissions. The joulie-simulator ClusterRole of charts/joulie-simulator grants get, list, watch, create and delete on pods and nodes, which both engines use; patch on pods, for the v1 completion annotation; get, list, watch, create and delete on batch jobs, for the v1 Job objects and their cleanup; and get, list and watch on joulie.io nodetwins, which a v1 run observes for each node’s schedulable class and never writes.
KWOK Stage. With SIM_WORKLOAD_COMPLETION=kwok, a pod ends only through a KWOK Stage named pod-complete that selects Running pods annotated sim.joulie.io/complete: "true": scripts/simcluster/manifests/stage-pod-complete.yaml, adapted from KWOK v0.8.0. It replaces KWOK’s own pod-complete Stage, which completes every Running pod a Job owns on a timer, before it did its work; the simulated cluster applies it after KWOK’s Stages. On another KWOK cluster, apply it the same way, or set SIM_WORKLOAD_COMPLETION=delete. simscenario run refuses a cluster whose pod-complete Stage does not select the annotation.
Scenario runner. scripts/simcluster/scenario.sh (make simcluster-scenario SCENARIO=<file>) reads these settings besides those of the simulated cluster scripts:
Variable Default Description SCENARIO (none) The scenario file, for make simcluster-scenario. Simulator telemetry export In emulate mode the simulator (simulator/cmd/simulator) pushes OpenTelemetry metrics of every emulated node and of the facility as OTLP JSON over HTTP, for example straight to a Prometheus started with --web.enable-otlp-receiver. Events are always written to events.jsonl and pushed only when a logs endpoint is set. Names and Prometheus spellings: Simulator Metrics.
In every mode the simulator also answers reads of one node over HTTP: GET /otlp/telemetry/{node} and GET /telemetry/{node} serve the same OTLP JSON ExportMetricsServiceRequest, the format TELEMETRY_CPU_HTTP_ENDPOINT and NODE_POWER_HTTP_ENDPOINT read. /telemetry/{node} used to serve the legacy packagePowerWatts JSON: a client that still parses it adds ?format=legacy, which is deprecated and removed in v0.4.0, and the simulator logs one warning per process when it is used. ?format=otlp asks for the default explicitly; any other format value is refused with 400.
