Each has _METRICS_ and _LOGS_ variants that win for their signal. OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL 60000 Milliseconds between metrics pushes. A rate() window over the pushed counters should cover at least 4 intervals. OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER, OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER otlp none turns off that signal’s push. The export follows the OpenTelemetry exporter specification with three deviations:
Only http/json is supported; the specification’s default is http/protobuf, and any other protocol stops the start. Nothing is pushed without an endpoint; the specification’s default is http://localhost:4318. A 404 from the logs endpoint turns the logs push off after one warning. Prometheus has no logs receiver, so a base endpoint pointing at Prometheus would otherwise fail on every push. Points are cumulative: Prometheus rejects delta temporality unless its otlp-deltatocumulative feature is on. A push is retried on 429, 502, 503 and 504, honouring Retry-After, and never on 400 (such as out-of-order samples) or 500. Each request carries at most 64 node resources, plus the facility. A per-signal endpoint is used exactly as given, so it needs the full path; a base URL there is a common mistake.
Helm values of charts/joulie-simulator, rendered only when emulate.enabled is true:
Value Default Effect otel.metricsEndpoint "" OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT. otel.logsEndpoint "" OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT. otel.exportIntervalMillis 10000 OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL, in milliseconds since Helm cannot parse durations. otel.resourceAttributes {} OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, joined as key=value pairs. For queries, Prometheus should promote k8s.node.name and host.name onto the data series (otlp.promote_resource_attributes); without that, the node name is joined from target_info. See Simulator Metrics.
Simulator hardware profiles The simulator (simulator/cmd/simulator) emulates a node from a hardware profile picked by name: one of the builtin profiles in simulator/pkg/hwemu/profiles/, or a local one. Local profiles stay outside the repository and are the only ones whose measured sources (measured: provenance) may name the machine they were measured on, such as a calibration of your own nodes. A builtin profile may cite a measurement too, but describes the machine by its hardware only.
Variable Default Description SIM_PROFILES_DIR (empty) Directory of local hardware profiles: every *.yaml file directly in it, each with a name equal to its file name without .yaml. Empty means the builtin profiles only, and so does a directory with no *.yaml in it, such as a mounted ConfigMap that holds no profile yet. Hidden entries (a leading dot) are skipped. A directory that does not exist, a path that is not a directory and a *.yml file, or a .yaml suffix in another case such as .YAML, are errors, never a fallback to the builtins. A local profile may extend (extends:) a builtin profile or another local one, by the same merge rules the builtins use. It may not take a builtin’s name, since one of the two would be hidden: give it a new name and extend the builtin instead. The simulator logs the local profiles once, as local profiles loaded dir=<dir> profiles=<names>.
kubectl plugin The kubectl joulie plugin requires no configuration. It reads your current kubeconfig context.
# Install go build -o kubectl-joulie ./cmd/kubectl-joulie mv kubectl-joulie /usr/local/bin/ # Usage kubectl joulie status # cluster energy overview

body:
This page describes runtime IO contracts:
how Joulie reads telemetry inputs, how Joulie sends control intents. If you want the CRD-level summary first, read CRD and Policy Model. This page is the detailed runtime reference for the telemetry and control contract.
It is not the /metrics exposition contract. For exported metrics, see Metrics Reference.
Why this abstraction exists Joulie must run in two worlds with the same control logic:
real hardware clusters, simulator/KWOK clusters. So agent/controller manager logic depends on provider interfaces, not directly on sysfs or simulator HTTP shape.
Backend selection in one sentence Environment variables tell the agent which telemetry backend to read from and which control backend to write to.
Conceptually:
NodeHardware defines discovered node capability NodeTwin.spec defines the target Agent environment variables define the wiring Backend configuration should not carry hardware identity. Its job is only backend routing. In particular:
do not conflate backend selection with CPU/GPU model or inventory identity, do not use it as a substitute for NodeHardware, do use it to route simulator HTTP or host backends. Telemetry provider model Telemetry input can come from:
host (real node interfaces), http (an endpoint serving the HTTP input format, such as the simulator), none. Cluster-level inputs come from Prometheus and are read by the controller manager, not the agent: see Input metrics (OpenTelemetry).
Quality handling should distinguish fresh, stale, and missing samples so policy can degrade safely.
Control provider model Control outputs are routed by backend:
host: write real interfaces (RAPL/cpufreq), http: send intents to simulator, none. Result semantics:
applied blocked error none (no intent selected for that control path) This allows desired vs applied behavior auditing.
Current CPU control intents Supported intent actions:
rapl.set_power_cap_watts dvfs.set_throttle_pct DVFS intent is normalized as throttlePct (0..100) to stay portable across heterogeneous CPUs. Backend-specific frequency writes remain implementation details.
GPU control intent Supported GPU intent action:
gpu.set_power_cap_watts Payload:
capWattsPerGpu Semantics:
node-level intent is translated to per-device enforcement, same cap is applied to all GPUs on the node, result is reported as applied|blocked|error in NodeTwin.status.controlStatus.gpu. Current HTTP contracts Telemetry endpoints:
GET /otlp/telemetry/{node}: one OTLP JSON document, the HTTP input format. Point TELEMETRY_CPU_HTTP_ENDPOINT and NODE_POWER_HTTP_ENDPOINT here. GET /telemetry/{node}: the same OTLP JSON document by default (?format=otlp asks for it explicitly). GET /telemetry/{node}?format=legacy: the legacy JSON below. It is deprecated and removed in v0.4.0, and the simulator logs one warning per process when it is read. The agent and the controller manager still read the legacy JSON, with a warning, until v0.4.0. Any other format is refused with 400. Accepted minimal legacy payloads include:
{ "packagePowerWatts": 245.3 } or
{ "cpu": { "packagePowerWatts": 245.3 } } The simulator exports a richer payload than this minimal contract. Important optional fields currently include:
top level: packagePowerWatts instantPackagePowerWatts cpu.*: packagePowerWatts instantPowerWatts utilization memoryIntensity ioIntensity freqScale temperatureC thermalThrottlePct gpu.*: powerWattsTotal avgPowerWattsTotal utilization memoryIntensity cpuFeedIntensity devices Controllers should treat these richer fields as additive observability, not as a replacement for the minimal contract above.
HTTP input format The agent (TELEMETRY_CPU_SOURCE=http) and the controller manager (NODE_POWER_SOURCE=http) read the same format: one OTLP JSON ExportMetricsServiceRequest per GET of the endpoint, with {node} replaced by the node name. It is the protobuf JSON mapping of OTLP: lowerCamelCase keys, 64-bit integers as decimal strings, integer enums. A body with a top-level resourceMetrics key is OTLP; any other body is read as the legacy JSON above, with one deprecation warning.
Node filter. A resource that carries k8s.node.name is read only when it names the node. A resource without it is always read, since an endpoint that serves one node need not name it. Power per component, a component being one (hw.type, hw.id): from a cumulative hw.energy series: the energy difference to the previous point over the difference of their timeUnixNano, the producer’s clock. A decrease or a new startTimeUnixNano is a reset, and an interval longer than the rate window (PROMETHEUS_RATE_WINDOW for the controller manager, 5 minutes for the agent) is too long; either interval is dropped and the series warms up again; from a delta hw.energy point: its value over its own interval; otherwise, and while its energy series warms up, from the hw.power gauge, as rate(energy) or power does in PromQL; duplicates of one component count once, with their maximum. Sum. The agent sums the hw.type=cpu components. The controller manager sums cpu and gpu, or reads hw.host.energy and hw.host.power as one component under NODE_POWER_SCOPE=host. Warm-up. A reading is unavailable while a selected component has only an energy series without a rate and no power gauge: its first point, or its first after a reset. The controller manager then writes 0 W with source: http for that reconcile. A minimal document for node worker-01 with one CPU package:
{"resourceMetrics": [{ "resource": {"attributes": [ {"key": "k8s.node.name", "value": {"stringValue": "worker-01"}}, {"key": "service.instance.id", "value": {"stringValue": "worker-01"}}]}, "scopeMetrics": [{"metrics": [ {"name": "hw.energy", "unit": "J", "sum": {"aggregationTemporality": 2, "isMonotonic": true, "dataPoints": [{"attributes": [{"key": "hw.id", "value": {"stringValue": "cpu0"}}, {"key": "hw.type", "value": {"stringValue": "cpu"}}], "startTimeUnixNano": "1760000000000000000", "timeUnixNano": "1760000060000000000", "asDouble": 15000}]}}, {"name": "hw.power", "unit": "W", "gauge": { "dataPoints": [{"attributes": [{"key": "hw.id", "value": {"stringValue": "cpu0"}}, {"key": "hw.type", "value": {"stringValue": "cpu"}}], "timeUnixNano": "1760000060000000000", "asDouble": 250}]}}]}]}]} Control endpoint:
POST /control/{node} Example request:
{ "node": "worker-01", "action": "dvfs.set_throttle_pct", "throttlePct": 20, "ts": "2026-02-27T00:00:00Z" } Expected response includes:
result (applied|blocked|error) message state (best-effort post-state) Input metrics (OpenTelemetry) The controller manager reads two measured inputs from Prometheus: the power of each node (NODE_POWER_SOURCE=prometheus, the chart default) and the facility readings (ENABLE_FACILITY_METRICS=true). Producers write them as OpenTelemetry metrics, pushed over OTLP to Prometheus’ OTLP receiver: the simulator in emulate mode, an OpenTelemetry Collector, or any exporter that follows the table below. The controller manager does not receive OTLP; it runs PromQL instant queries, GET <PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS>/api/v1/query. Only the controller manager queries Prometheus; the scheduler extender reads NodeTwin.
Each input is one grouped query per reconcile (node power) or per poll (facility). The query aggregates by the key label, so the answer holds one series per node, cooling zone or rack, and every component of a node is in its sum; the answer is never read by keeping the first series returned. A key that comes back twice is refused (the result is counted as error), since it means two producers that Prometheus stores as one target. A node missing from the answer has no reading (source: prometheus-no-data), which is never the value of an earlier reconcile.
The contract All names come from pkg/otel/semconv, and their Prometheus spellings from pkg/otel/promname, which is checked against the translator Prometheus uses (tests/promql). The hw.* names are OpenTelemetry semantic conventions v1.44.0 (Development stability); the joulie.* names are Joulie’s own.
OTel name Unit Instrument Point attributes Prometheus name (default strategy) Read as hw.energy J Counter hw.id, hw.type, hw.name, hw.parent hw_energy_joules_total node power, scope components: rate of the cpu and gpu components hw.power W Gauge the same hw_power_watts node power, scope components: a component without an energy counter hw.host.energy J Counter hw.id=host hw_host_energy_joules_total node power, scope host hw.host.power W Gauge hw.id=host hw_host_power_watts node power, scope host, without an energy counter joulie.facility.ambient_temperature Cel Gauge joulie_facility_ambient_temperature_celsius outdoor ambient temperature (avg) joulie.facility.it.energy J Counter joulie_facility_it_energy_joules_total IT power, as a rate joulie.facility.it.power W Gauge joulie_facility_it_power_watts IT power without an energy counter joulie.facility.cooling.energy J Counter joulie_facility_cooling_energy_joules_total cooling power, as a rate joulie.facility.cooling.power W Gauge joulie_facility_cooling_power_watts cooling power without an energy counter joulie.cooling_zone.ambient_temperature Cel Gauge joulie.cooling_zone.name joulie_cooling_zone_ambient_temperature_celsius ambient temperature of each cooling zone joulie.rack.energy J Counter joulie.rack.name joulie_rack_energy_joules_total power of each rack, as a rate joulie.rack.power W Gauge joulie.rack.name joulie_rack_power_watts power of each rack without an energy counter hw.host.ambient_temperature Cel Gauge hw.id=host hw_host_ambient_temperature_celsius inlet temperature of each node (the hottest sensor) Resource attributes every producer sets:
k8s.node.name: the node a resource describes. It is the node identity of every node metric, and Prometheus keeps it on target_info and, when promoted, on every series. service.instance.id: unique per producer and node. Prometheus derives the instance label from it, so two producers that share one are stored as one target. service.name: the job label. Producer rules, which the simulator follows and tests:
One cpu component per CPU package (hw.id cpu<socket>) and one gpu component per GPU (gpu<index>). RAPL core, uncore and psys zones are never cpu; DRAM is memory (hw.parent=cpu<socket>) and is not part of node power. Whole-host energy only as hw.host.energy and hw.host.power, never as hw.energy; hw.host.* carries no hw.type. Counters never decrease, also across a producer restart (the simulator keeps them in a ledger). A counter that does go back is read as a reset: rate() counts it as a restart from zero and the HTTP reader drops that interval, so neither reads negative power, but rate() reads a spike. The cooling zone and rack names are the values of the nodes’ joulie.io/cooling-zone and joulie.io/rack labels; see Node topology.
The queries With the default window [5m] and the default naming, the otel presets run:
# node power, scope components, labels form sum by (k8s_node_name) (max by (k8s_node_name, hw_type, hw_id) (rate(hw_energy_joules_total{hw_type=~"cpu|gpu"}[5m])) or on (k8s_node_name, hw_type, hw_id) max by (k8s_node_name, hw_type, hw_id) (hw_power_watts{hw_type=~"cpu|gpu"})) # node power, target_info form: every inner selector X becomes X * on (job, instance) group_left (k8s_node_name) max by (job, instance, k8s_node_name) (target_info and on (job, instance) X) # node power, scope host max by (k8s_node_name) (rate(hw_host_energy_joules_total[5m])) or on (k8s_node_name) max by (k8s_node_name) (hw_host_power_watts) # facility avg(joulie_facility_ambient_temperature_celsius) sum(rate(joulie_facility_it_energy_joules_total[5m])) or sum(joulie_facility_it_power_watts) sum(rate(joulie_facility_cooling_energy_joules_total[5m])) or sum(joulie_facility_cooling_power_watts) avg by (joulie_cooling_zone_name) (joulie_cooling_zone_ambient_temperature_celsius) sum by (joulie_rack_name) (rate(joulie_rack_energy_joules_total[5m])) or on (joulie_rack_name) sum by (joulie_rack_name) (joulie_rack_power_watts) max by (k8s_node_name) (hw_host_ambient_temperature_celsius{k8s_node_name!=""} or hw_host_ambient_temperature_celsius{k8s_node_name=""} * on (job, instance) group_left (k8s_node_name) max by (job, instance, k8s_node_name) (target_info and on (job, instance) hw_host_ambient_temperature_celsius{k8s_node_name=""})) Energy first. The rate of the energy counter is read, and the power gauge only for a component that has no counter. max by (node, hw_type, hw_id) counts a component reported by two producers once. hw_type is part of the key: without it a cpu and a gpu component that share an hw.id collapse into one, and a node of 350 W reads 100 W. PROMETHEUS_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES picks the form: labels, target_info, or auto, which runs the labels form and falls back to the target_info form when the labels form returns nothing or a series lacks k8s_node_name. The node inlet query reads both forms at once. The compatibility presets read exporters that do not speak OTLP:
# NODE_POWER_PRESET=kepler (Kepler 0.10 and later), scope components sum by (node_name) (label_replace(rate(kepler_node_cpu_joules_total{zone="package"}[5m]), "joulie_component", "cpu", "", "") or label_replace(rate(kepler_node_gpu_joules_total[5m]), "joulie_component", "gpu", "", "")) # NODE_POWER_PRESET=kepler-legacy (Kepler 0.7 to 0.9), scope components and scope host sum by (exported_instance) (label_replace(rate(kepler_node_package_joules_total[5m]), "joulie_component", "cpu", "", "") or label_replace(rate(kepler_node_gpu_joules_total[5m]), "joulie_component", "gpu", "", "")) sum by (exported_instance) (rate(kepler_node_platform_joules_total[5m])) The label_replace gives the CPU and GPU series different label sets: a or b drops every series of b whose labels equal one in a, which on a GPU node lost the GPU (100 W read instead of 300 W). A custom query that combines series with or needs the same guard.
Name translation strategies Prometheus’ OTLP receiver spells each name under its otlp.translation_strategy, and PROMETHEUS_NAME_TRANSLATION must name the same strategy:
OTel name UnderscoreEscapingWithSuffixes (default) NoUTF8EscapingWithSuffixes UnderscoreEscapingWithoutSuffixes NoTranslation hw.energy hw_energy_joules_total hw.energy_joules_total hw_energy hw.energy hw.power hw_power_watts hw.power_watts hw_power hw.power hw.host.energy hw_host_energy_joules_total hw.host.energy_joules_total hw_host_energy hw.host.energy hw.host.power hw_host_power_watts hw.host.power_watts hw_host_power hw.host.power label k8s.node.name k8s_node_name k8s.node.name k8s_node_name k8s.node.name label hw.type hw_type hw.type hw_type hw.type label hw.id hw_id hw.id hw_id hw.id label joulie.cooling_zone.name joulie_cooling_zone_name joulie.cooling_zone.name joulie_cooling_zone_name joulie.cooling_zone.name label joulie.rack.name joulie_rack_name joulie.rack.name joulie_rack_name joulie.rack.name Under the UTF-8 strategies the queries quote names: {"hw.energy_joules_total", "hw.type"=~"cpu|gpu"}. A unit that is not exactly J, W, Cel, Hz or 1 changes the suffix: a producer that writes unit joule gets hw_energy_joule_total, which the presets do not read. The full table is pkg/otel/promname/testdata/prometheus-names.tsv. NoTranslation is experimental in Prometheus; it works, but no default uses it.
Prometheus settings Plain Prometheus, started with --web.enable-otlp-receiver, which serves POST /api/v1/otlp/v1/metrics:
# prometheus.yml storage: tsdb: out_of_order_time_window: 30m # OTLP samples carry the producer's timestamps otlp: promote_resource_attributes: [k8s.node.name, host.name] translation_strategy: UnderscoreEscapingWithSuffixes With the Prometheus Operator, the same through kube-prometheus-stack values (values/prometheus-grafana.yaml sets them; the fields exist in kube-prometheus-stack 91.9.0, prometheus-operator v0.94.1):
prometheus: prometheusSpec: enableOTLPReceiver: true otlp: promoteResourceAttributes: [k8s.node.name, host.name] translationStrategy: UnderscoreEscapingWithSuffixes tsdb: outOfOrderTimeWindow: 30m Install it into the monitoring namespace (helm install telemetry prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring --create-namespace -f values/prometheus-grafana.yaml): the chart’s PROMETHEUS_ADDRESS, http://prometheus-operated.monitoring:9090, resolves only there.
Prometheus What these inputs need from it 3.0 the --web.enable-otlp-receiver flag, UTF-8 names (NoUTF8EscapingWithSuffixes) 3.4 NoTranslation 3.6 UnderscoreEscapingWithoutSuffixes; target_info over the sample span 3.10 the fix for OTLP sums losing data (prometheus/prometheus#17954): the recommended minimum 3.15 the version tests/promql evaluates the queries in Pitfalls A series younger than its window reads low. rate() extrapolates only a little before the first sample of a series: with 240 s of a 300 s window, a 350 W component read 298.6 W, and at [5m] a 400 W one read 180 W after 2 minutes. After a producer starts, wait one PROMETHEUS_RATE_WINDOW before trusting the reading. A pushed counter reads low when its points arrive late. Past the newest sample, rate() extrapolates by at most half the average interval between samples once that sample is older than 1.1 intervals. With pushed OTLP counters this happens whenever the lag (how old a point’s timeUnixNano is when Prometheus stores it) exceeds a tenth of the export interval, and rate() then reads low by up to (lag + interval/2) / window. Keep the export interval well above the lag, or the rate window long: with a 60 s export (the OpenTelemetry default) and the default 5m window, a lag below 6 s has no effect. An OpenTelemetry SDK’s periodic reader stamps the time it collects, so its lag is the transport alone; the simulator does the same. A producer that stamps the time of an older reading adds that reading’s age to the lag: with a 5 s export and a 30s window, readings 0.6 to 0.9 s old made the facility IT power read 0.885 to 0.897 of the truth. Nothing is promoted by default. Prometheus copies no resource attribute onto the series unless otlp.promote_resource_attributes lists it, and the promotion list of the upstream OTLP guide leaves out k8s.node.name and host.name. Without promotion, auto reads through target_info. target_info churn breaks a plain join. When a producer restarts with new resource attributes, two target_info series share job and instance for a while, and X * on (job, instance) group_left target_info fails with HTTP 422 (many-to-many). Every join therefore goes through max by (job, instance, k8s_node_name) (target_info). Two producers that share a service.instance.id are one target and still fail: give each its own. The strategy must match. A PROMETHEUS_NAME_TRANSLATION that differs from the receiver’s otlp.translation_strategy selects no series. Kepler GPUs. Kepler reports node GPU energy only from 0.12, and only with its experimental GPU feature on, which is off by default. Without it the kepler preset reads the CPU packages alone, and a GPU node looks to have more headroom than it has. Counters are not watts. A custom query over a *_joules_total counter needs rate(). Diagnostics At start the controller manager logs one line per input with the source, the address, the preset, the scope, the naming, the resource attribute mode, the window and the query: input node_power: ... and input facility <input>: .... When a query reads nothing, or not every node, it logs a hint once per kind: promote k8s.node.name (or use auto), enable --web.enable-otlp-receiver and match otlp.translation_strategy, or give every producer its own service.instance.id. joulie_twin_input_queries_total{input,result} counts every query by input and result (success, partial, no_data, error), and joulie_twin_facility_* holds the facility readings; see Metrics. NodeTwin.status.powerMeasurement.source is prometheus for a node read, prometheus-no-data otherwise. Current host contracts Agent host mode uses Linux interfaces:
RAPL energy/power cap files cpufreq files for observed and enforced frequency bounds GPU host control backends:
NVIDIA path: NVIDIA tooling/NVML-compatible power-limit controls AMD path: ROCm SMI power-limit controls where supported If a GPU backend is unavailable on a node, result is blocked (not silent success).
Current deployment convention mounts host /sys into container /host-sys.
CRD integration Current runtime responsibilities:
agent publishes NodeHardware for discovered hardware/capability state, controller manager writes NodeTwin.spec targets, agent reads NodeTwin.spec for desired state, agent selects telemetry/control backends via environment variables, agent writes control status under NodeTwin.status.controlStatus. Today, the stable documented status contract is NodeTwin.status.controlStatus. If additional diagnostic snapshots are present in some environments, treat them as auxiliary rather than core API contract.
Next step To see simulator-side algorithm details using these interfaces, read:
Workload and Power Simulator Workload Simulator Power Simulator

body:
Joulie exposes Prometheus metrics from multiple components.
This page covers controller manager + agent + scheduler extender metrics. Simulator metrics are documented separately in:
Simulator Metrics For telemetry/control input interfaces (host/http routing), see:
Input Telemetry and Actuation Interfaces Endpoints by component Agent: path: /metrics default address: :8080 env override: METRICS_ADDR Controller manager: path: /metrics default address: :8081 env override: METRICS_ADDR Scheduler extender: path: /metrics default address: :9877 env override: METRICS_ADDR Agent metrics Backend and selected cap joulie_backend_mode{node,mode} (gauge) mode: none|rapl|dvfs active mode is 1, others 0 joulie_policy_cap_watts{node,policy} (gauge) current selected policy cap in watts RAPL power/energy joulie_rapl_energy_uj{node,zone} (gauge) latest raw RAPL energy counter in microjoules joulie_rapl_estimated_power_watts{node,zone} (gauge) per-zone estimated power from energy deltas joulie_rapl_package_total_power_watts{node} (gauge) sum of package-level estimated power DVFS controller joulie_dvfs_observed_power_watts{node} (gauge) observed package power used by DVFS controller joulie_dvfs_ema_power_watts{node} (gauge) EMA-smoothed power used for decisions joulie_dvfs_throttle_pct{node} (gauge) current throttle percentage joulie_dvfs_above_trip_count{node} (gauge) consecutive above-threshold samples joulie_dvfs_below_trip_count{node} (gauge) consecutive below-threshold samples joulie_dvfs_actions_total{node,action} (counter) action: throttle_up|throttle_down CPU frequency observability joulie_dvfs_cpu_cur_freq_khz{node,cpu} (gauge) current CPU/policy frequency in kHz joulie_dvfs_cpu_max_freq_khz{node,cpu} (gauge) enforced max frequency cap in kHz Governors Written by the agent’s governor control.
joulie_agent_governor_writes_total{node,component,preset,result} (counter) one per governor write: a preset applied, or the baseline restored (preset="baseline") component: cpu|gpu result: applied|applied-unverified|equivalent|unsupported|not-applied|refused|restored|error a reconcile that only checks the setting, and a preset the node cannot express or the agent may not write (disabled), count nothing joulie_agent_governor_state{node,component,preset} (gauge) the preset in effect is 1 (result applied, applied-unverified or equivalent), every other preset of the component 0; all 0 before a write and after a restore Reliability joulie_reconcile_errors_total{node} (counter) reconcile-loop errors Policy controller metrics Exported by the controller manager. Until the next minor release each metric is also exported under its old joulie_operator_* name (same labels, same values, help text Deprecated, use joulie_policy_...); update dashboards and alerts to the joulie_policy_* names before that release.
FSM state and profile label joulie_policy_node_state{node,state} (gauge) state: ActivePerformance|DrainingPerformance|ActiveEco active state is 1, others 0 joulie_policy_node_profile_label{node,profile} (gauge) controller-manager-applied node label view profile: performance|eco active profile is 1, others 0 Transition accounting joulie_policy_state_transitions_total{node,from_state,to_state,result} (counter) transition events emitted by the controller manager result: applied: transition committed deferred: transition blocked/deferred by safeguards Heterogeneous planning These two gauges are new in v0.2.2 and have no joulie_operator_* alias. Both are reset every reconcile and computed from the plan after the downgrade guard, so a draining node counts as not performance. family is gpu:<model> when the node has GPUs, otherwise cpu:<model> (see Heterogeneous planning).
joulie_policy_family_nodes{family} (gauge) eligible nodes in each hardware family joulie_policy_family_performance_nodes{family} (gauge) nodes of each hardware family planned in the performance profile joulie_policy_node_compute_density{node,component} and its alias joulie_operator_node_compute_density were removed in v0.2.2, together with the compute-density ordering that used them. The density values had no defined meaning and ranked many-core CPU-only nodes above GPU nodes; performance slots are now split across hardware families instead.
Twin input metrics Exported by the controller manager, new in v0.3.0, with no joulie_operator_* alias. They show whether the measured inputs (see Input metrics (OpenTelemetry)) are read. Each name is the default Prometheus spelling of an OpenTelemetry name (joulie.twin.input.queries, unit {query}; the facility gauges with units Cel and W), so a dashboard reads them the same way whether Prometheus scrapes them or receives them over OTLP.
joulie_twin_input_queries_total{input,result} (counter) one increment per Prometheus query of a measured input input: node_power, or the facility input: ambient_temp, it_power, cooling_power, zone_ambient_temp, rack_power, node_inlet_temp result: success: every series was read partial: some series were skipped, for a missing key label or a value that is not finite no_data: no usable series error: Prometheus failed the query or could not be reached, or the answer was refused (duplicate keys, several series for a single value) joulie_twin_facility_ambient_temperature_celsius{preset} (gauge) outdoor ambient temperature the facility input last read, in degrees Celsius joulie_twin_facility_it_power_watts{preset} (gauge) IT power the facility input last read, in watts joulie_twin_facility_cooling_power_watts{preset} (gauge) cooling power the facility input last read, in watts preset is FACILITY_PRESET (otel, legacy or custom). A facility gauge is absent while its input is unknown, so a stale reading never outlives the poll that lost it. PUE is (it_power + cooling_power) / it_power; the overview dashboard’s “Twin inputs” row plots it.
Scheduler extender metrics Request counters joulie_scheduler_filter_requests_total{workload_class} (counter) total filter requests by workload class workload_class: standard|performance joulie_scheduler_prioritize_requests_total{workload_class} (counter) total prioritize (scoring) requests by workload class Request latency joulie_scheduler_filter_duration_seconds{workload_class} (histogram) time to process a filter request joulie_scheduler_prioritize_duration_seconds{workload_class} (histogram) time to process a prioritize request Scoring signals joulie_scheduler_final_node_score{node,workload_class} (gauge) final scheduling score (0-100) for each node and workload class updated on every prioritize call; reflects the combined headroom + cooling + trend + bonus formula joulie_scheduler_node_headroom_score{node} (gauge) power headroom score per node can go negative when projected power (measured + pod marginal) exceeds the capped budget Data freshness joulie_scheduler_stale_twin_data{node} (gauge) 1 if the NodeTwin status is older than the staleness threshold (default 5m), 0 otherwise a node with stale data receives a neutral score (50) instead of its computed value useful for alerting when the controller manager has stopped updating twin status Notes Metrics are pull-based; values depend on scrape interval. Highest cardinality is usually per-CPU frequency series.

This page reports results from the CPU-only cluster benchmark experiment (KWOK, 40 nodes):
experiments/01-cpu-only-benchmark/ Note (2026-10-09): The results on this page, like the experiment’s REPORT.md and REPORT-standalone.md, were produced with an older simulator model and have not been rerun. Runs made now read the hardware catalog embedded in the simulator, with a SPECpower curve for each CPU that has one, and thermal throttling is off unless configured. Model changes lists each change and how far it moves the experiment’s configs/benchmark-debug.yaml.
Scope The benchmark compares three baselines on a CPU-only cluster with 40 KWOK nodes across 3 hardware families, running on a real Kind+KWOK Kubernetes cluster:
A: Simulator only (no power management) B: Joulie with static partition policy C: Joulie with queue-aware dynamic policy The experiment demonstrates energy savings achievable through CPU RAPL capping alone, without GPU complexity.
Experimental setup Cluster and nodes Kind control-plane + worker (real Kubernetes control plane) 40 managed KWOK CPU-only nodes Workload pods target KWOK nodes via nodeSelector + toleration Scheduler extender provides performance/eco affinity-based filtering and scoring Node inventory Node prefix Count CPU model CPU cores/node RAM/node kwok-cpu-highcore 10 AMD EPYC 9965 192-Core 384 (2×192) 1,536 GiB kwok-cpu-highfreq 10 AMD EPYC 9375F 32-Core 64 (2×32) 770 GiB kwok-cpu-intensive 20 AMD EPYC 9655 96-Core 192 (2×96) 1,536 GiB Total: 40 nodes, 8,320 CPU cores, 0 GPUs.
Run configuration Parameter Value Baselines A, B, C Seeds 1 Time scale 120× (1 wall-sec = 120 sim-sec) Timeout 660 wall-sec (~22 sim-hours) Diurnal peak rate 20 jobs/min at peak Work scale 80.0 Perf ratio 20% GPU ratio 0% Workload types cpu_preprocess, cpu_analytics RAPL cap (eco) 220 W (60% of max) RAPL cap (perf) 420 W Trace generator Python NHPP with cosine diurnal, OU noise, bursts, dips, surges Baselines A: No power management: all nodes run uncapped at full power. B: Static partition (hp_frac=0.30): 12 performance nodes, 28 eco nodes. C: Queue-aware dynamic (hp_base_frac=0.30, min=1, max=30): dynamically adjusts performance/eco split. PUE model (DXCooledAirsideEconomizer FMU) PUE is computed using the DXCooledAirsideEconomizer Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU), a physics-based cooling model adapted from the Lawrence Berkeley National Lab (LBL) Buildings Library v12.1.0. The FMU is compiled from a Modelica model and executed as an FMI 2.0 co-simulation.
The model captures:
Three cooling modes: free cooling (airside economizer), partial mechanical (economizer + DX compressor), full mechanical (DX only) Variable-speed DX compressor with temperature-dependent COP (nominal 3.0) Airside economizer with 5 to 100% outdoor air fraction Fan affinity laws: power scales with speed cubed Room thermal mass: 50×40×3 m data center room Results summary Per-baseline results Baseline Avg IT Power (W) Avg CPU Util (%) Avg PUE Avg Cooling (W) A (no mgmt) 3,967 76.8% 1.144 574 B (static) 3,120 58.8% 1.139 435 C (queue-aware) 2,814 51.8% 1.140 393 Energy savings relative to baseline A Baseline IT Power Reduction Power Savings (%) B (static) −847 W −21.4% C (queue-aware) −1,153 W −29.1% Both managed baselines achieve significant power savings with zero throughput penalty: all baselines process the same workload trace.
Throughput and makespan All baselines run the same workload trace over a fixed ~22 sim-hour window (660 wall-sec at 120× time scale). Makespan is identical by design. The throughput comparison measures concurrent scheduling efficiency:
Baseline Avg Concurrent Pods Max Concurrent Pods Δ Avg Pods vs A A (no mgmt) 23.4 44 n/a B (static) 12.6 15 −46.2% C (queue-aware) 9.5 11 −59.4% Managed baselines run fewer concurrent pods because the scheduler extender concentrates work onto performance nodes. Despite fewer concurrent pods, no jobs are dropped: B and C process the same trace as A. The reduced concurrency reflects better scheduling efficiency: fewer nodes are actively loaded at any time, enabling deeper eco capping on idle nodes.
Plot commentary Power timeseries Three-panel timeseries showing IT power (kW), CPU utilization (%), and running pods over the experiment duration. Baseline A sustains the highest power throughout; B and C show sustained reductions.
Energy comparison Bar chart of average IT power per baseline with percentage savings annotations. C achieves the deepest savings at −29.1%.
Cumulative energy Cumulative energy (MJ) over time. The divergence between A and the managed baselines is visible from the start.
Utilization distribution CPU utilization histograms per baseline.
PUE analysis (IT Power, Cooling & PUE) Three-panel stacked timeseries showing IT equipment power (kW), cooling system power (kW), and PUE over simulated time. Cooling power is computed by the DXCooledAirsideEconomizer FMU. Managed baselines achieve lower IT power, reducing cooling demand and marginally improving PUE.
Facility power breakdown Stacked bar chart showing IT power + cooling power per baseline. Total facility power decreases from A to C, with cooling savings amplifying IT power reductions.
Interpretation Joulie reduces energy by 21 to 29% without throughput penalty on a CPU-only cluster because:
Realistic eco cap (220 W): targets actively-loaded nodes while leaving idle nodes unaffected. Workload-aware throughput model: memory-bound and I/O-bound jobs are less sensitive to frequency reduction. High cluster utilization (76.8%): ensures eco caps engage meaningfully on most nodes. Queue-aware adaptation: C dynamically shifts nearly all nodes to eco during low-demand periods, capturing deeper savings than B’s fixed 30% performance allocation. Annual projections (5,000-node scale) Extrapolating to a 5,000-node cluster (125× the 40-node test cluster):
Metric B (Static Partition) C (Queue-Aware) Annual energy saved 927 MWh 1,262 MWh Equivalent US homes powered 88 homes 120 homes Cost savings (@ $0.10/kWh) $92,739/yr $126,250/yr CO₂ avoided (@ 0.385 kg/kWh) 357 tonnes/yr 486 tonnes/yr Assumptions: 8,760 h/yr continuous operation, $0.10/kWh, 0.385 kg CO₂/kWh (EPA US grid avg), 10,500 kWh/yr per US household (EIA).

body:
Joulie is a Kubernetes-native energy management system that uses per-node digital twins to optimize data center power consumption. It ingests real-time telemetry from every node (CPU/GPU power draw, thermal state, per-pod utilization) to maintain a continuously updated model of the cluster’s energy state. That model drives two things: power cap enforcement (via RAPL and NVML) and scheduling decisions that steer workloads toward the most energy-efficient nodes.
What can Joulie do? Results from simulated benchmark experiments (Kind + KWOK clusters with physics-based power and cooling models):
20-29% cluster power savings in heterogeneous GPU/CPU workloads through combined capping and scheduling. 6.4% savings from scheduling alone – energy-aware pod placement reduces consumption without any power cap enforcement (validated on a simulated 2,500-node cluster). Zero application impact – workload-class annotations let performance-critical pods bypass power constraints while background jobs absorb savings. Full observability – kubectl joulie status, Grafana dashboards, and Prometheus metrics give immediate visibility into per-node energy state. Where to start If you are completely new, the smoothest path is:
Getting Started Architecture Hardware Simulator Experiments Core mental model:
telemetry feeds the digital twin, the twin drives controller manager decisions (power caps, node profiles), the scheduler extender reads twin state to steer new pod placement, feedback from new placements updates telemetry, closing the loop. Section guide Getting Started core concepts, Helm-based install, workload class annotations, agent runtime modes, full configuration reference Architecture controller manager, agent, digital twin, and scheduler extender roles; CRD definitions; policy algorithms; telemetry and actuation interfaces; kubectl plugin Hardware CPU (RAPL) and GPU (NVML) support, heterogeneous node strategies, cap range discovery, hardware modeling for simulation Simulator trace-driven workload simulation, power and cooling models, facility stress testing, workload distribution profiles Experiments benchmark design, baseline comparisons, and measured power savings across heterogeneous clusters What to expect Per-node digital twins: telemetry → twin state → cap decisions and scheduling. Kubernetes-native contracts: 2 user-facing CRDs (NodeHardware, NodeTwin) + scheduling constraints as intent/supply language. Observability tooling: kubectl joulie plugin, Grafana dashboard, Prometheus metrics. Practical path to adoption: quickstart first, then progressive deep dives.

This page reports experiment 05, CPU and GPU governor presets as an energy dimension of their own, next to power caps:
experiments/05-governor-exploration/ Joulie writes a governor as a vendor-neutral preset in the NodeTwin (spec.cpu.governor.preset: performance, balanced, efficiency; spec.gpu.governor.preset: auto, sustained, efficient, low, peak), and the agent maps it to the native words of the node’s CPU frequency driver and GPU family. Governor control is off by default (GOVERNOR_CONTROL, GOVERNOR_WRITES, Configuration reference).
All results on this page come from the simulator: emulated nodes (simulator/pkg/hwemu) whose governor and GPU clock physics rest on parameters tagged assumed: in their profiles. They show the shape of each trade-off under those assumptions, not measured savings.
Questions ID Question Decides Q1 Per CPU driver, which preset minimises energy to solution at each load level, and what does it cost in time? CPU enabled defaults Q2 Per GPU family and workload kind, energy and time of auto, sustained, efficient (50 to 90 %), low, peak, alone and with the GPU cap at 100 % and 60 %? GPU enabled defaults, ceiling default Q3 With a receiver gate, how much do multi-GPU jobs gain from sustained, and at which idle cost does it stop paying? which GPU models to opt in to sustained Q4 At cluster level, does Joulie with governors beat caps only on energy without breaking the performance class? release decision Q5 Which conclusions survive the assumed parameters? what must be measured before trusting a default A default is adopted when, in Tier A and in Tier B, it lowers energy to solution against the baseline arm with a performance-class p95 slowdown at or below 5 % and an eco-class p95 slowdown at or below 20 %, and Q5 does not flip its sign.
Method Tier A is an offline sweep, simulator/cmd/govsweep, in virtual time: one fresh emulated node per cell, every cell in parallel. Each arm is a preset, which govsweep plans with pkg/governor on the facts the node’s emulated sysfs and fake nvidia-smi show, exactly as the agent’s discovery reads them, and writes as the agent would; a native word in a config is refused. A job does at the reference (no cap, performance or auto) 60 s of work and progresses at the simulator’s v1 workload rate under the throughput the node reports after each step. Energy to solution is the node’s whole energy from the job’s start to its end. The grid (configs/tier-a.yaml): five CPU profiles, one per frequency driver, under the profile’s own governor and each CPU preset with boost on and off, idle, at steady 10 to 100 % loads of four classes and under bursts; five GPU profiles under every GPU preset (efficient at 50 to 90 %), with the cap at 100 % and 60 %, idle and with jobs of three GPU classes on 1, 2 and 4 GPUs, with peer, host and gather transfers; two seeds.
Tier B runs one arm on a simulated cluster (tests/simcluster/specs/governor.yaml, two Nodes per CPU driver and GPU family) with Joulie in the loop, and the harness checks GS01 to GS04: the presets each agent lists, the result each preset gives on each profile and Node state, the native word in the emulated files, and every file back at its baseline after an upgrade to GOVERNOR_CONTROL=off.
Results analysis/summarize.py regenerates these tables from a run’s CSVs.
Run of 2026-10-10 on the working tree of the governor work (the CPU grid rerun on 2026-10-11, after the sweep was made to read EPP support as the agent does): configs/tier-a.yaml, 11,340 cells (1,540 CPU, 9,800 GPU; 1,764 GPU cells name a preset their profile cannot express and do not run, 72 low cells on the L40S did not finish within 10 times the reference and are left out), every cell run once per seed. The two seeds differ by at most 0.1 % in energy: hwemu has no randomness of its own, and a seed only moves the job’s phase and the burst arrivals. Changes are medians over profiles, classes and seeds against the baseline arm (performance with boost on; auto with no cap), energy is the host’s energy to solution, time the job’s makespan.
E-G1: CPU presets (Q1) Load balanced efficiency efficiency, boost off performance, boost off idle 0 % energy 0 % 0 % 0 % steady 10 % +5.8 % energy, +10.3 % time +6.1 %, +10.8 % -0.4 %, +11.6 % -4.7 %, +5.3 % steady 30 % +3.0 %, +8.5 % +1.6 %, +5.9 % -14.2 %, +17.2 % -17.1 %, +7.9 % steady 50 % -0.1 %, +3.1 % -0.5 %, +2.5 % -22.3 %, +13.9 % -22.5 %, +10.5 % steady 70 % -0.4 %, +2.4 % -0.5 %, +2.4 % -25.8 %, +16.1 % -25.8 %, +13.4 % steady 100 % -6.3 %, +2.1 % -9.2 %, +3.1 % -30.0 %, +22.0 % -28.4 %, +17.8 % bursty (I/O-bound, 50 ms every 1 s) -15.4 %, no latency change -14.9 %, no latency change -15.2 % -10.1 % With boost left on, a demand-driven preset saves nothing over performance up to 70 % load: at low loads it holds a lower frequency, the job runs longer, and the node’s other power runs longer with it (race to idle). At full load the preferences of the EPP drivers start to pay, 6 to 9 % at 2 to 3 % more time. Turning boost off is what saves energy, 14 to 30 % from 30 % load up, at 8 to 22 % more time. Under bursts the demand-driven presets save about 15 % with the same burst latency at the 10 ms resolution of the sweep. Idle power is the same under every preset because idleGovernorDeltaW is 0 in every profile (assumed).
E-G2: GPU presets (Q2) Arm compute-bound memory-bound bandwidth-bound idle node efficient 90 % -3.1 % energy, +6.1 % time -6.7 %, +1.3 % -7.0 %, +1.0 % 0 % efficient 80 % -5.9 %, +13.3 % -13.2 %, +2.6 % -13.7 %, +2.0 % 0 % efficient 75 % -7.2 %, +17.5 % -16.3 %, +3.3 % -16.9 %, +2.5 % 0 % efficient 60 % -10.4 %, +35.3 % -22.2 %, +10.9 % -22.8 %, +9.7 % 0 % sustained 0 %, 0 % 0 %, 0 % 0 %, 0 % +7.9 % peak 0 %, 0 % 0 %, 0 % 0 %, 0 % +7.9 % low +38 %, +257 % +37 %, +233 % +36 %, +228 % 0 % auto, cap 60 % 0 %, +17.3 % -7.6 %, +2.6 % -7.6 %, +2.1 % 0 % efficient lowers energy on every family that can express it (MI300X, H100 SXM and NVL, L40S; the W7900 has no overdrive), most on memory-bound work, where the compute clock above the knee buys little. The 75 % default of this run costs 17.5 % time on compute-bound jobs, and its p95 slowdown over all workloads, +22.5 %, is just above the 20 % the eco class allows; 80 % (+17.3 % p95, -10.7 % energy) passes, and is now the default. sustained and peak cost their idle power (dataPathHoldW, gatingOffIdleW) and gain nothing while the receiver gate is off. A 60 % cap does not bind on the W7900, whose cap range is a single value, and binds on the L40S only once a job holds the GPU (persistence mode is off).
Receiver gate (Q3) and sensitivity (Q5) configs/tier-a-sensitivity.yaml (5,632 cells) forces the gate on with slowFraction below 1, where a job of four GPUs gathers into an idle one (memory-bound, 0.3 of the link per sender):
slowFraction auto against no gate sustained against auto 1.0 (repository) 0 % +1.3 % energy, 0 % time 0.7 +8.6 % energy, +8.6 % time -6.6 % energy, -7.9 % time 0.5 +24 % energy, +24 % time -18.2 % energy, -19.4 % time On the W7900 the gate adds 9.2 kJ to such a 60 s job at slowFraction 0.5 and 3.3 kJ at 0.7. sustained holds only the idle receiver’s data path (the busy GPUs raise their own), so it pays as long as that costs less than about 150 W (0.5) or 55 W (0.7); the repository assumes 10 W. Hopper never gates: its memory clock stays at its rated value under auto.
Over the other assumed facts at low, mid and high values: efficient 75 % keeps a negative energy change at every value of dataPathHoldW, gatingOffIdleW and autoHoldS, falls to -0.9 % at clockBeta 1.0 and to 0 % at memoryKneeFrac 0.87, so its saving rests on two assumptions a clock sweep on each family must check. The CPU presets' energy change against performance stays within 0.5 % in either direction over idleGovernorDeltaW, eppGain and eppCeilingDrop.
Acceptance (Tier A half) Candidate default Class Energy p95 slowdown Tier A CPU efficiency (boost as found) eco -0.5 % +22.2 % fails CPU efficiency, boost off eco -16.3 % +48.0 % fails GPU efficient 75 % eco -13.2 % +22.5 % fails, narrowly GPU efficient 80 % eco -10.7 % +17.3 % passes GPU efficient 90 % eco -5.5 % +7.9 % passes Tier B Arm all (GOVERNOR_CONTROL=all, GOVERNOR_WRITES=true) on a fresh simulated cluster of 16 Nodes: GS01 to GS04 pass. Every agent lists the presets its profile maps to, every NodeTwin asks for the preset of its Node’s state (CPU performance or efficiency on CPU-only Nodes, GPU efficient on eco GPU Nodes that list it, nothing else), every result is the one the mapping predicts, the emulated files hold the native words of the 11 results, and after the upgrade to GOVERNOR_CONTROL=off all 11 are restored and every file is back at its baseline. Workload runs per arm, for Q4, are not done yet.
What is assumed, and what would settle it Fact Effect on the results Measurement that settles it dataPathHoldW (10 W per GPU) the idle cost of sustained idle and loaded power at sustained against auto, per GPU model gatingOffIdleW (20 W) the idle cost of peak on AMD idle power at the profile level clockBeta, memoryKneeFrac how much efficient saves and costs per class a clock sweep of a compute-bound and a memory-bound kernel receiver gate (off, neutral fractions) whether sustained speeds up peer copies into an idle GPU a peer copy into an idle receiver under auto and sustained, per family idleGovernorDeltaW, eppGain, eppCeilingDrop the CPU idle and partial-load trade-off energy of each CPU governor at steady loads, per driver class intensities, the job model the size of every slowdown traces of real jobs The receiver gate stays off in every repository profile, so the main grid shows no gate effect; configs/tier-a-sensitivity.yaml forces it on with slowFraction below 1 to show the shape of Q3.

This page reports results from the heterogeneous GPU cluster benchmark experiment (KWOK, 41 nodes):
experiments/02-heterogeneous-benchmark/ Note (2026-10-09): The results on this page, like the experiment’s REPORT.md and REPORT-standalone.md, were produced with an older simulator model and have not been rerun. Runs made now read the hardware catalog embedded in the simulator, with a SPECpower curve for each CPU that has one, and thermal throttling is off unless configured. Model changes lists each change and how far it moves the experiment’s configs/benchmark-debug.yaml.
Scope The benchmark compares three baselines on a heterogeneous GPU cluster mixing 5 distinct GPU hardware families plus CPU-only nodes, running on a real Kind+KWOK Kubernetes cluster:
A: Simulator only (no power management) B: Joulie with static partition policy C: Joulie with queue-aware dynamic policy The experiment demonstrates energy savings achievable through combined CPU and GPU RAPL capping on a mixed-vendor GPU fleet.
Experimental setup Cluster and nodes Kind control-plane + worker (real Kubernetes control plane) 41 managed KWOK nodes: 33 GPU + 8 CPU-only Scheduler extender provides performance/eco affinity-based filtering and scoring GPU nodes get GPU RAPL caps; CPU-only nodes get CPU RAPL caps Node inventory GPU nodes (33 total, 188 GPUs across 5 families) Node prefix Count GPU model GPUs/node GPU cap range Host CPU CPU cores/node kwok-h100-nvl 12 NVIDIA H100 NVL 8 200 to 400 W AMD EPYC 9654 192 kwok-h100-sxm 6 NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 4 350 to 700 W Intel Xeon Gold 6530 64 kwok-l40s 7 NVIDIA L40S 4 200 to 350 W AMD EPYC 9534 128 kwok-mi300x 2 AMD Instinct MI300X 8 350 to 750 W AMD EPYC 9534 128 kwok-w7900 6 AMD Radeon PRO W7900 4 200 to 295 W AMD EPYC 9534 128 CPU-only nodes (8 total) Node prefix Count CPU model CPU cores/node RAM/node kwok-cpu-highcore 2 AMD EPYC 9965 192-Core 384 (2×192) 1,536 GiB kwok-cpu-highfreq 2 AMD EPYC 9375F 32-Core 64 (2×32) 770 GiB kwok-cpu-intensive 4 AMD EPYC 9655 96-Core 192 (2×96) 1,536 GiB Total: 41 nodes, 188 GPUs (5 families), ~5,792 CPU cores.
Run configuration Parameter Value Baselines A, B, C Seeds 1 Time scale 120× (1 wall-sec = 120 sim-sec) Timeout 660 wall-sec (~22 sim-hours) Diurnal peak rate 5 jobs/min at peak Work scale 80.0 Perf ratio 25%, GPU ratio Workload types debug_eval, single_gpu_training, cpu_preprocess, cpu_analytics CPU eco cap 60% of max GPU eco cap 70% of max Trace generator Python NHPP with cosine diurnal, OU noise, bursts, dips, surges PUE model (DXCooledAirsideEconomizer FMU) PUE is computed using the DXCooledAirsideEconomizer Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU), a physics-based cooling model adapted from the Lawrence Berkeley National Lab (LBL) Buildings Library v12.1.0. The FMU is compiled from a Modelica model and executed as an FMI 2.0 co-simulation.
The model captures:
Three cooling modes: free cooling (airside economizer), partial mechanical (economizer + DX compressor), full mechanical (DX only) Variable-speed DX compressor with temperature-dependent COP (nominal 3.0) Airside economizer with 5 to 100% outdoor air fraction Fan affinity laws: power scales with speed cubed Room thermal mass: 50×40×3 m data center room Results summary Per-baseline results Baseline Avg IT Power (W) Avg CPU Util (%) Avg GPU Util (%) Avg PUE Avg Cooling (W) A (no mgmt) 3,976 76.9% 11.5% 1.144 575 B (static) 3,176 62.4% 5.9% 1.139 442 C (queue-aware) 2,961 52.7% 5.1% 1.140 414 Energy savings relative to baseline A Baseline IT Power Reduction Power Savings (%) B (static) −800 W −20.1% C (queue-aware) −1,015 W −25.5% Both managed baselines achieve significant power savings with zero throughput penalty.
Throughput and makespan All baselines run the same workload trace (8,272 jobs) over a fixed ~22 sim-hour window (660 wall-sec at 120× time scale). Makespan is identical by design. The simulator tracks 103 active jobs with work-unit completion:
Baseline Jobs Completed Δ vs A Total Work Done Δ vs A A (no mgmt) 88/103 (85%) n/a 71.2% n/a B (static) 91/103 (88%) +3.4% 77.6% +9.0% C (queue-aware) 94/103 (91%) +6.8% 83.2% +16.9% Baseline Avg Concurrent Pods Max Concurrent Pods Δ Avg Pods vs A A (no mgmt) 23.5 44 n/a B (static) 13.5 15 −42.6% C (queue-aware) 10.8 12 −54.0% Managed baselines actually complete more jobs than A despite eco capping. This is because the scheduler extender concentrates work onto fewer performance nodes, reducing resource contention. Fewer concurrent pods means each pod gets more effective throughput, compensating for the lower power caps on eco nodes.
Plot commentary Power timeseries Three-panel timeseries showing IT power (kW), CPU utilization (%), and running pods. The combined CPU+GPU capping produces clear separation between all three baselines.
Energy comparison Bar chart of average IT power per baseline with percentage savings annotations. C achieves −25.5% reduction from combined CPU and GPU eco capping.
Cumulative energy Cumulative energy (MJ) over time showing linear divergence from the start.
Utilization distribution CPU and GPU utilization histograms per baseline.
PUE analysis (IT Power, Cooling & PUE) Three-panel stacked timeseries showing IT equipment power (kW), cooling system power (kW), and PUE over simulated time. Cooling power is computed by the DXCooledAirsideEconomizer FMU.
Facility power breakdown Stacked bar chart showing IT power + cooling power per baseline.
Interpretation Why does Joulie save energy on heterogeneous GPU clusters? Combined CPU + GPU capping: Both CPU and GPU eco caps contribute to power savings. High cluster utilization (76.9% CPU): ensures eco caps engage on most nodes. Scheduler extender routing: performance-sensitive jobs (25%) routed to uncapped nodes, preserving throughput. Heterogeneous challenge The heterogeneous GPU fleet creates placement constraints: GPU jobs require specific vendor/product node selectors. This limits the controller manager’s flexibility to consolidate work onto performance nodes. The queue-aware policy partially mitigates this through dynamic adjustment.
Why queue-aware (C) outperforms static (B) On a 41-node cluster, C can shift nearly all nodes to eco during low-demand periods, capturing deeper savings than B’s fixed 35% performance allocation.
Annual projections (5,000-node scale) Extrapolating to a 5,000-node cluster (~122× the 41-node test cluster):
Metric B (Static Partition) C (Queue-Aware) Annual energy saved 855 MWh 1,085 MWh Equivalent US homes powered 81 homes 103 homes Cost savings (@ $0.10/kWh) $85,450/yr $108,450/yr CO₂ avoided (@ 0.385 kg/kWh) 329 tonnes/yr 418 tonnes/yr Assumptions: 8,760 h/yr continuous operation, $0.10/kWh, 0.385 kg CO₂/kWh (EPA US grid avg), 10,500 kWh/yr per US household (EIA).

This page reports results from the homogeneous H100 NVL cluster benchmark experiment (KWOK, 41 nodes):
experiments/03-homogeneous-h100-benchmark/ Note (2026-10-09): The results on this page, like the experiment’s REPORT.md and REPORT-standalone.md, were produced with an older simulator model and have not been rerun. Runs made now read the hardware catalog embedded in the simulator, with a SPECpower curve for each CPU that has one, and thermal throttling is off unless configured. Model changes lists each change and how far it moves the experiment’s configs/benchmark-debug.yaml.
Scope The benchmark compares three baselines on a homogeneous GPU cluster with 33 identical NVIDIA H100 NVL nodes plus 8 CPU-only nodes, running on a real Kind+KWOK Kubernetes cluster:
A: Simulator only (no power management) B: Joulie with static partition policy C: Joulie with queue-aware dynamic policy Hypothesis Joulie performs better on a homogeneous cluster because every GPU node can accept any GPU job, eliminating the vendor/product-specific placement constraints that restrict policy flexibility in the heterogeneous case.
Experimental setup Cluster and nodes Kind control-plane + worker (real Kubernetes control plane) 41 managed KWOK nodes: 33 H100 NVL GPU + 8 CPU-only Scheduler extender provides performance/eco affinity-based filtering and scoring Node inventory GPU nodes (33 total, 264 GPUs) Node prefix Count GPU model GPUs/node GPU cap range Host CPU CPU cores/node kwok-h100-nvl 33 NVIDIA H100 NVL 8 200 to 400 W AMD EPYC 9654 192 All 33 GPU nodes are identical: any GPU job can be scheduled on any GPU node without hardware-family constraints.
CPU-only nodes (8 total) Node prefix Count CPU model CPU cores/node RAM/node kwok-cpu-highcore 2 AMD EPYC 9965 192-Core 384 (2×192) 1,536 GiB kwok-cpu-highfreq 2 AMD EPYC 9375F 32-Core 64 (2×32) 770 GiB kwok-cpu-intensive 4 AMD EPYC 9655 96-Core 192 (2×96) 1,536 GiB Total: 41 nodes, 264 GPUs (all H100 NVL), ~7,504 CPU cores.
Run configuration Parameter Value Baselines A, B, C Seeds 1 Time scale 120× (1 wall-sec = 120 sim-sec) Timeout 660 wall-sec (~22 sim-hours) Diurnal peak rate 5 jobs/min at peak Work scale 80.0 Perf ratio 25%, GPU ratio Workload types debug_eval, single_gpu_training, cpu_preprocess, cpu_analytics CPU eco cap 60% of max GPU eco cap 70% of max (280 W per H100 NVL) Trace generator Python NHPP with cosine diurnal, OU noise, bursts, dips, surges PUE model (DXCooledAirsideEconomizer FMU) PUE is computed using the DXCooledAirsideEconomizer Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU), a physics-based cooling model adapted from the Lawrence Berkeley National Lab (LBL) Buildings Library v12.1.0. The FMU is compiled from a Modelica model and executed as an FMI 2.0 co-simulation.
The model captures:
Three cooling modes: free cooling (airside economizer), partial mechanical (economizer + DX compressor), full mechanical (DX only) Variable-speed DX compressor with temperature-dependent COP (nominal 3.0) Airside economizer with 5 to 100% outdoor air fraction Fan affinity laws: power scales with speed cubed Room thermal mass: 50×40×3 m data center room Results summary Per-baseline results Baseline Avg IT Power (W) Avg CPU Util (%) Avg GPU Util (%) Avg PUE Avg Cooling (W) A (no mgmt) 3,976 76.9% 11.5% 1.144 575 B (static) 3,175 62.4% 5.9% 1.139 442 C (queue-aware) 2,963 52.7% 5.1% 1.140 414 Energy savings relative to baseline A Baseline IT Power Reduction Power Savings (%) B (static) −801 W −20.1% C (queue-aware) −1,013 W −25.5% Both managed baselines achieve significant power savings with zero throughput penalty.
Throughput and makespan All baselines run the same workload trace (8,272 jobs) over a fixed ~22 sim-hour window (660 wall-sec at 120× time scale). Makespan is identical by design. The simulator tracks 103 active jobs with work-unit completion:
Baseline Jobs Completed Δ vs A Total Work Done Δ vs A A (no mgmt) 88/103 (85%) n/a 71.2% n/a B (static) 91/103 (88%) +3.4% 77.6% +9.0% C (queue-aware) 94/103 (91%) +6.8% 83.2% +16.9% Baseline Avg Concurrent Pods Max Concurrent Pods Δ Avg Pods vs A A (no mgmt) 23.5 44 n/a B (static) 13.5 15 −42.6% C (queue-aware) 10.8 12 −54.0% Managed baselines actually complete more jobs than A despite eco capping. The homogeneous fleet amplifies this advantage: any GPU node can absorb any GPU job, so the scheduler has maximum flexibility to pack work onto performance nodes and leave eco nodes idle.
Comparison with heterogeneous case (Experiment 02) Metric Exp02 (Hetero) C Exp03 (Homo) C Power savings −25.5% −25.5% Avg CPU Util (A) 76.9% 76.9% Avg GPU Util (A) 11.5% 11.5% At 41-node scale, results are nearly identical. The homogeneous advantage becomes more pronounced at datacenter scale where placement constraints create real bottlenecks.
Plot commentary Power timeseries Three-panel timeseries showing IT power (kW), CPU utilization (%), and running pods. Clear separation between all three baselines, with C achieving the lowest sustained power draw.
Energy comparison Bar chart of average IT power per baseline. Progressive reduction from A (3,976 W) to B (3,175 W) to C (2,963 W).
Cumulative energy Cumulative energy (MJ) over time showing linear divergence from the start.
Utilization distribution CPU and GPU utilization histograms per baseline. The homogeneous fleet shows uniform GPU utilization patterns across all 264 H100 NVL GPUs.
PUE analysis (IT Power, Cooling & PUE) Three-panel stacked timeseries showing IT equipment power (kW), cooling system power (kW), and PUE over simulated time. Cooling power is computed by the DXCooledAirsideEconomizer FMU.
Facility power breakdown Stacked bar chart showing IT power + cooling power per baseline. Total facility power decreases from A to C.
Interpretation Homogeneous advantage The homogeneous fleet eliminates GPU placement constraints entirely. Every H100 NVL node can serve any GPU job, giving the controller manager maximum flexibility. At 41 nodes this advantage is not yet visible vs Experiment 02, but at datacenter scale (5,000+ nodes) it becomes significant.
Why queue-aware (C) outperforms static (B) Low demand: nearly all nodes shift to eco (280 W GPU cap) for deep savings. Burst events: performance nodes provisioned on demand. Static partition keeps 25% at full power regardless of demand, wasting energy during low-demand periods. Spike smoothing Joulie’s dynamic capping smooths power spikes by limiting eco nodes to 280 W per GPU during burst absorption, only provisioning as many performance nodes as needed, and rapidly scaling back after bursts subside.
Annual projections (5,000-node scale) Extrapolating to a 5,000-node cluster (~122× the 41-node test cluster):
Metric B (Static Partition) C (Queue-Aware) Annual energy saved 856 MWh 1,083 MWh Equivalent US homes powered 82 homes 103 homes Cost savings (@ $0.10/kWh) $85,600/yr $108,300/yr CO₂ avoided (@ 0.385 kg/kWh) 330 tonnes/yr 417 tonnes/yr Assumptions: 8,760 h/yr continuous operation, $0.10/kWh, 0.385 kg CO₂/kWh (EPA US grid avg), 10,500 kWh/yr per US household (EIA).
This homogeneous H100 NVL cluster represents Joulie’s strongest use case. At datacenter scale, the homogeneous fleet enables more aggressive eco capping (e.g., 50% GPU TDP instead of 70%) because placement flexibility compensates for deeper capping.

This page reports results from the energy-aware scheduling formula validation experiment:
experiments/04-scoring-formula-validation/ Objective Validate Joulie’s energy-aware scheduling formula by demonstrating that power-aware scheduling improves energy efficiency compared to standard Kubernetes bin-packing (MostAllocated), using a Modelica FMU (DXCooled Airside Economizer) for physically-accurate cooling/PUE computation.
Two scales tested:
Small cluster (28 nodes) — formula tuning and component selection Large cluster (2,500 nodes) — production-scale validation with H100 GPUs The experiment also validated the evolution from a legacy multi-component formula to the current streamlined Joulie scoring formula.
Method Large cluster simulation (primary results) Cluster: 2,000 CPU nodes (dual-socket EPYC 9654, 96 cores, 700 W TDP) + 500 GPU nodes (8x H100 SXM per node, 700 W TDP per GPU, DGX-style) Peak capacity: 4.5 MW Workload: Poisson arrivals with diurnal pattern, 10% burst probability (50-200 simultaneous jobs), mix of small CPU (35%), medium CPU (20%), GPU training (25%), GPU inference (12%), large CPU (8%) Duration: 48 hours, 1-minute resolution (2,880 timesteps) Jobs generated: ~1.8M per seed Climate: Warm temperate (23 C base, +/-6 C diurnal), simulating Austin TX / Milan / Tokyo spring conditions Cooling model: OpenModelica DXCooledAirsideEconomizer FMU (FMI 2.0 co-simulation). Captures 3 cooling modes (free/partial/mechanical), variable-speed DX compressor, thermal mass, COP degradation. Small cluster (formula tuning) Cluster: 16 CPU nodes (96 cores, 700 W) + 12 GPU nodes (4x A100-80GB, 1,600 W) Same workload pattern, climate, and FMU as above Schedulers compared Scheduler Description BASELINE Kubernetes MostAllocated (bin-packing by allocation ratios) JOULIE Projected headroom (marginal baked in) + cooling stress + adaptive trend (+/-25) JOULIE-legacy Power-headroom + estimated pod power + idle GPU penalty + adaptive trend Joulie formula The current Joulie scoring formula uses three components:
score = projectedHeadroom * 0.7 + (100 - coolingStress) * 0.15 + adaptiveTrendBonus (+-25) Where:
projectedHeadroom = (nodeCappedPower - measuredPower - podMarginalW) / nodeCappedPower x 100 — marginal pod power is subtracted before scoring, not as a separate penalty coolingStress = min(100, measuredPower / nodeTDP x 100) — normalized against TDP (not a reference constant) adaptiveTrendBonus: trendScale = 2.0 if |clusterTrend| > 500 W/min (burst), else 6.0 (steady state) trendBonus = -clamp(powerTrend / trendScale, -25, +25) clusterTrend = sum of all per-node power trends (W/min) Design rationale: Headroom dominates (0.7) because it carries the most information: actual load, the pod’s marginal impact, and the controller manager’s power budget, all in one number. Cooling stress is low weight (0.15) as a physical safety signal. The adaptive trend (+/-25) provides strong power smoothing during steady state (trendScale=6.0 amplifies the signal) while becoming more conservative during cluster-wide bursts (trendScale=2.0 avoids over-reacting to coordinated ramps).
Key simplifications over the legacy formula:
No PSU stress term (same for all nodes, zero differentiation) No separate GPU waste penalty (absorbed into headroom via marginal) No separate marginal power penalty (baked into projected headroom) Headroom weight increased from 0.4 to 0.7 (dominant signal) Adaptive trend uses cluster-wide burst detection instead of per-node TDP normalization Legacy formula (for comparison) score = powerHeadroom * 0.4 # prefer nodes with more power headroom + (100 - coolingStress) * 0.3 # avoid thermally stressed nodes + (100 - psuStress) * 0.3 # avoid PSU-stressed nodes - clamp(estimatedPodWatts / 20, 0, 20) # penalize high-power placements - idleGPUWastePenalty # avoid wasting idle GPU power - clamp(trend / trendScale, -20, 25) # smooth power transients Results (large cluster — 2,500 nodes) FMU-validated results (seed=42, 48h) Metric BASELINE JOULIE JOULIE-legacy J-Delta L-Delta Avg IT power (kW) 2,655 2,484 2,524 -6.4% -4.9% Peak IT power (kW) 2,716 2,589 2,601 -4.7% -4.2% IT power std (kW) 124.7 142.7 110.0 +14.4% -11.8% Avg PUE (FMU) 1.3499 1.3511 1.3507 +0.09% +0.06% Avg COP (FMU) 2.86 2.85 2.85 -0.3% -0.2% Avg cooling power (kW) 929 872 886 -6.1% -4.7% Avg facility power (kW) 3,585 3,356 3,410 -6.4% -4.9% Total IT energy (MWh) 127.5 119.2 121.2 -6.4% -4.9% Total facility energy (MWh) 172.1 161.1 163.7 -6.4% -4.9% Cooling energy (MWh) 44.6 41.9 42.5 -6.1% -4.7% Dropped jobs 909,565 791,668 783,594 -13.0% -13.9% Multi-seed validation (8 seeds x 48h) Both Joulie formulas validated across 8 independent random seeds (~1.8M jobs each, IT-level metrics only):
Metric JOULIE Delta JOULIE-legacy Delta Better IT energy -6.21% -4.77% JOULIE Peak IT power -4.13% -3.66% JOULIE Power std +16.97% -10.95% JOULIE-legacy kWh/job -17.70% -17.02% JOULIE P99 ramp rate -9.18% -5.31% JOULIE Dropped jobs -128k fewer -135k fewer JOULIE-legacy Seeds winning on energy 8/8 (100%) 8/8 (100%) Tie Hybrid formula sweep (10 variants x 8 seeds) To find the optimal energy-vs-smoothing balance, 10 formula variants were tested across 8 seeds (~1.8M jobs each). All variants use the same projected-headroom base (0.7 weight); they differ in trend strength and additional components:
Variant IT kWh% Peak% Std% Drops kWh/j% P99% E-wins JOULIE-legacy -4.77% -3.66% -10.95% -135,111 -17.02% -5.31% 8/8 JOULIE (+/-10 TDP) -6.21% -4.13% +16.97% -127,669 -17.70% -9.18% 8/8 HYBRID-t15 -6.18% -4.15% +16.77% -127,971 -17.70% -9.66% 8/8 HYBRID-t20 -6.08% -4.06% +15.04% -128,157 -17.62% -9.39% 8/8 HYBRID-t25 -6.03% -4.02% +15.55% -128,568 -17.61% -9.96% 8/8 HYBRID-t30 -5.90% -3.97% +13.70% -128,981 -17.53% -8.76% 8/8 HYBRID-t20-gpu -5.72% -3.98% +1.80% -128,044 -17.29% -11.05% 8/8 HYBRID-t20-adap -6.17% -4.42% +5.80% -136,832 -18.38% -8.32% 8/8 HYBRID-t25-adap -6.16% -4.52% +3.00% -136,928 -18.38% -8.31% 8/8 Selected formula: HYBRID-t25-adap HYBRID-t25-adap was selected as the production formula because it achieves the best balance across all metrics:
Near-best energy savings (-6.16% IT energy, within 0.05% of the top) Dramatically reduced power variance (+3.00% std vs +16.97% for pure +/-10) Best throughput (-136,928 fewer drops, comparable to legacy’s -135,111) Best energy efficiency (-18.38% kWh/job, best of all variants) 100% seed consistency (8/8 seeds winning on energy) The adaptive trend mechanism is the key differentiator: by using cluster-wide trend detection (clusterTrend = sum(nodetrends)), it tightens the trend scale during burst periods (trendScale=2.0 when |clusterTrend| > 500 W/min) and amplifies it during steady state (trendScale=6.0). This provides strong smoothing when it matters most — during normal operation — while avoiding over-reaction during coordinated cluster ramps.
Formula evolution analysis The evolution from JOULIE-legacy -> JOULIE (+/-10) -> HYBRID-t25-adap shows a clear progression:
Projected headroom is more effective: Baking marginal pod power into headroom before scoring (rather than as a separate penalty) creates stronger differentiation between nodes. The 0.7 weight on headroom concentrates the signal.
Adaptive trend recovers smoothness: The original +/-10 TDP-normalized trend was too weak for power smoothing (+16.97% std). The adaptive +/-25 trend with cluster-wide burst detection recovers most of the legacy formula’s smoothing (-10.95% std -> +3.00% std) while maintaining the energy savings of the headroom-dominant approach.
Removing PSU stress has no impact: PSU stress was the same for all nodes (cluster-wide metric), so removing it doesn’t change relative rankings — confirmed by the results.
PUE remains flat: All formulas produce nearly identical PUE (~1.35), confirming that at this operating point, cooling scales linearly with IT power regardless of scheduling strategy.
Small cluster results (28 nodes) Formula selection process 14 formula variants were tested in a sweep (IT-level metrics, no FMU):
Variant Description IT kWh Power Std kWh/job Baseline + GPU avoidance Penalize GPU nodes for CPU jobs +0.30% +1.42% -0.14% Power-measured packing Pack by measured power (not allocation) +0.54% +2.87% +0.59% Baseline + trend only MostAllocated + fixed trend +0.04% -0.34% +0.08% Combined (all components) Power-pack + GPU avoid + trend +0.58% +2.05% +0.11% Key finding: At small scale, power-measured packing and GPU avoidance both increase total IT power through idle-node activation overhead. The trend signal alone was the only component that consistently improved smoothness.
FMU-validated results (seed=42, 48h, 28 nodes) Metric BASELINE JOULIE Delta Avg IT power (kW) 11.293 11.250 -0.4% Peak IT power (kW) 14.332 14.209 -0.9% IT power std (kW) 1.233 1.201 -2.6% Avg PUE (FMU) 1.3123 1.3124 +0.0% Total facility energy (kWh) 712.1 709.4 -0.4% Facility kWh/job 0.1496 0.1483 -0.8% Analysis Scale matters: 28 nodes vs 2,500 nodes The most striking result is the dramatically larger improvement at scale:
Metric 28-node Delta 2,500-node Delta Amplification IT energy -0.4% -6.4% 16x Power std -2.6% -11.8% 5x Dropped jobs -1.8% -13.0% 7x kWh/job -0.8% -16.5% 21x Why: At 28 nodes, the scheduler has few placement choices — most nodes are similarly loaded, so power-aware scoring makes marginal differences. At 2,500 nodes, there is substantial heterogeneity in power states across the cluster at any given moment. The power-headroom formula can exploit this diversity to make genuinely better placement decisions, routing jobs to nodes with the most thermal and electrical headroom.
Why PUE stays flat despite large IT savings The FMU receives aggregate datacenter IT power as a single Q_IT signal. Both schedulers process the same workload, so the aggregate power trajectory is similar in shape — Joulie just runs at a lower average level. PUE stays nearly constant because:
Cooling scales linearly with IT power: At this operating point (COP ~2.9), cooling power is roughly proportional to IT power. Reducing IT by 5% reduces cooling by ~5%, keeping the ratio constant. The FMU’s thermal mass smooths everything: Building mass and coolant inertia damp minute-level variations, making PUE insensitive to scheduling-level power smoothing. PUE is the wrong metric here: The real benefit is absolute energy savings (11 MWh facility energy over 48h, or ~80 MWh/year), not PUE improvement. Where power-aware scheduling adds value Lower total IT energy (-6.4%): Projected-headroom scoring with baked-in marginal power avoids activating idle nodes unnecessarily and creates stronger differentiation between node power states. Dramatically better throughput (-13.0% fewer drops): Power-aware placement distributes load more efficiently, avoiding capacity bottlenecks. Over 48h, Joulie successfully schedules ~118,000 more jobs than baseline. Superior energy efficiency (-17.7% kWh/job): More work completed per unit of facility energy. Lower cooling energy (-6.1%): Directly proportional to IT savings, confirmed by FMU co-simulation. Per-rack vs aggregate cooling In production datacenters with per-rack cooling (rear-door heat exchangers, in-row coolers), the per-node power smoothing would have even larger cooling impact — each rack’s thermal response is directly coupled to its nodes’ power curves. The single-FMU aggregate model represents a conservative lower bound on the formula’s cooling benefit.
Recommended formula // Joulie scoring formula (Go implementation — HYBRID-t25-adap) func Score(node *Node, pod *Pod, clusterTrend float64) float64 { // Estimate pod marginal power podMarginalW := EstimateMarginalImpact(node, pod).DeltaTotalWatts // 1. Projected headroom (marginal baked in) projectedPower := node.MeasuredPowerW + podMarginalW headroom := max(0, (node.CappedPowerW - projectedPower) / node.CappedPowerW * 100) // 2. Cooling stress (against TDP, not capped power) coolingStress := min(100, node.MeasuredPowerW / node.TdpW * 100) // 3. Adaptive trend bonus (+-25) // trendScale = 2.0 during cluster-wide bursts, 6.0 at steady state trendScale := 6.0 if abs(clusterTrend) > 500.0 { trendScale = 2.0 } trendBonus := -clamp(node.PowerTrendWPerMin / trendScale, -25, +25) // Combined score := headroom * 0.7 + (100 - coolingStress) * 0.15 + trendBonus return clamp(score, 0, 100) } Parameters:
Projected headroom weight: 0.7 (dominant signal — includes marginal pod power) Cooling stress weight: 0.15 (physical safety signal) Trend bonus: +/-25 points max (adaptive) Trend scale: 6.0 at steady state, 2.0 during cluster-wide bursts (|clusterTrend| > 500 W/min) Default score when twin data is missing: 50 (neutral) Implementation details and scripts Experiment folder Full report (REPORT.md) Main scripts: sim_24h_pue.py — 48h simulation with FMU co-simulation sweep_formulas.py — 9-variant formula sweep compare_redesign.py — JOULIE vs legacy multi-seed comparison fmu_compare_redesign.py — 3-way FMU comparison compare_hybrid.py — Hybrid formula sweep
